If the method is idempotent, the client retries without risk. If it is not, the client faces an ambiguous state: retry and risk a duplicate, or give up and risk losing the operation. This is why distributed systems prefer `PUT` for updates that might be retried.

The idempotency key pattern extends idempotency to `POST`. The client sends a unique key in a header — Stripe uses `Idempotency-Key`. The server stores the key with the response. A second request with the same key returns the stored response instead of creating a second resource. The key makes the non-idempotent method behave idempotently for that client. The server must store the key long enough to outlast any plausible retry window, and must handle the race where two requests with the same key arrive simultaneously — typically by locking on the key.

Idempotency is a contract about repeated calls. The method declares it. The server honors it. The client relies on it for safe retries.

Okay — explain how DNS resolves a name to an address, plain register, every sentence a fact.

A browser asks for `example.com`. The operating system hands that question to a resolver, and the resolver chases the name through a chain of servers until one of them answers with an IP address.

The resolver first checks its own cache. If it asked for `example.com` recently and kept the answer, it returns the address without contacting anything else. If the cache is empty, the resolver asks a root nameserver.

There are 13 root nameserver IP addresses, distributed across hundreds of physical machines via anycast. The resolver picks one by round-trip time and sends the query. The root server does not know `example.com`'s address. It knows which servers hold the top-level domain `.com`. It returns a list of those servers.

The resolver picks a `.com` server and asks the same question. The `.com` server does not know the address either. It knows which nameservers are authoritative for `example.com` — the servers operated by whoever registered the domain. It returns those.

The resolver asks the authoritative server for `example.com`. This server holds the actual record. It reads the A record for `example.com`, finds `93.184.216.34`, and returns it. The resolver caches that answer for the time-to-live listed in the record — often 300 seconds — and hands the address to the operating system, which hands it to the browser.

The whole chase is recursive. The resolver asks, gets a referral to the next server, asks again, gets another referral, and repeats until it reaches a server that answers instead of referring. A single name lookup can produce four round trips: cache miss, root, TLD, authoritative. Each round trip adds latency proportional to the network distance to that server.

Most resolvers are run by the internet service provider, but the protocol does not require it. Google's `8.8.8.8` and Cloudflare's `1.1.1.1` are public resolvers that perform the same chase from their own locations. A machine can also run a local resolver — `systemd-resolved` or `dnsmasq` — that caches answers on the machine itself, cutting the round trips to zero for repeated lookups.

DNS over HTTPS and DNS over TLS encrypt the connection between the client and the resolver. Traditional DNS sends queries in cleartext over UDP port 53, which a network observer can read and alter. DNSSEC adds cryptographic signatures to the records themselves, so the resolver can verify that the authoritative server's answer was not tampered with in transit. Neither changes the resolution chain. The root, TLD, and authoritative servers still do the same work in the same order.

The name becomes an address because each server in the chain knows exactly one thing: not the final answer, but who to ask next. The resolver follows that chain to the end and caches what it finds.

Okay — explain a deadlock and one way to avoid it, plain register, every sentence a fact.

A deadlock is two threads stopped forever, each waiting for a lock the other holds. Thread A locks mutex 1, then tries to lock mutex 2. Thread B locks mutex 2, then tries to lock mutex 1. A waits for B. B waits for A. Neither moves.

Four conditions must hold at once. The threads hold their locks and wait at the same time — no thread releases its lock until it gets the next one. The locks are not shared — a mutex belongs to one thread. The locks do not come back out of order — a thread holding mutex 1 will not release it just because mutex 2 is unavailable. The wait forms a circle — A waits on B, B waits on A, and the chain closes.

Break any one condition and the deadlock cannot happen. The simplest to break is the circle. Give every mutex a number, and make every thread lock its mutexes in ascending order. Thread A locks 1 then 2. Thread B locks 1 then 2. Both threads reach for mutex 1 first. Whichever thread gets it, the other blocks at the first lock and never touches the second. The thread holding mutex 1 acquires mutex 2, does its work, and releases both. The second thread wakes, gets mutex 1, gets mutex 2, and proceeds. The circle never closes.

The rule is a lock-ordering protocol. It works when every piece of code that touches the same set of mutexes agrees on the order. A single function that locks mutex 2 before mutex 1 breaks the guarantee for the whole program. The discipline is global: the order is a property of the mutexes, not the function that happens to use them this time.

A hash map turns a key into an array index, then stores the value at that index. Two keys can land on the same index. That is a collision, and every hash map has a policy for it.

**Chaining** hangs a linked list off each bucket. On insert, the map walks the list, replaces the value if the key matches, and appends a new node if it does not. On lookup, it walks the same list. The cost grows with chain length: O(1) when keys spread evenly, O(n) when they pile into one bucket. Java's `HashMap` and C++'s `std::unordered_map` both chain. Java chains with entries that carry a `next` pointer; C++ chains through a singly linked list of node pointers stored per bucket.

**Open addressing** stores entries in the bucket array itself. On collision, the map probes neighboring slots by a fixed rule and takes the first empty one. Three rules cover most implementations:

- *Linear probing* checks `index + 1`, then `+ 2`, then `+ 3`. Cache-friendly, because the probe stays in one contiguous run. It clusters: a block of filled slots grows, and every key that hashes inside the block walks through it.
- *Quadratic probing* jumps by `1`, then `4`, then `9` — the step grows quadratically. It breaks up primary clusters but can miss slots if the table size and the probe sequence share a factor.
- *Double hashing* computes a second hash to set the probe step. The step varies with the key, so keys that collide on the first hash scatter on the second. It avoids both primary and secondary clustering at the cost of a second hash call per probe.

Python's `dict` uses open addressing with a perturbed probe sequence derived from the hash, not a textbook rule. Robin Hood hashing, used in Rust's `HashMap`, is open addressing with a twist: on insert, the probe walks and compares the "distance from home bucket" of the existing entry against the incoming one's. If the existing entry has a shorter distance, the two swap. This keeps the worst-case probe length low — every key is as far from home as the least-fortunate key in its probe chain.

Deletion in open addressing cannot just empty the slot. A probe sequence that hits a gap stops early and misses keys placed beyond it. The fix is a tombstone: the slot is marked deleted, probes skip past it, and inserts can reuse it. Tombstones accumulate; a table with many tombstones degrades lookup until it is rehashed.

Every policy degrades when the table fills. The **load factor** — entries divided by buckets — is the dial. Chaining tolerates a factor above 1, because chains can grow past the bucket count. Open addressing caps at 1, because there are no more slots than buckets; most implementations rehash well before that. Go's `map` rehashes when the load exceeds 6.5 entries per bucket on small maps. Java's `HashMap` doubles the array when the load factor hits 0.75. The rehash picks a larger array, recomputes every key's index, and moves every entry — O(n), amortized to O(1) per insert across a growth sequence.

A database index is a second data structure stored alongside the table. It trades write speed and disk space for read speed.

The structure is usually a B-tree. A B-tree keeps sorted keys in blocks, with child pointers splitting the key range. A lookup touches four or five blocks instead of scanning the whole table. On a million-row table, that is the difference between four disk reads and a hundred thousand.

The database stores this tree separately. Every insert, update, or delete on a column with an index must also update the tree. One index on a table means two writes per row change. Five indexes mean six. A table that takes inserts all day slows down in proportion to its index count.

Indexes also cost disk and memory. A B-tree node holds keys and pointers, not row data, but on a wide table the index can approach the table's own size. The database caches index pages in RAM. More index pages compete for that cache, pushing out table pages and forcing more disk reads.

An index hurts when the query does not use it. A query that filters on `last_name` gains nothing from an index on `customer_id`. The database still scans the full table, and the index sits unused, collecting write overhead. A query that selects most of the rows in a table also bypasses the index. Reading two blocks to find a row, then reading the row itself, is cheaper than scanning — but only when the query returns a small fraction of the table. At ten percent of rows, the scan often wins, because sequential reads are faster than the random reads the index forces.

A composite index on `(last_name, first_name)` serves queries that filter on `last_name` alone, because the tree sorts by `last_name` first. It does not serve queries that filter on `first_name` alone, because `first_name` is sorted only within each `last_name` group. The order of columns in the index fixes which queries it helps.

The index that earns its place is the one a real query uses, on a column that cuts the result set to a small fraction, on a table that takes fewer writes than reads. Every other index is overhead.

TCP gives each byte a number. The sender picks a starting sequence number in the initial handshake and counts forward from there: the first byte of data is sequence number plus one, the second is plus two, and so on. Every TCP segment carries the sequence number of its first byte in its header.

The network delivers segments out of order. Segment 5 can arrive before segment 3. A router delay, a retransmission, a path change — any of these scrambles the arrival order. TCP on the receiving side puts the bytes back by their numbers.

The receiver holds bytes in a buffer and tracks the next number it expects. Bytes that arrive in order go to the application. Bytes that arrive early sit in the buffer until the gap fills. If segment 3 is missing, segments 4 and 5 wait. When 3 arrives, the receiver releases 3, 4, and 5 together.

The receiver tells the sender what it has. Every acknowledgment carries the next sequence number the receiver expects — an acknowledgment of 1001 means "I have everything through byte 1000, send 1001 next." This is a cumulative acknowledgment. It does not say which later bytes sit in the buffer, only that everything up to the number is complete.

A gap means a segment was lost or delayed. The sender keeps bytes in its own buffer until the receiver acknowledges them. If the acknowledgment number does not advance for a while, the sender retransmits the oldest unacknowledged segment. When the delayed segment finally arrives, the receiver's acknowledgment jumps forward by the full length of the gap, because the buffered bytes were already there.

The sequence number is a 32-bit field. It wraps at 2³² bytes, roughly 4 GB, and TCP handles the wrap by comparing numbers with modular arithmetic so an old segment from before the wrap is not mistaken for a new one. The handshake randomizes the starting number so an attacker cannot guess the sequence and inject segments into the stream.

The ordering guarantee is narrow. TCP delivers bytes to the application in sequence number order, no gaps. It does not deliver segments in order, it does not deliver messages in order, and it does not guarantee that two sends from the sender appear as two separate reads at the receiver — the bytes arrive as a continuous, ordered stream, and the boundary between sends can be lost.

A mutex protects one thing: the invariant a thread needs while it touches shared memory.

A thread that wants a shared resource calls `lock` on the mutex. The call blocks until no other thread holds the lock, then returns. The thread does its work — reads a counter, appends to a list, updates a struct — and calls `unlock`. While the lock is held, every other thread that calls `lock` on the same mutex waits. The mutex serializes access to whatever the programmer wrapped between `lock` and `unlock`.

The danger it prevents is the interleaved read-modify-write. Two threads read the same counter at value 7. Both add 1. Both write 8. The counter should be 9. The mutex makes the second thread wait until the first finishes, so the second reads 8, adds 1, writes 9. Without the lock, the increment is two instructions apart and the write clobbers the other thread's write. This is a data race: two threads access the same memory, at least one writes, and the result depends on timing.

A mutex does not protect against everything. It does not protect against deadlock — two threads each holding one mutex and waiting for the other's. It does not make a data structure thread-safe on its own; the programmer must lock the mutex on every path that touches the shared state, and forgetting one path leaves the race open. It does not protect memory that threads reach through separate pointers if those paths skip the lock. It does not compose: locking mutex A then mutex B in one thread and B then A in another is deadlock, and the mutex itself does not prevent the mismatch.

The lock is a promise the programmer makes and keeps by discipline. The mutex enforces the promise among threads that call `lock`. Threads that do not call it are outside the contract.

Garbage collection finds memory the program no longer reaches and frees it.

The collector starts from the roots: the stack, the CPU registers, the global variables. These are the pointers the program holds directly. Every object a root points to is live. Every object a live object points to is also live. The collector walks this graph, marking each object it reaches. When the walk finishes, every unmarked object is garbage — no root, no live object, no path to it. The collector frees the unmarked and leaves the marked behind.

This is **tracing**, and it is the core of most collectors. The mark phase walks the graph. The sweep phase frees the unmarked. The two phases together are mark-and-sweep.

The walk must see a consistent picture of the graph. If the program mutates the heap while the collector walks it, the collector can miss a pointer: it marks object A, the program moves a pointer from A to B, the collector has already passed A and never visits B, and B gets freed while the program still reaches it. The collectors differ in how they handle this.

A **stop-the-world** collector pauses the program for the whole mark and sweep. Simple, correct, and the source of the freezes that give garbage collection its reputation. The program stops, the collector walks, the program resumes. No mutation during the walk means no missed pointers.

A **concurrent** collector runs the mark phase alongside the program. The program allocates and mutates while the collector traces. The hard part is the pointer that moves after the collector passes its source. Concurrent collectors solve this with a **write barrier**: when the program stores a pointer into an already-marked object, the runtime notes the target so the collector revisits it. The barrier adds overhead to every pointer write, and the collector must handle the case where the program creates new garbage faster than the collector traces it.

**Incremental** collectors split the work into small steps interleaved with program execution, bounding pause time at the cost of more total work. **Parallel** collectors use multiple threads to trace the graph faster, reducing wall-clock pause time on multi-core machines.

**Generational** collectors bet on a pattern observed in real programs: most objects die young. A function allocates a temporary list, returns, and the list is garbage. The collector splits the heap into a young generation and an old generation. It collects the young generation frequently — it is small, the collection is fast, and most of its contents are already dead. It collects the old generation rarely. Objects that survive several young-generation collections get promoted to the old generation. The bet pays off because a young collection scans a small heap and frees most of it, instead of scanning the whole heap to find a few dead objects scattered across it. The cost is a write barrier on pointers from old objects to young objects, so a young collection can find its roots without scanning the entire old heap.

**Reference counting** is a different approach. Every object carries a count of pointers to it. Assignment increments the target's count and decrements the old target's count. When the count hits zero, the object is unreachable and gets freed immediately. The cost is overhead on every pointer assignment, and the failure mode is cycles: two objects pointing to each other have counts of 1 and no external references, but neither count reaches zero. Python and Swift use reference counting and require cycle collection or manual breaking of cycles. C++ uses it in `shared_ptr` and leaves cycle-breaking to the programmer.

The collector does not know which objects the program will reach in the future. It knows only what the program reaches now, through the roots and the live object graph. Garbage is what falls outside that graph, and the collector's job is to find it without freeing something the program still holds.

A race condition is a bug where the result depends on the timing of two operations that run at the same time. The program is correct if one finishes first, correct if the other finishes first, and wrong if they overlap.

A bank account holds a balance of 100. Two threads each withdraw 40. The code reads the balance, subtracts 40, and writes it back. Thread A reads 100. Thread B reads 100, before A writes. A subtracts 40, writes 60. B subtracts 40, writes 60. The balance is 60. It should be 20. Forty dollars vanished.

The subtraction itself is not one step. The CPU loads the balance into a register, subtracts, and stores it back. Between the load and the store, the other thread loads the same old value. Both threads compute from the same starting point, and the second store overwrites the first. The lost update is the visible damage.

The bug is timing-dependent. Run the same code a thousand times and it might produce 20 every time, because the scheduler happened to serialize the threads. Run it once more and it produces 60. A test that passes does not prove the race is absent; it proves the race did not trigger on that run.

The fix is to make the read-modify-write atomic. A mutex around the balance update forces thread B to wait until A finishes its store. An atomic compare-and-swap does the same without a lock: it writes only if the balance has not changed since the read, and retries if it has. Either way, the two operations no longer overlap, and the result no longer depends on which thread got there first.

A CPU cache is a small block of fast memory sitting between the processor and main memory. Main memory takes roughly 100 nanoseconds to answer a request. The cache takes one.

The processor does not fetch memory one byte at a time. It fetches in blocks called cache lines, usually 64 bytes. When the CPU loads a byte from address 1000, the hardware pulls the whole line — bytes 1000 through 1063 — from main memory and copies it into the cache. The next load from address 1004 hits the cache, because that byte arrived in the same line. The load completes in one nanosecond instead of a hundred.

This works because real programs touch memory in patterns. An array stored contiguously in memory is walked front to back, and each cache line brings in the next several elements. A struct's fields sit next to each other, so reading one field prefetches the rest. The cache turns a hundred-nanosecond memory system into something that answers in one nanosecond most of the time.

The cache is small. A typical L1 cache holds 32 or 48 kilobytes. Main memory holds gigabytes. The cache keeps only what the processor used recently, and evicts the rest. When the processor asks for data that is not in the cache — a cache miss — it pays the full main-memory latency, plus the cost of writing an evicted line back if it was modified. A program that jumps through memory at random addresses misses on most accesses. Each miss stalls the processor for the hundred nanoseconds it takes to fetch the line.

Caches are layered. The L1 cache is smallest and fastest, built into each core. The L2 cache is larger, around 256 kilobytes to 2 megabytes, still per-core, slower. The L3 cache is shared across all cores, 8 to 64 megabytes on a desktop chip. A load checks L1, then L2, then L3, then main memory. Each level is larger and slower than the one above it. The hierarchy exists because a cache fast enough to feed the processor cannot be large, and a cache large enough to hold the working set cannot be fast.

The speedup is not from the processor running faster. It is from the processor not waiting. A 4 GHz core issues an instruction every quarter-nanosecond. A main-memory load makes it wait four hundred cycles. A cache hit makes it wait four. The cache does not add speed; it removes stalls. A program that fits its working set into L1 runs at full speed. A program that misses on every access runs at memory speed, which is a hundred times slower.

Okay — explain idempotency as it applies to HTTP APIs, in the plain register already established.

An HTTP method is idempotent when sending the request twice produces the same server state as sending it once. The second call does not duplicate the first; it either repeats the same result or recognizes that the work is already done.

`GET` is idempotent because it reads. Two identical GETs return the same representation, and neither changes anything. `PUT` is idempotent because it replaces. A PUT that sets resource 42's name to "Alice" leaves the resource in the same state whether it runs once or ten times — each call overwrites with the same value. `DELETE` is idempotent because the resource is gone after the first call. A second delete finds nothing to remove and returns the same outcome.

`POST` is not idempotent. A POST that creates a new order processes the request body and allocates a new resource each time. Two identical POSTs create two orders. The server has no instruction from the method itself that the second call is a repeat of the first.

The distinction matters because networks retry. A client sends a PUT, the server applies it, the response is lost on the way back, and the client does not know whether the request landed. The client sends the PUT again. Because PUT is idempotent, the retry is safe: the server applies the same state change a second time, the resource ends up where it should, and the client gets its confirmation. The same scenario with POST creates a duplicate order.

Idempotency is a property of the method's contract, not a guarantee the server enforces. A handler that increments a counter inside a PUT breaks the contract — the second call produces a different state than the first. The HTTP specification defines which methods are idempotent so clients and intermediaries — proxies, load balancers, retry layers — can repeat those requests without corrupting state. A server that honors the contract gets correct retries for free. A server that violates it forces every client to build its own deduplication.

The contract is about server state, not about the response. A DELETE that returns 200 the first time and 404 the second is still idempotent. The resource is gone in both cases; the status code reflects what the server found, not a change in state. What stays constant is the effect on the resource, not the bytes in the reply.

Okay — explain DNS resolution from name to address, in the plain register.

A browser asks the operating system to resolve `www.example.com`. The operating system hands the query to a resolver, usually a stub resolver inside the libc layer that knows nothing but the address of a recursive resolver — typically the one the ISP runs, or a public one like 8.8.8.8.

The recursive resolver does the work. It starts with no answer and builds one by walking the DNS hierarchy, which is a tree of servers split by the dots in the name.

The first question goes to a root server. There are 13 root server addresses, backed by hundreds of anycast instances. The resolver asks: where is `com`? The root server does not know `www.example.com`, and it does not ask anyone. It answers with a referral — a list of authoritative servers for the `com` top-level domain.

The resolver caches that referral, then asks a `com` server: where is `example.com`? The `com` server holds records for every registered `.com` domain. It answers with a referral to the authoritative servers for `example.com`.

The resolver asks the `example.com` server: what is the address of `www.example.com`? This server holds the actual record. It answers with an A record — a 32-bit IPv4 address, or an AAAA record carrying a 128-bit IPv6 address. The resolver hands the address back to the operating system, which hands it to the browser.

Each answer carries a time-to-live. The resolver stores it for that many seconds and serves it from cache until the TTL expires. A cached answer skips the walk. A cold query for a popular domain usually hits the recursive resolver's cache, because someone else asked recently. A cold query for a domain nobody has visited in hours makes the full three-hop walk.

The authoritative server for `example.com` is the one the domain owner configured through their registrar. The registrar pushed the nameserver names into the `com` zone, which is how the `com` server knew where to refer. The chain of trust from root to `com` to `example.com` is the hierarchy: each level delegates the next, and each referral narrows the question.

DNS runs over UDP port 53. A query and its answer each fit in a single UDP packet, up to 512 bytes by default, with larger responses handled by TCP or EDNS0 padding. The resolver sends one UDP packet per question and waits for one UDP packet back. If the answer does not arrive, it retransmits — same packet, same port, same question.

Okay — explain deadlock and one avoidance strategy, in the plain register.

A deadlock is two threads frozen, each holding a lock the other needs. Thread A holds lock 1 and waits for lock 2. Thread B holds lock 2 and waits for lock 1. Neither releases what it has until it gets what it wants. Both wait forever.

Four conditions must hold at once. The threads hold locks exclusively — no two threads share a lock. They hold while waiting — a thread does not release its lock before requesting the next. The locks are not preempted — the operating system does not force a thread to give up a held lock. There is a circular wait — a ring of threads where each holds a lock the next one needs, and the last points back to the first. Break any one and the deadlock cannot form.

The circular wait is the easiest to break. Impose a global order on every lock in the program. Every thread acquires locks in that order, always. Thread A wants lock 1 and lock 2: it acquires lock 1 first, then lock 2. Thread B wants the same two: it also acquires lock 1 first, then lock 2. If A gets lock 1, B blocks on lock 1 before it touches lock 2. A finishes, releases both, B proceeds. The ring never closes.

The fix costs nothing at runtime. It costs discipline: every path that takes two or more locks must know the order, and every new lock must slot into the ordering. A lock taken out of order, once, reopens the deadlock. The order can be arbitrary — memory address, ID number, declaration sequence — as long as it is total and every thread follows it.

A hash map stores key-value pairs in an array. It computes an integer from the key, maps that integer to an array index, and places the pair there. Two keys can produce the same index. That is a collision, and the map has to resolve it.

**Chaining** keeps a linked list at each array slot. When two keys land on index 7, both pairs go into the list at position 7. A lookup walks that list, comparing each stored key against the target. The list is short on average — the load factor (entries divided by slots) keeps it bounded, and the map resizes the array when the load factor crosses a threshold, typically 0.75. Java's `HashMap` and C++'s `std::unordered_map` both chain. The cost: a pointer per entry, and cache misses when the list nodes scatter across the heap.

**Open addressing** stores every pair directly in the array. A collision at index 7 triggers a probe sequence — a rule for trying other slots. Linear probing checks 8, 9, 10, and so on. Quadratic probing jumps by squares: 7, 8, 11, 16. Double hashing computes a second hash from the key to set the step size, spreading entries more evenly. Python's `dict` uses open addressing with a perturbed probe sequence. Robin Hood hashing, used in Rust's `HashMap`, is a variant of open addressing that evicts entries that traveled fewer probes from their home slot, keeping the worst-case probe length low.

The tradeoff is locality against deletion. Open addressing keeps everything in one contiguous array, so a probe sequence hits cache lines. But deleting a pair leaves a gap: a later lookup that probes through that slot would stop early and miss entries placed beyond it. Open-addressing maps mark deleted slots with a tombstone flag, and the slot stays usable for insertion but skipped during probing. Chaining deletes by unlinking a list node, no tombstone needed.

Load factor governs both schemes. As the array fills, collisions rise, and probe sequences or chain lists lengthen. The map allocates a larger array — usually double the size — rehashes every entry into its new slot, and discards the old array. This rehash is O(n) but amortized O(1) per insertion, the same way a dynamic array's growth is.

A database index is a second data structure stored alongside a table. It trades disk space and write speed for read speed.

The structure is usually a B-tree. The B-tree keeps the indexed column's values in sorted order, with the corresponding row's location attached to each value. A query that filters on that column — `WHERE last_name = 'Smith'` — walks the tree from root to leaf, comparing a handful of values at each level, and arrives at the matching rows without scanning the table. A table with ten million rows might need ten million disk reads to find every Smith without an index. With a B-tree index on `last_name`, the database reads four or five tree pages, then reads only the rows the leaf nodes point to. That is the point of the structure: turn a linear scan into a logarithmic one.

A table can have many indexes. Each one answers a different query. An index on `last_name` does nothing for `WHERE zip_code = '90210'`; that query still scans unless a separate index on `zip_code` exists. A composite index on `(last_name, first_name)` serves queries that filter on both columns, and also queries that filter on `last_name` alone, because the tree sorts by `last_name` first. It does not serve a query that filters on `first_name` alone, because `first_name` is only sorted within each `last_name` group.

Indexes hurt on writes. Every `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, and `DELETE` that changes an indexed column must update the index tree as well as the table. A table with five indexes pays six writes for one inserted row — one to the table's heap, five to the B-trees. On a system that reads far more than it writes, that cost is invisible. On a system that logs high-frequency events — say, ten thousand inserts per second — five indexes can cut throughput by more than half, because each insert forces random I/O across six different on-disk structures.

Indexes also hurt when the optimizer decides not to use them. A B-tree lookup is only cheaper than a scan when the index narrows the result set enough to justify the tree traversal plus the random reads back to the table. A query that matches thirty percent of a table's rows will usually scan, because reading the table sequentially beats jumping between index pages and row locations hundreds of thousands of times. An index built for that query wastes the space it occupies and the writes it costs, because the optimizer ignores it. The database's `EXPLAIN` output shows this: a query plan that lists a sequential scan where an index scan was expected means the index is dead weight.

The cost is concrete. An index consumes disk space proportional to the table size — a B-tree on a ten-million-row table might occupy 400 MB. It slows every write to that table by a factor roughly equal to the number of indexes. And it provides zero benefit on queries the optimizer will not route through it. An index earns its place only when a real query runs often enough, and matches few enough rows, that the read savings outweigh the write cost across the workload.

TCP sends data as numbered bytes, not as messages. Each byte gets a sequence number, and the receiver uses those numbers to put the bytes back in the order they were sent.

The sender stamps every segment with two values: the sequence number of the first byte in that segment, and the number of bytes it carries. A segment carrying bytes 1001 through 1500 has sequence number 1001 and length 500. The next segment starts at 1501. The numbers run continuously across segment boundaries — byte 1500 in one segment and byte 1501 in the next are adjacent, regardless of how the data was chunked for transmission.

The receiver collects these segments and places them in a buffer keyed by sequence number. If segment 1501 arrives before segment 1001, the receiver holds it. When 1001 arrives, the two fit together. The receiver then sends an acknowledgment back: "I have everything up to byte 1500, send 1501 next." That acknowledgment carries the next expected sequence number, which is also the cumulative count of bytes received in order. A gap means the receiver acknowledges only up to the gap, not past it.

Gaps happen because IP, the protocol underneath TCP, delivers packets independently with no ordering guarantee. Packet 3 can beat packet 2 to the destination. TCP sits above IP and reconstructs the order using the sequence numbers. The receiver never hands data to the application out of order. It holds later segments in the buffer until the missing ones fill the gap, then delivers the contiguous run to the application.

The sender detects the gap through duplicate acknowledgments. If the receiver gets bytes 1001 and 2001 but not 1501, it acknowledges 1001 twice — once for the 1001 segment, once for the 2001 segment, both saying "next expected: 1501." The sender sees the second acknowledgment as a signal that 1501 was lost and retransmits it. This is TCP's fast retransmit: three duplicate acknowledgments trigger a resend before the retransmission timer expires.

The sequence number space is finite — 32 bits, wrapping at roughly 4.3 billion bytes. For a high-throughput connection sending data faster than the sequence space cycles, two segments could theoretically carry the same number. TCP prevents this by limiting the send rate through the sliding window: the sender cannot transmit beyond what the receiver has acknowledged plus the advertised window size. The window keeps the unacknowledged data within bounds so that old segments expire from the network before their sequence numbers recycle.

A mutex protects one thing: the interleaving of operations on shared state.

Two threads running on separate cores can read and write the same memory at the same time. A thread increments a counter: it reads the value 7 into a register, adds 1, writes 8 back. If a second thread reads the same counter between the first thread's read and its write, it also reads 7, adds 1, writes 8. Two increments produced one. The counter should be 9. It is 8. This is a data race — two accesses to the same memory, at least one a write, with no synchronization between them.

A mutex is a lock with two operations: acquire and release. Only one thread can hold the lock at a time. A thread that calls acquire when the mutex is free gets it immediately. A thread that calls acquire when another thread holds it blocks — the operating system parks it until the holder calls release. The kernel maintains a wait queue of blocked threads and hands the mutex to the next one when it is released.

The mutex turns concurrent access into serial access. Code wrapped between acquire and release is a critical section: two threads cannot both be inside it at once. The counter increment becomes read, add, write — uninterrupted, because any other thread trying to enter the same section waits outside the lock. The lost update cannot happen.

A mutex protects against data races on the specific state it guards. It does not protect against races on other variables. It does not make a thread-safe data structure by existing — the mutex must be acquired on every path that touches the shared state, or the protection fails. A function that locks the mutex, updates the counter, and unlocks is safe. A second function that updates the same counter without locking the mutex breaks the guarantee, because the first function can be inside its critical section when the second function writes.

A mutex does not protect against deadlock. Two threads can deadlock if each holds one mutex and waits for the other. Thread A locks mutex 1, then tries to lock mutex 2. Thread B locks mutex 2, then tries to lock mutex 1. Both wait forever. The mutex prevents the data race but introduces a coordination problem: locks acquired in a consistent order across all threads prevent the cycle.

A mutex does not protect against priority inversion. A low-priority thread holding a mutex can block a high-priority thread that needs it, while a medium-priority thread keeps the low-priority thread from running and releasing the lock. The high-priority thread waits behind the medium-priority thread's work, inverting the priority the scheduler intended. Priority inheritance — the holder temporarily inherits the priority of the highest thread waiting on the mutex — is one fix, implemented in the kernel's mutex implementation, not in the mutex concept itself.

The protection is narrow and absolute within its scope. Every access to the shared state goes through the same mutex. The critical section is as short as it can be, because the mutex serializes every thread that needs it, and long sections reduce concurrency. The lock is released before any operation that might block — I/O, sleeping, acquiring another lock — because a held mutex blocks every other thread waiting for it, and holding one across a blocking call turns a brief wait into a system-wide stall.

Garbage collection reclaims memory that a program can no longer reach. The collector's job is to distinguish garbage from live objects, and the criterion is reachability: an object is live if a chain of references connects it to a root, and garbage if no such chain exists.

The roots are the starting points. In a Java or .NET runtime, the roots are the references on every thread's call stack — local variables holding objects — plus static fields and active JNI handles. The collector walks from these roots through every reference they contain, then through the references inside those objects, and so on. Every object it touches is marked live. Every object it never touches is unreachable, and unreachable means dead.

This is the mark phase. The collector starts at the roots and sets a flag on each object it reaches. The traversal is a graph search — depth-first or breadth-first, the choice is implementation detail — through the reference graph. When the traversal finishes, the collector knows which objects are live. It then sweeps the heap: it walks every allocated object, checks the flag, and frees the ones left unmarked. This is mark-and-sweep, the algorithm McCarthy described in 1960 and the foundation of most tracing collectors since.

Mark-and-sweep leaves gaps. Freed objects scatter holes across the heap, and allocating a new object means finding a hole big enough — a search that fragments over time. A compaction pass fixes this. After the sweep, the collector slides every live object toward one end of the heap, closing the gaps. Every moved object's references must be updated to point at the new addresses. The result is a contiguous block of free space at the other end, and allocation becomes a pointer bump: advance the free pointer by the object's size, return that address. The JVM's serial and parallel collectors compact. Go's GC does not — it trades fragmentation for pause-time predictability and relies on the allocator to manage spans.

Compaction costs time proportional to the number of live objects, because each one may move. A heap that is mostly garbage sweeps cheaply but compacts expensively if the surviving objects are many. This asymmetry drives generational collection, built on the weak generational hypothesis: most objects die young. A program allocates temporary buffers, intermediate strings, loop variables — objects created and discarded within a single function call. The collector splits the heap into a young generation and an old generation. New objects go into the young generation, which is small and collected often. A young-generation collection marks and sweeps a small heap, finds most objects dead, and copies the few survivors into the old generation. The old generation, large and stable, is collected rarely. The JVM's G1 and ZGC, and .NET's managed heap, are generational.

Copying collection is the mechanism that makes young-generation collection fast. The collector divides the young generation into two semi-spaces. It copies live objects from the active semi-space to the empty one, packing them contiguously as it goes. Dead objects are never touched — they simply vanish when the active semi-space is overwritten on the next cycle. Copying costs time proportional to the number of live objects, not the total heap, so a space that is 95% garbage costs almost nothing to collect. The survivors land in the old generation or the other semi-space, compacted by the act of copying.

The alternative to tracing is reference counting. Each object carries a counter of how many references point to it. A new reference increments the counter; a dropped reference decrements it. When the counter hits zero, the object is unreachable and can be freed immediately, no traversal needed. CPython uses this for most objects. The weakness is cycles: two objects that reference each other keep each other's count at 1 forever, even when nothing else references either. A separate cycle detector must run periodically to find and break these. Reference counting also pays a cost on every assignment — incrementing and decrementing counters, checking for zero — where a tracing collector batches the work into discrete collection cycles.

The hard problem is pause time. A tracing collector that stops the application while it marks and sweeps the full heap can pause for hundreds of milliseconds on a large heap. That is intolerable for a system with latency targets. Concurrent collectors reduce the pause by doing most of the work while the application runs. The collector marks live objects as the application mutates the heap, which means the application can change the reference graph mid-traversal. The collector handles this with write barriers: every reference update triggers a small piece of bookkeeping that records what changed, so the collector can revisit those objects and correct its marks. Go's collector is concurrent and uses a write barrier to track mutations during the mark phase. ZGC, introduced in JDK 11 and production-ready in JDK 15, does marking, relocation, and remapping concurrently with colored pointers and load barriers, keeping pauses under one millisecond on multi-gigabyte heaps.

The collector finds unused memory by tracing from the roots through the reference graph, marking what is reachable, and reclaiming what is not. Everything else — generational layout, copying, compaction, concurrency, barriers — is engineering to make that traversal cheap enough and fast enough that the program does not notice it running.

A race condition is a bug that appears only when the timing of two operations lands a certain way. The program's correctness depends on the order of events, and that order is not controlled.

Consider a bank account with a balance of 100 dollars. Two threads transfer money out at the same time. Thread A checks the balance: 100. Thread B checks the balance: 100. Both see enough funds. Thread A subtracts 30 and writes 70. Thread B subtracts 40 and writes 60. The final balance is 60. One of the two withdrawals vanished. The account lost 30 dollars that no one withdrew.

The operations were not atomic. Each thread performed three steps: read the balance, subtract, write it back. The threads interleaved between the read and the write. Thread A read 100, then Thread B read 100 before A wrote 70. Both worked from the same stale value, and the second write clobbered the first.

The fix is synchronization. A mutex around the read-subtract-write block forces the threads to take turns. Thread A acquires the lock, reads 100, subtracts 30, writes 70, releases. Thread B acquires the lock, reads 70, subtracts 40, writes 30, releases. The balance is correct. The lock made the three steps indivisible, so no thread can read a value the other is about to overwrite.

Races are hard to find because they do not reproduce on every run. The interleaving depends on the operating system's scheduler, which decides when each thread gets a core and for how long. A program can run a million times with the threads always landing in a safe order, then fail on the million-and-first because the scheduler preempted a thread at the wrong instruction. Testing rarely catches them. The code looks correct step by step; the bug is in the gap between the steps.

A CPU cache is a small, fast memory that sits between the processor and main memory. It speeds up a program by keeping the data the processor is most likely to need next close enough to fetch in a few cycles instead of hundreds.

Main memory is slow. A 3 GHz processor executes an instruction every 0.33 nanoseconds, but a read from DRAM takes roughly 100 nanoseconds — 300 cycles of waiting. The cache, built from SRAM on the same die as the processor, returns a value in 3 to 5 cycles. That gap is the entire reason the cache exists.

The cache works because of locality. A program that reads `array[0]` almost always reads `array[1]` next. That is spatial locality: nearby memory gets accessed close in time. The cache exploits it by fetching data in blocks, not single bytes. A cache line is 64 bytes on most x86 and ARM processors. When the CPU reads one byte from memory, the hardware pulls the entire 64-byte line containing it into the cache. The next seven reads from that line hit the cache and cost 3 cycles each instead of 100.

A program that reads the same variable in a loop — a counter incremented ten thousand times — shows temporal locality. The value stays in the cache because it keeps getting used. The cache holds it, and every read after the first is fast.

Modern processors have three cache levels. L1 is smallest and fastest: 32 to 48 kilobytes, 3 to 5 cycles, split into separate caches for data and instructions. L2 is larger and slower: 256 kilobytes to 1 megabyte, 10 to 15 cycles, unified. L3 is largest and shared across cores: 8 to 64 megabytes, 30 to 50 cycles. A request checks L1, then L2, then L3, then main memory. A hit at any level avoids the slower levels below. A miss at all three costs the full DRAM latency.

The cache is finite, so it evicts. When a new line arrives and the cache is full, the hardware discards an old line to make room. The replacement policy is usually least-recently-used: the line that has gone longest without a read or write gets removed. A program that streams through a large array — reading 10 megabytes of data once, never revisiting — fills the cache and evicts every line it loaded. Each read misses. The cache provides no benefit, because the access pattern has no reuse. A program that repeatedly scans a 100-kilobyte table fits the table in L2 and hits the cache on every pass. The table size relative to the cache determines whether the workload runs fast or slow.

Cache misses come in three kinds. A compulsory miss is the first read of a line — the data was never in the cache, so it must be fetched. A capacity miss happens when the cache is too small to hold the working set, so lines get evicted and reloaded. A conflict miss happens when multiple lines map to the same cache set — the cache is not fully associative, so a direct-mapped or set-associative cache forces evictions even when total capacity is available. A 4-megabyte L2 with 8-way set associativity holds 8 lines per set; a ninth line mapping to that set evicts one regardless of how empty the other sets are.

The cache also speeds up writes. A store instruction writes to L1 and moves on — the data reaches main memory later. This is a write-back cache: the line is marked dirty, and the cache writes it to DRAM only when the line is evicted or another core requests it. The processor does not wait for the full memory latency on every store. A write-through cache, simpler but slower, writes to both cache and memory on every store. Most modern processors use write-back for L1 and L2.

The speedup is measurable. A matrix multiplication that accesses data row by row — the cache-friendly order — can run ten times faster than the same computation accessing data column by column, because the column-wise traversal jumps across cache lines and misses on nearly every read. The arithmetic is identical. The memory access pattern is not. The cache rewards programs that touch memory in the order it was laid out, and penalizes programs that jump.

Okay — explain idempotency in the context of an HTTP API, plain register, every sentence carrying a fact.

An HTTP request is idempotent when sending it once produces the same result as sending it twice. The second call does not change the server's state again. It may return a different response — a 200 the first time, a 404 the second — but the underlying state is the same after both.

`DELETE /users/42` is idempotent. The first call removes the user. The second call finds no user at 42 and returns 404. The server's state after the second call is identical to its state after the first: user 42 is gone. The response body differs. The state does not.

`POST /users` is not idempotent. Each call creates a new user. Two calls produce two users. Three calls produce three. The server's state changes with every request, and the change is cumulative.

The HTTP specification marks `GET`, `PUT`, `DELETE`, and `HEAD` as idempotent methods. `POST` and `PATCH` are not. The spec defines idempotency as a property of the method's semantics, not a guarantee about a particular implementation. A `DELETE` endpoint that logs each attempt to an audit table is not idempotent in the strictest sense, because the log grows with every call. The spec's concern is the resource state, not side effects like logging or metrics.

Idempotency matters for retries. Network infrastructure — proxies, load balancers, cellular gateways — drops connections and resends requests. A client that times out waiting for a response cannot tell whether the server received the request. If the method is idempotent, the client resends safely. The second `DELETE /users/42` either confirms the deletion or reports the user already gone. No harm done.

A client that resends `POST /users` after a timeout risks creating a duplicate. The first call may have succeeded; the response was lost. The second call creates a second user with the same data. This is the problem idempotency exists to solve, and `POST` does not solve it by default.

The fix for non-idempotent operations is an idempotency key. The client generates a unique identifier — a UUID — and sends it in a header, typically `Idempotency-Key`. The server stores the key with the result of the first request. On the second request with the same key, the server returns the stored result instead of executing the operation again. Stripe's API uses this pattern: a `POST /v1/charges` with `Idempotency-Key: 7c8d2f1a` creates one charge, no matter how many times that exact key is sent. The key scopes to the request path and body, so a different charge amount with the same key is rejected as a conflict, not silently ignored.

`PUT` is idempotent by construction. `PUT /users/42` with a body sets the user's state to that body. The tenth call with the same body produces the same state as the first. The server overwrites whatever was there with the provided representation. Partial updates via `PUT` — sending only changed fields and expecting the server to merge them — break this guarantee, because the result depends on the state the server held before the call. A `PUT` that merges is really a `PATCH` wearing a `PUT`'s method name, and it loses the retry safety that `PUT`'s idempotency provides.

Okay — explain DNS resolution from name to IP, plain register, every sentence carrying a fact.

A browser asks the operating system for the address of `www.example.com`. The operating system hands the question to a resolver, which is usually a library inside the C runtime. The resolver checks its own cache first. If the answer is there and still valid, it returns the address and the process stops.

If the cache is empty, the resolver sends a UDP packet to a recursive resolver — the machine configured in the system's network settings, often the ISP's server at `192.168.1.1` or a public one like Google's `8.8.8.8`. The recursive resolver's job is to chase the answer across the DNS hierarchy and bring it back.

The hierarchy is a tree. The root is the top. Below it sit the top-level domains: `.com`, `.org`, `.net`, the country codes like `.uk` and `.jp`. Below each TLD sit the authoritative servers for individual domains. `example.com` has its own set of name servers that hold the actual records for that domain.

The recursive resolver starts at the root. It sends a query for `www.example.com` to one of the thirteen root server clusters. The root server does not know the answer. It knows which servers hold the `.com` TLD, and it returns that list in the response as a referral. The referral is a set of NS records — name server records — each pointing at a `.com` TLD server.

The resolver picks one and sends the same query to it. The TLD server does not know `www.example.com` either. It knows which servers are authoritative for `example.com`, and it returns those as another referral. The domain's authoritative servers are the ones the domain owner configured when registering the domain — the names listed in the registrar's delegation record.

The resolver sends the query to one of `example.com`'s authoritative servers. This server holds the zone file for `example.com`, which is the set of records the domain administrator published. The zone file contains an A record for `www` — a mapping from the hostname to an IPv4 address, say `93.184.216.34`. The authoritative server returns that record.

The resolver caches the answer for the duration specified in the record's TTL field — time to live, measured in seconds. A TTL of 3600 means the resolver will return the cached address for the next hour without asking anyone. When the TTL expires, the resolver discards the cached entry and repeats the full lookup on the next request.

The resolver hands the address back to the operating system, which hands it to the browser. The browser opens a TCP connection to that address and sends the HTTP request.

One lookup can return more than an address. A CNAME record maps one name to another instead of to an address. `www.example.com` might be a CNAME pointing to `example.com`, which in turn has an A record. The resolver follows the chain: it queries for `www.example.com`, gets back the CNAME, then queries for `example.com` and gets the A record. The chain can be several links long, and each link is a separate DNS query with its own TTL.

The protocol runs on port 53. The queries are small enough to fit in a single UDP datagram, and most lookups use UDP because the round-trip is faster than TCP's handshake. A response that exceeds 512 bytes — a large TXT record, or a domain with many name servers — triggers a fallback to TCP, or uses EDNS0, an extension that lets the resolver advertise a larger UDP buffer size. DNSSEC, which signs records cryptographically, adds enough data that EDNS0 is effectively required.

The system is layered caching. The browser caches. The operating system caches. The recursive resolver caches. Each layer holds the answer for its own TTL and serves subsequent lookups from memory. A cold lookup — nothing cached anywhere — can take four round trips: resolver to root, resolver to TLD, resolver to authoritative, and the original query from the machine to the resolver. A warm lookup takes one: the resolver returns the cached address in under a millisecond. The difference between a 40-millisecond cold resolution and a sub-millisecond cached one is why the TTL exists. The hierarchy distributes the work across thousands of servers, and the caching keeps most queries from reaching them.

A deadlock is a state where two threads each hold a resource the other needs, and neither will give up what it has. Both wait forever. The program stops.

Thread A locks file 1, then tries to lock file 2. Thread B locks file 2, then tries to lock file 1. A holds file 1 and wants file 2. B holds file 2 and wants file 1. Neither can proceed. The locks never release, because a thread must hold its first lock to do the work that needs the second, and neither thread will release its first lock until it gets the second and finishes. The cycle is the bug.

Four conditions must hold at once for a deadlock to occur. The resources must be held exclusively — one thread at a time. The threads must hold while waiting — a thread does not release its lock before requesting the next. The resources cannot be taken away — the kernel does not revoke a held lock. And there must be a circular wait — a chain of threads where each holds what the next one needs, and the last holds what the first one needs. Break any one condition and the deadlock cannot form.

The simplest fix breaks the circular wait. Require every thread to acquire locks in the same order. If both threads lock file 1 first, then file 2, the deadlock vanishes. Thread A locks file 1. Thread B tries to lock file 1 and blocks, because A holds it. Thread A locks file 2, does its work, releases both. Thread B gets file 1, then file 2, does its work, releases both. The order turns the cycle into a line.

The rule is a lock-ordering protocol: every mutex in the system has a rank, and every thread acquires locks in ascending rank order. A thread holding a rank-2 lock may acquire a rank-5 lock, but a thread holding a rank-5 lock may never acquire a rank-2 lock. The ranks are assigned at design time and fixed. The protocol costs nothing at runtime — no extra locks, no checks — but it demands discipline. A single function that acquires locks in the wrong order opens the deadlock the protocol was meant to prevent.

The protocol fails when the lock order is not global. Two modules written independently, each with its own internal lock ordering, can deadlock when they interact. Module X locks its internal mutex, then calls into Module Y, which locks its own internal mutex. Module Y's code, called from a different path, locks its mutex first, then calls into Module X, which locks its mutex. The two modules each follow their own order, but the combined order is circular. The fix is to define the ranking across module boundaries, or to avoid holding locks across module calls — release before calling out, reacquire on return.

A hash map turns a key into an integer with a hash function, then uses that integer as an index into an array of buckets. Two keys can produce the same index. That is a collision, and the map has to store both.

The oldest fix is chaining. Each bucket holds a pointer to a linked list. When a key lands on an occupied bucket, the map appends the new entry to that list. A lookup walks the list and compares keys until it finds a match. The cost grows with list length. If every key hashes to the same bucket, the map degrades to a linked list, and lookup becomes O(n).

Open addressing takes a different shape. There is one array and no lists. When a key's bucket is taken, the map probes other slots by a rule: linear probing checks the next slot, then the next. Quadratic probing jumps by squares of the index. Double hashing uses a second hash function to set the step size. A lookup follows the same probe sequence until it finds the key or an empty slot.

Open addressing is faster on modern hardware because the array stays in cache and the map avoids the pointer chase that linked lists require. The trade is fragility. As the array fills, probe sequences lengthen fast. Most implementations keep the array at most two-thirds full and rebuild a larger array when that threshold is crossed. That rebuild rehashes every entry, which is expensive, but it keeps average lookup near O(1).

Deletion adds a problem under open addressing. Removing an entry and leaving an empty slot breaks the probe chain for any key that was inserted past it. The fix is a tombstone: the slot is marked deleted rather than empty, so probes continue past it. Tombstones accumulate, though, and they raise the load factor without holding live data, which is why a map that sees many deletes needs periodic rehashing to clear them.

Robin Hood hashing is a variant of open addressing that reduces the worst-case probe length. On insert, it tracks how far each entry sits from its home bucket. A new entry that has probed farther can evict an entry that probed less, taking its slot. The evicted entry continues probing. This spreads probe lengths evenly and keeps the longest chain short.

The choice between chaining and open addressing comes down to load and access pattern. Chaining tolerates high load factors without catastrophic degradation and handles deletion cleanly. Open addressing is more cache-friendly and uses less memory per entry, but it demands a low load factor and a good hash function, because a weak hash clusters entries and the probe chains grow long.

A database index is a second data structure stored alongside the table. It holds a sorted copy of one or more columns, each entry paired with a pointer back to the full row. Without an index, a query that filters on a column must read every row in the table and test the predicate against each. With an index on that column, the database seeks the matching entries in the sorted structure and fetches only the rows they point to. On a million-row table, a query for `users WHERE email = 'x'` reads one index entry instead of scanning a million rows.

The common structure is a B-tree. It keeps keys in sorted order inside a balanced tree, so a point lookup takes O(log n) comparisons and a range scan walks the leaf nodes in order. Hash indexes serve only equality checks, since a hash destroys ordering. Postgres, MySQL, and SQL Server all default to B-tree for this reason.

An index hurts in three places. The first is write speed. Every insert, update, or delete on an indexed column must update the index as well as the table. A table with five indexes takes roughly six times as long to insert a row as a table with none, because each index is a separate structure that must be rebalanced.

The second is storage. The index is a copy of the data, not a view of it. An index on a large text column can approach the size of the table itself. A table with four such indexes can consume five times the disk space of the bare rows.

The third is the planner's choice. A query that returns a large fraction of the table is slower through an index than through a full scan, because the index forces random I/O — one seek per row — while a sequential scan reads the table in one pass. The planner estimates how many rows a predicate will match and switches to a scan when the fraction crosses a threshold, often around five to ten percent. A bad estimate, caused by stale statistics or a correlated column the planner does not model, makes the planner pick the wrong path.

An index earns its cost when it serves queries that run often and return few rows relative to the table size. A unique index on a primary key is the clear case: every join and every lookup by id uses it, and it enforces uniqueness at the same time. An index on a foreign key serves join queries. A composite index on `(last_name, first_name)` serves queries that filter on both columns or on `last_name` alone, since the B-tree sorts by the leftmost column first. It does not serve a query that filters on `first_name` alone, because the sort order is by `last_name` and `first_name` values are scattered across the leaves.

The rule is arithmetic, not aesthetic. If the read time saved across all queries exceeds the write time added plus the storage cost, the index pays for itself. If a query runs once a month on a ten-thousand-row table, no index is needed. If it runs a thousand times a second on a hundred-million-row table, the index is the difference between a millisecond and a minute.

TCP sends data as numbered bytes, not as detached packets. Each byte gets a sequence number drawn from a 32-bit counter, and the receiver uses that number to reassemble the stream in order.

The sender writes application data into a buffer. TCP breaks that buffer into segments, and each segment carries the sequence number of its first byte. Segment one might start at byte 0, segment two at byte 1000, segment three at byte 2000. The numbers are byte positions, not segment indices.

The receiver keeps a buffer of its own. When a segment arrives, TCP checks the sequence number against what it expects next. If the segment carries bytes 2000 through 2999 and the receiver has already delivered bytes 0 through 1999 to the application, it writes the new segment into the buffer at the correct offset and sends an acknowledgment back: "I have everything up to byte 3000, send 3000 next."

If segments arrive out of order, the receiver keeps them. Segment 3000 can arrive before segment 2000. The receiver stores it, notes the gap, and sends a duplicate acknowledgment for byte 2000 — the next byte it still needs. When segment 2000 arrives, the gap closes, and TCP releases bytes 2000 through 3999 to the application in one contiguous pass.

A missing segment stalls delivery. If bytes 2000 through 2999 never arrive, the receiver holds bytes 3000 through 5000 in its buffer and delivers nothing past 1999. The application sees a continuous stream; it never sees the hole.

The sender retransmits to close the gap. It starts a timer when it sends a segment. If the acknowledgment does not return before the timer expires, the sender sends the segment again. TCP also infers loss from duplicate acknowledgments: three duplicate acks for byte 2000 tell the sender that byte 2000 was lost but later segments arrived, so it retransmits 2000 without waiting for the timer. This is fast retransmit.

The sequence number wraps at 2³². A 4 GB stream exhausts the counter and the numbering starts over. TCP handles this with the window scale and by ensuring old segments from a previous connection age out before the counter recycles their numbers, using the time-wait state and a four-tuple of source address, source port, destination address, destination port to distinguish connections.

The result is that the application reads a byte stream in the order it was written, regardless of the order the segments crossed the network. The sequence numbers turn an unreliable packet service into an ordered byte pipe.

A mutex protects one thing: shared memory touched by more than one thread at the same time.

Two threads run a bank balance update. Thread A reads the balance at 100. Thread B reads the balance at 100. Thread A adds 50, writes 150. Thread B subtracts 30, writes 70. The final balance is 70. It should be 120. Thirty dollars of deposits vanished. The problem is not the arithmetic. The problem is that read-modify-write is not one operation. It is three, and the scheduler can switch threads between any of them.

A mutex serializes those operations. Before touching the balance, a thread locks the mutex. Any other thread that tries to lock it stalls. The operating system puts the second thread to sleep, not spinning, until the first thread unlocks. The second thread wakes, acquires the lock, and proceeds. The balance update now runs start to finish without interruption.

The mutex protects the data, not the code. Two threads can run the same function at the same time under a mutex, as long as they touch different data. Two threads touching the same balance without a mutex corrupt it, even if they run different functions. The lock follows the memory, not the instruction.

A mutex does not protect against reentrancy from the same thread. If a function locks a mutex and then calls another function that locks the same mutex, the thread deadlocks against itself. A recursive mutex solves this by tracking ownership and allowing the same thread to lock it again, but recursive mutexes mask design problems. The cleaner fix is to restructure so the inner function does not need the lock.

Deadlock is the other failure. Thread A locks mutex 1, then tries to lock mutex 2. Thread B locks mutex 2, then tries to lock mutex 1. Both stall. The fix is lock ordering: every thread acquires mutexes in the same sequence, so the cycle cannot form.

A mutex is the blunt instrument. It turns concurrent access into serial access for the span of the lock. The cost is that the second thread waits. Hold the lock for the minimum work needed to keep the data consistent, and release it before anything slow — disk I/O, network calls, sleeping — because those operations block every other thread waiting on the same lock.

Okay, explain how garbage collection identifies unused memory, written in plain White/Orwell register.

A program allocates memory on a heap. It asks the runtime for a block, receives a pointer, and stores data there. When the program no longer needs the data, it drops the pointer. The block becomes garbage: still allocated, still holding data, unreachable by any code that runs.

The collector's job is to find those blocks and return them to the heap. It works from a simple principle: memory is live if the program can reach it, and dead if it cannot. Reachability starts from a fixed set of roots — the stack variables, the CPU registers, and the global variables that the running code can name directly. From those roots, the collector traces every pointer it can follow, marks every block it arrives at as live, and treats everything unmarked as garbage.

That is the mark phase. The collector walks the object graph the way a program would: it reads the roots, follows their pointers to the objects they reference, follows those objects' pointers in turn, and stamps each one. When the walk finishes, every reachable object carries a mark. The sweep phase then scans the entire heap and frees any block without one.

The mark-and-sweep collector leaves gaps. Freed blocks scatter across the heap, and new allocations must fit into whatever hole is large enough. The heap fragments. A program can have enough total free memory to satisfy a request and still fail, because no single gap is big enough. Compaction fixes this. After marking, the collector slides every live object to one end of the heap, closing the gaps. Pointers that referenced moved objects get rewritten to the new addresses. The heap is contiguous again, and allocation is a simple pointer bump from the free end.

Copying collection takes a different approach. It splits the heap into two halves. The program allocates in one half only. When that half fills, the collector copies every reachable object from the full half to the empty half, packing them contiguously as it goes. The old half becomes the new free space. Dead objects never get copied; they simply vanish when the old half is overwritten. This trades half the heap for automatic compaction and fast allocation, with no sweep phase at all.

The cost of all these methods is the pause. While the collector runs, the program stops. The runtime freezes every thread, runs the collection, and resumes. On a small heap this takes microseconds. On a large heap with a deep object graph, it can take hundreds of milliseconds, and a program that must respond in real time stalls during that window.

Generational collection cuts that pause. It rests on an empirical observation: most objects die young. A loop that builds a temporary string each iteration allocates and discards thousands of objects, and nearly all of them become garbage before the next collection. The collector divides the heap into generations. New objects go in the young generation, which is small and collected often. The collection is fast because the heap region is small. Objects that survive several young-generation collections get promoted to an older generation, which is large and collected rarely.

The generational collector faces one complication. A pointer from an old object to a new object makes the new object reachable, but the collector does not scan the old generation during a young collection. It would defeat the purpose. Instead the runtime maintains a remembered set: a list of old-to-new pointers, updated whenever the program writes one. The young collection treats the remembered set as additional roots, so it can find new objects referenced by old ones without scanning the old generation.

Reference counting takes a fourth shape. Each object carries a count of the pointers that reference it. The program increments the count when it stores a new pointer to the object and decrements when it drops one. When the count hits zero, no pointer references the object, and the collector frees it immediately. No pause, no separate scan. The cost is two arithmetic operations on every pointer assignment, and a failure mode: two objects that reference each other hold counts of one, never reach zero, and never get freed. A cycle of references keeps garbage alive under reference counting, which is why most runtimes pair it with a periodic tracing collector or forbid cycles at the language level.

The collector reclaims memory the program forgot. It traces from the roots, marks what is reachable, frees what is not, and compacts what remains so the heap stays usable. The trade across every variant is the same: CPU time spent collecting versus pause time imposed on the program, and memory held in reserve versus memory available for work.

A race condition is a bug where the result of a program depends on the order in which two operations run, and that order is not controlled.

Two threads share a counter. Both read it at 5. Both add 1. Both write 6. The counter should be 7. One increment is lost. The read and the write are separate instructions, and the scheduler can pause one thread between them and let the other run. The threads race for the same memory, and the loser's write overwrites the winner's.

The counter is not the only victim. A printer queue that appends a job to a linked list while another thread removes one can lose a job or corrupt the list pointers. A bank transfer that reads a balance, computes a withdrawal, and writes the result can drop a deposit that arrived between the read and the write. Any data that two threads touch without synchronization is open to the race.

The fix is to make the read and the write atomic. A mutex around the counter serializes the increment: one thread finishes before the other starts. An atomic integer does the same without a lock, using a CPU instruction that reads, modifies, and writes in one indivisible step. Either way the second thread sees the first thread's result, not the stale value it read before the first thread wrote.

The bug is hard to find because it does not reproduce on every run. The scheduler decides when to switch threads, and two executions of the same program can take different paths. A test passes a thousand times and fails on the thousandth because the operating system paused the thread at the wrong instruction on that one run. The failure looks random, and randomness sends the search in the wrong direction.

A race condition is a concurrency bug. It appears when shared state changes between the moment one thread reads it and the moment that thread acts on it. The window is the gap between read and write, and closing that gap is the whole job.

Okay, explain how a CPU cache speeds up a program, in plain White/Orwell register.

A CPU runs at four gigahertz. Main memory runs at three hundred megahertz. The processor can execute billions of instructions per second, but fetching data from DRAM takes roughly one hundred nanoseconds — two hundred forty cycles where the core sits idle, waiting for a number to cross the bus.

The cache closes that gap. It is a small block of SRAM built onto the processor die, six to twelve nanoseconds from the execution units. A cache hit returns data in three or four cycles. A cache miss falls back to main memory and pays the full two hundred forty.

Caches work because programs do not access memory at random. They access it in patterns. A loop that sums an array reads element zero, then element one, then element two. A function that calls `sqrt` will probably call it again soon. The first is spatial locality: touched addresses sit near each other. The second is temporal locality: a touched address will probably be touched again. The cache exploits both.

The hardware loads data in blocks, not bytes. A cache line is sixty-four bytes on most x86 and ARM processors. When the CPU reads address 0x1000, it pulls the entire line — 0x1000 through 0x103F — into the cache. The next read at 0x1004 hits the line already in the cache and returns in three cycles instead of one hundred. The program did not ask for those extra bytes. The cache guessed it would, and the guess is right often enough to matter.

The cache sits in levels. L1 is smallest and closest: thirty-two kilobytes, two or three cycles, one for instructions and one for data.
