L2 is larger and one step farther: two hundred fifty-six kilobytes to one megabyte, ten to twelve cycles. L3 is largest and shared across cores: eight to thirty-two megabytes, thirty to forty cycles. A request checks L1, then L2, then L3, then main memory. Each miss costs more time, and the average access time depends on how often the request stops at each level.

The hit rate determines the speedup. A program whose working set — the data it touches in a tight loop — fits in L1 runs at full speed. The same program on a working set three times the L1 size misses on most accesses and spends most of its time stalled. This is why an algorithm that touches memory sequentially can beat one that does less computation but jumps across the heap: the sequential version stays in cache, the jumping version does not.

The replacement policy decides what stays when the cache is full. Most processors use a variant of least-recently-used: when a new line arrives and the cache has no room, the hardware evicts the line that went longest without a read. LRU bets that data not touched recently will not be touched soon, and it loses badly on patterns that stream through memory faster than the cache can hold — a loop scanning a hundred-megabyte array evicts every line it loads, because each line is touched once and never again.

Cache misses come in three kinds. A compulsory miss is the first read of a line; the data was never in the cache, so it must be fetched. A capacity miss happens when the working set exceeds the cache size and lines are evicted before the program finishes with them. A conflict miss happens when the cache's mapping scheme forces multiple addresses to the same set, evicting lines that the program still needs even though the cache has room elsewhere. Direct-mapped caches, where each address maps to exactly one line, suffer conflict misses. Set-associative caches, where each address maps to a small group of lines, reduce them at the cost of more hardware.

The cache turns slow main memory into fast local storage by betting on the program's own patterns. When the bet wins, the processor runs at full speed. When it loses, the processor waits. Writing code that respects those patterns — sequential access, small working sets, data laid out so related fields sit on the same cache line — is the difference between a program that runs at four gigahertz and one that runs at three hundred megahertz.

Okay, explain what idempotency means for an HTTP API, in plain White/Orwell register.

Idempotency means a client can send the same request twice and the server ends in the same state as if it had been sent once. The second call does not duplicate the first. It does not charge the card twice, create two rows, or append a second record. It either repeats the original result or returns the current state, but the effect on the server is unchanged.

HTTP defines this in RFC 9110. The methods `GET`, `PUT`, `DELETE`, and `HEAD` are idempotent. `POST` and `PATCH` are not. The distinction is not about safety — `DELETE` is idempotent and it destroys data. The distinction is about repetition. Sending `DELETE /users/42` once removes the user. Sending it again finds no user at 42 and returns 404, but the server state is the same as after the first call: no user 42. The resource is gone either way.

`PUT` is idempotent because it replaces a resource wholesale. `PUT /users/42` with a body sets user 42 to exactly that body. Send it ten times and user 42 holds the same values after the tenth as after the first. `POST /users` with the same body creates a new user each time, because `POST` appends rather than replaces. Ten calls produce ten users with ten different IDs. That is the failure mode idempotency exists to prevent.

Networks retry. A client sends `POST /payments`, the server processes it, the response drops on the floor, and the client does not know whether the payment succeeded. It sends the request again. Without an idempotency mechanism, the server charges the customer twice. The problem is not the server's logic. The problem is that the server cannot tell the second request from the first.

The fix is an idempotency key. The client generates a unique token — a UUID — and sends it in a header, conventionally `Idempotency-Key`. The server stores the key on first receipt, processes the request, and persists the response. On the second request with the same key, the server returns the stored response without reprocessing. Stripe's API documents this pattern in detail: the key is stored for twenty-four hours, and a repeat request within that window returns the original result verbatim, including the original status code and body.

The key makes `POST` behave like `PUT` for a given request. The server treats the key as the resource identifier and the request body as the replacement. A second arrival with the same key is not a new operation. It is a retransmission of the old one, and the server answers from its record rather than from its logic.

Idempotency has a boundary. The server state is unchanged only with respect to the resource the request targets. A `DELETE /users/42` that also logs an audit entry appends one log row per call, and the log grows. The method is still idempotent by the HTTP definition because the target resource — user 42 — reaches the same state. The side effect on the log is outside the contract. An API that promises end-to-end idempotency, including side effects, must handle those separately, and the idempotency key is the mechanism for that scope.

The practical value is resilience. A client that can retry without fear of duplicate effects can treat the network as unreliable and still deliver exactly-once semantics to the user. The server absorbs the duplication, deduplicates by key, and returns a consistent answer. Without it, the client must guess whether the first call landed, and guessing wrong costs money.

Okay, explain how DNS resolves a hostname to an IP address, in plain White/Orwell register.

A browser asks for `example.com`. The operating system hands that name to a resolver, and the resolver asks a chain of servers until one of them returns an address.

The chain starts at the root. The root servers hold the addresses of the top-level domain servers for every suffix — `.com`, `.org`, `.net`, the country codes. There are thirteen root server addresses, served by over a thousand physical instances scattered across the world, and the resolver picks one by proximity.

The resolver asks the root server for `example.com`. The root server does not know the address. It knows only the `.com` servers. It returns those addresses — a referral, not an answer. The resolver takes the referral and asks a `.com` server the same question.

The `.com` server does not know the address either. It knows the authoritative servers for `example.com` — the name servers that the domain's owner configured when registering the domain. It returns those addresses. The resolver asks one of them.

The authoritative server holds the actual record. It reads the zone file for `example.com`, finds the A record, and returns `93.184.216.34`. The resolver caches that answer for the record's time-to-live — the number of seconds the owner permits the cache to hold it — and hands the address to the operating system, which hands it to the browser.

The full walk is three round trips: root, top-level, authoritative. Each adds latency. A resolver in New York asking a root server in Virginia, a `.com` server in Chicago, and an authoritative server in Frankfurt pays roughly 20 ms, 15 ms, and 80 ms, and the page does not load until the last one returns.

Caching collapses those trips. The operating system caches the answer. The browser caches it. The resolver caches it. A second request for `example.com` within the TTL window returns from the resolver's cache in under a millisecond, and no server upstream sees the question. The root servers see roughly a thousand queries per second each, a number that has stayed flat for years despite traffic growth, because caching absorbs nearly everything.

The resolver is the only piece the client controls. Most machines use the resolver provided by the ISP or a public resolver like Google's `8.8.8.8` or Cloudflare's `1.1.1.1`. The resolver performs the three-step walk on the client's behalf, caches the result, and serves subsequent requests from cache. It is the middleman, and the cache is what makes the system scale.

DNS runs over UDP port 53. A query is a single packet, and a response is a single packet, so the round trip costs one network delay rather than the handshake-and-data sequence that TCP requires. A response larger than 512 bytes — common with DNSSEC signatures — switches to TCP, and the protocol negotiates that switch with a flag in the UDP response.

The system turns a name into an address by asking a hierarchy of servers, each of which knows only the next step down. The root points to `.com`. The `.com` server points to the authoritative server. The authoritative server holds the record. Caching at every level keeps the walk from happening twice.

A deadlock is a state where two threads each hold a resource the other needs, and neither will give up what it holds. Both wait forever. The program freezes.

Thread A locks file one. Thread B locks file two. Thread A asks for file two. Thread B asks for file one. Thread A waits for B. Thread B waits for A. The cycle closes and neither moves.

The four conditions were named by Coffman in 1971. Mutual exclusion: a resource belongs to one thread at a time. Hold and wait: a thread holds one resource while asking for another. No preemption: the system will not force a release. Circular wait: a ring of threads each holds what the next one needs. Break any one and deadlock cannot happen.

Lock ordering breaks the circular wait. Every thread acquires locks in the same sequence. If the rule is "file one before file two," thread B cannot lock file two first. It must ask for file one, stall behind thread A, and only then take file two. Thread A finishes, releases both, and thread B proceeds. The ring never forms.

The cost is rigidity. A function deep in the call stack cannot grab a lock out of order without knowing which locks the caller already holds. The ordering convention must thread through every layer of the program, and a single violation reintroduces the deadlock the rule was built to prevent.

A hash map turns a key into an integer, then uses that integer as an index into an array of buckets. The hash function spreads keys across the array; the map stores each key-value pair in the bucket the hash points to.

Two keys can hash to the same index. That is a collision, and every hash map has to handle it, because the array has fewer slots than the hash function has possible outputs.

Two strategies dominate. **Chaining** stores a linked list (or a small array, or a tree) at each bucket. When a key lands on an occupied bucket, the map walks the list, compares keys, and either updates the matching pair or appends a new node. Lookups in that bucket degrade to a linear scan of the list. If the hash distributes keys evenly, each list stays short and the scan stays cheap. If many keys collide on one bucket, the list grows and that one bucket slows down.

**Open addressing** stores all pairs in the array itself. When a key's bucket is taken, the map probes a sequence of alternative slots — next index, index plus a quadratic offset, index doubled and rehashed — until it finds an empty one. Lookups follow the same probe sequence until they hit the key or an empty slot. Deletion is harder: removing a pair and leaving a hole would break the probe chain, so the map marks the slot as a tombstone, a slot that is empty for insertion but still occupied for probing. Tombstones accumulate and slow lookups until the map rehashes.

Both strategies share a failure mode. As the load factor — the ratio of stored pairs to array slots — rises, collisions multiply. Chained lists lengthen; probe sequences stretch. Most maps hold a threshold, commonly 0.75, and when the load crosses it, the map allocates a larger array, rehashes every key into its new position, and discards the old array. That rehash is O(n) but amortized across insertions, so individual operations stay near O(1) on average. Worst case, every key collides into one bucket, and every operation degrades to O(n) regardless of strategy.

A database index is a second data structure stored alongside a table. It trades disk space and write speed for read speed.

The structure is usually a B-tree. The tree sorts the values of one or more columns and pairs each value with a pointer to the row that holds it. To find the rows where `last_name` is `Smith`, the database walks the tree to `Smith` and follows the pointers. Without the index, it reads every row in the table and checks each one. On a million-row table, the index turns a million reads into a handful.

The cost is paid on every write. An insert, update, or delete that touches an indexed column must also update the tree. The tree must stay sorted, so a write can split a node and shift data on disk. Three indexes on a table triple that maintenance work. A table that takes a thousand inserts per second with no indexes might sustain three hundred with four indexes in place.

An index also hurts when the query never uses it. A query that filters on `last_name` gains nothing from an index on `email`. The database still scans the full table, and the index sits on disk, consuming space and slowing writes for no benefit. Multi-column indexes carry the same trap: an index on `(last_name, first_name)` serves queries that filter on `last_name`, but a query that filters only on `first_name` cannot use it, because the tree is sorted by `last_name` first.

The clearest case where an index hurts is a small table. If a table fits in a few disk pages, a full scan reads those pages in one pass. The index adds a tree walk and a pointer chase, which is more work than the scan it was meant to avoid. Indexing a 500-row lookup table wastes write capacity and buys nothing back.

A table with many indexes and heavy write traffic slows down at the insert point before any read ever benefits. The database spends its time maintaining trees instead of accepting rows. The fix is not more indexes; it is fewer, chosen for the queries that actually run.

TCP sends data as a stream of numbered bytes, not as discrete messages. Each byte gets a sequence number. The first byte the connection sends carries an initial sequence number agreed during the handshake; every byte after increments by one.

A sender transmits segments, each labeled with the sequence number of its first byte. Segments can take different network paths and arrive out of order. Segment 200 might reach the receiver before segment 100.

The receiver uses the sequence number on each segment to place the bytes back in order. It holds arriving bytes in a receive buffer and delivers them to the application only in contiguous order from the lowest unreceived byte forward. If bytes 100 through 199 are present but byte 99 is missing, the receiver holds 100 through 199 and waits.

For every segment that arrives, the receiver sends an acknowledgment back. The acknowledgment carries the sequence number of the next byte the receiver expects — the lowest byte not yet received. An ACK of 300 means bytes 1 through 299 are in place and the receiver wants 300 next. This is cumulative: one ACK confirms everything up to that number, even if earlier segments arrived out of order.

If a segment is lost, the receiver keeps acknowledging the last contiguous byte it has. The sender sees the same ACK repeated and infers the loss. It retransmits the missing segment. When that segment arrives, the receiver fills the gap, advances its contiguous window, and sends a single ACK for everything now in place.

The receive buffer has a fixed size, and the receiver advertises that size in the TCP header as the window. The sender cannot push more unacknowledged data than the window allows, which keeps the buffer from overflowing and forcing drops that would break ordering.

Sequence numbers are 32-bit and wrap after 4,294,967,295 bytes. TCP handles the wrap by comparing sequence numbers modularly, so a low number after a high one still reads as "later" within the current window.

A mutex protects one thing: shared memory seen by more than one thread.

Two threads run the same code at the same time. Both read a balance of 100. Both subtract 10. Both write 90. The balance should be 80. It is 90. One withdrawal vanished. That is a data race, and a mutex is the standard fix.

The mutex is a lock with two states, locked and unlocked. Before a thread touches the shared data, it calls `lock`. If the mutex is already locked, the thread blocks — the operating system parks it until the mutex frees. When the thread that holds the lock calls `unlock`, the scheduler wakes one of the waiting threads and hands it the lock.

The result is serialization. The section of code between `lock` and `unlock` — the critical section — runs on one thread at a time. The second thread cannot enter until the first exits. The lost update cannot happen, because the read, the subtract, and the write complete as one indivisible step.

A mutex does not protect against everything. It does not protect memory that no thread shares. It does not protect against deadlocks, which it creates: two threads each holding one mutex and waiting for the other's will stop forever. It does not protect against priority inversion, where a low-priority thread holds a lock a high-priority thread needs, blocking the high thread behind it. It does not make operations atomic across multiple locks; it guards one scope at a time.

The mutex protects the data inside the critical section and nothing outside it. The discipline is: lock, touch the shared data, unlock. Hold the lock for the shortest time possible. Never hold two locks at once unless the order is fixed and agreed. The protection is mechanical, but it depends on the programmer drawing the boundary in the right place.

A program allocates memory for objects it creates. It cannot free that memory while any part of the program can still reach it. Garbage collection is the process of finding which objects are no longer reachable and returning their memory to the heap.

The collector starts from a fixed set of roots: the registers on the CPU stack, the local variables in each thread's call stack, and the global variables the program holds for its entire run. These are the things the program can touch directly. Everything reachable from a root, by following pointers through fields and array elements, is live. Everything not reachable is garbage.

The tracing collector walks that graph. It marks every object it reaches. When the walk finishes, the heap holds two kinds of objects: marked and unmarked. The marked objects are live. The unmarked objects are garbage. The collector sweeps the unmarked objects and returns their space.

That is mark-and-sweep, and it leaves the heap fragmented. Free space is scattered among surviving objects, so a large allocation may fail even when enough total free space exists. A compacting collector fixes this by sliding the marked objects to one end of the heap, leaving a single contiguous free block. The collector must rewrite every pointer that moved, which adds work but removes fragmentation.

A copying collector splits the heap into two halves. The program allocates in one half. When that half fills, the collector copies every reachable object from the full half to the empty half, packing them tightly. The old half becomes the new free space. This approach compacts for free, because the copy itself is the compaction. It costs half the heap, since only one half is usable at a time.

The cost of tracing is proportional to the number of live objects. A program with ten million live objects pays to trace all ten million, even if it freed only a thousand. Generational collection cuts that cost by exploiting a pattern: most objects die young. The collector divides the heap into generations. New objects go in the young generation. The collector traces the young generation frequently and the old generation rarely. An object that survives several young-generation collections moves to the old generation, where it is traced less often.

The hard part is the roots. A register or stack slot can hold a pointer that the collector must find, but the hardware does not tag it as a pointer. The collector must know which stack slots and registers hold pointers and which hold integers. A conservative collector treats any value that could be a pointer as one, which is safe but can keep dead objects alive if an integer happens to match a heap address. A precise collector knows exactly where the pointers are, which requires the compiler to record that information at every point in the code where collection can run.

The collector must also stop the program from changing the graph while it traces. Most collectors pause every thread, trace, then resume. The pause length grows with the number of live objects and the depth of the pointer graph. Concurrent collectors trace while the program runs, which shortens the pause but adds complexity: the program can move an object the collector has already visited, so the collector must track changes to the graph during the trace.

A race condition is a bug where the outcome depends on the order in which two operations run, and that order is not controlled.

A bank account holds 100. Two threads each withdraw 10 at the same time. The first thread reads the balance: 100. The second thread reads the balance: 100. The first thread subtracts 10 and writes 90. The second thread subtracts 10 and writes 90. The balance should be 80. It is 90. One withdrawal is gone.

The operations are not atomic. A read, a subtract, and a write are three steps, and the scheduler can pause a thread between any of them. The second thread read a value the first thread was about to overwrite. That stale value became the basis for the second write, and the first write disappeared.

The name comes from the threads racing for the same data. Neither knows the other touched it. The bug is nondeterministic: run the same code a thousand times and the balance might be 80 on 999 runs and 90 on one. That makes race conditions hard to reproduce and hard to debug. A test that passes a million times does not prove the race cannot happen.

The fix is to make the read, the subtract, and the write one indivisible step. A mutex around the withdrawal serializes the two threads: the second cannot read until the first has written. An atomic operation does the same at the hardware level, combining the steps into a single instruction the CPU will not interrupt. Either way, the second thread sees 90, subtracts 10, and writes 80.

Race conditions are not limited to memory. Two processes writing to the same file can interleave their writes and corrupt the record. Two requests to a cache can both find it empty, both fetch the same value from the database, and both write it back, wasting the work. The shared element is uncontrolled access to a resource whose correct state depends on the full sequence completing before another sequence begins.

A CPU runs a thousand times faster than the memory it talks to. A modern processor can execute several instructions in a single nanosecond, but fetching a value from main memory takes a hundred nanoseconds or more. The processor spends most of its time waiting. A cache closes that gap.

The cache is a small block of fast memory built into the CPU chip. It sits between the processor cores and main memory, and it holds copies of the data and instructions the processor is most likely to need next. Reading from the cache takes one to three nanoseconds instead of a hundred.

The cache works because programs do not access memory at random. They access it in patterns. A loop that sums an array reads element 0, then element 1, then element 2, in order. A function that executes one instruction tends to execute the next one right after it. The cache exploits two patterns: spatial locality, the tendency to touch nearby memory, and temporal locality, the tendency to touch the same memory again soon.

When the CPU requests a byte from memory, the cache does not fetch one byte. It fetches a block — typically 64 bytes — called a cache line. The requested byte arrives with its 63 neighbors. If the program reads the array sequentially, the next seven 8-byte values are already in the cache. The processor gets them in two nanoseconds instead of waiting a hundred for each one.

The cache checks every memory request against the lines it holds. If the requested address is present, that is a cache hit, and the CPU reads from the cache. If the address is absent, that is a cache miss, and the CPU fetches the line from main memory, writes it into the cache, and delivers the byte. The hit rate determines the speedup. A program with a 95 percent hit rate spends most of its time reading from the cache and rarely waits for memory.

Caches are organized in levels. The L1 cache is smallest and fastest, usually 32 to 64 kilobytes, one or two nanoseconds away, one per core. The L2 cache is larger, 256 kilobytes to a megabyte, around ten nanoseconds, also per core. The L3 cache is shared across all cores, several megabytes to tens of megabytes, around 40 nanoseconds. Main memory sits behind all three at a hundred or more. A request misses L1, checks L2, misses, checks L3, misses, and goes to memory. Each miss adds latency.

The cache is finite, so it must evict. When a new line arrives and the cache is full, the controller picks an old line to remove. The common policy is least-recently-used: the line that has gone longest without a read gets replaced. A program that streams through a large array once, never revisiting a byte, fills the cache and evicts every line it loaded. Each access misses. The cache buys nothing, because the access pattern has no temporal locality. A program that works on a small block of data repeatedly hits the same lines and runs at cache speed.

The practical consequence is that two algorithms with the same big-O complexity can run at very different speeds. A loop that strides through memory sequentially hits the cache on every element. A loop that jumps across a linked list, following pointers to scattered addresses, misses on every node. Both are O(n), but the sequential loop runs ten or twenty times faster, because the cache line prefetch turns each miss into seven hits. The algorithm that respects the cache line size wins, and the one that chases pointers waits for memory.

Okay: explain idempotency as it applies to HTTP APIs, in plain register.

An HTTP request is idempotent when sending it once produces the same result as sending it any number of times. The server's observable state after the first request is the state it holds after every repeat. A client can retry the request without changing the outcome beyond what the first call already did.

`GET` is the straightforward case. It reads a resource and changes nothing, so ten identical `GET` requests return the same representation and leave the server in the same state. `PUT` is idempotent by contract. A `PUT` to `/users/42` with a body of `{"name": "Ada"}` sets user 42's name to Ada. Sending it again sets the name to Ada again. The second request overwrites the first, and the resource ends in the same place. `DELETE` is idempotent because the operation is "remove this resource." The first call deletes it. The second call finds nothing to delete, but the resource is still gone, which is the state the first call produced.

`POST` is the one that breaks idempotency. A `POST` to `/users` with `{"name": "Ada"}` creates a new user. Sending it again creates a second user. Each call appends a row, and the server's state diverges with every retry. `POST` is not idempotent because its semantics are "process this," not "set this."

The distinction matters when a call fails mid-flight. A client sends a `PUT`, the server applies it, and the response drops on the network. The client does not know whether the request landed. With `PUT`, it resends. The server applies the same value, the state is correct, and no harm is done. With `POST`, the client faces a trap. Resend, and the server might create a second order, charge the card twice, send the email again. The state after a retry is not the state after one call.

The fix for non-idempotent operations is an idempotency key. The client sends a unique identifier in a header, and the server records it alongside the first request's result. On a retry with the same key, the server finds the recorded result and returns it without reprocessing. The operation becomes idempotent by contract, not by method. The server must store the key, check it before processing, and return the original response on a match. The key turns a retry-unsafe `POST` into a retry-safe one, at the cost of server-side storage and a lookup on every call.

Idempotency is a property of the operation, not the method label. A `DELETE` that decrements a counter on each call is not idempotent, even though `DELETE` is supposed to be. A `POST` guarded by an idempotency key is idempotent, even though `POST` is not. The contract is what the server does on a repeat, and the HTTP method is only the default that contract starts from.

DNS turns a name into an address by walking a tree of servers, each one answering a narrower question than the last.

A browser asks the operating system's resolver for `www.example.com`. The resolver is usually a program run by the ISP or a service like 1.1.1.1, and it does the actual work. The browser itself never talks to the DNS hierarchy directly.

The resolver does not know `www.example.com`. It knows where the root servers are. The root servers sit at the top of the DNS tree, and there are thirteen of them, identified by the letters A through M. The resolver asks one of them for `www.example.com`.

The root server does not know the address either. It knows which servers hold the top-level domains — the `.com` servers, the `.org` servers, the country-code servers. It hands the resolver a list of the `.com` servers and says, ask them.

The resolver asks a `.com` server for `www.example.com`. The `.com` server does not know the address. It knows which servers hold the `example.com` zone, the authoritative servers for that domain. It hands the resolver their addresses.

The resolver asks the `example.com` authoritative server for `www.example.com`. This server holds the actual record. It reads the A record for `www`, finds the IPv4 address `93.184.216.34`, and returns it. The resolver caches that answer for the time-to-live the record specifies, then hands the address to the operating system, which hands it to the browser. The browser opens a TCP connection to that address.

Four servers touched, three round trips. The root, the top-level domain, the authoritative server, and the resolver's own cache. The cache is what makes the system bearable. Without it, every page load would trigger the full walk. With it, the resolver answers most queries from memory, and the root servers see a fraction of the traffic they otherwise would.

The system is hierarchical because the names are. `www.example.com` reads right to left: the root, then `.com`, then `example`, then `www`. Each server delegates the left part to the server below it. No single server holds the whole map. Each holds one zone and points to the next.

Okay: explain deadlock, concretely, and one avoidance method.

Two threads each need two locks to finish their work. Thread A takes lock 1, then waits for lock 2. Thread B takes lock 2, then waits for lock 1. A holds what B needs. B holds what A needs. Neither lets go. Both wait forever. That is a deadlock.

The deadlock needs four conditions, all present at once: resources that cannot be shared, threads holding resources while waiting for more, resources that cannot be taken by force, and a circular chain of waits. Break any one and the deadlock cannot form.

The simplest break is a lock ordering rule. Every thread acquires locks in the same sequence. If the rule is "lock 1 before lock 2," thread A takes lock 1, then lock 2. Thread B takes lock 1, then lock 2. Thread B cannot take lock 2 until thread A releases lock 1, so the circular wait never closes. One thread waits, the other finishes and frees both, the waiter proceeds.

The rule costs nothing at runtime. It costs discipline at design time: every lock acquisition in the program must follow the global order, and a new lock added out of order reintroduces the deadlock the rule was meant to prevent.

A hash map turns a key into an integer, then uses that integer as an index into an array. When two keys produce the same index, the map has a collision, and every implementation has to pick a policy for it.

The oldest policy is **chaining**. Each slot in the array holds the head of a linked list. A key that hashes to slot 4 gets appended to the list at slot 4; a lookup walks that list comparing keys until it finds the match or reaches the end. The cost of a lookup is therefore the cost of hashing plus the cost of walking one list, and that list length is the load factor — the ratio of stored entries to array slots. At a load factor of 0.75, the average list holds under one element, and lookups stay near constant time. If the load factor climbs and the lists grow, the map resizes: it allocates a larger array, re-hashes every entry into it, and discards the old one. Java's `HashMap` and C++'s `std::unordered_map` both chain.

The second policy is **open addressing**. There is no list; the entry lives in the array itself. A key that hashes to slot 4 finds it occupied, so the map applies a **probe sequence** to check the next candidate slot, and the next, until it finds either an empty slot or the matching key. The simplest sequence is linear probing: check slot 4, then 5, then 6. Linear probing is cache-friendly — the CPU's prefetcher pulls consecutive memory lines — but it suffers from **primary clustering**, where a long run of occupied slots grows longer with every collision, because any key landing anywhere inside the run extends it. Quadratic probing jumps by squares (1, 4, 9…) to break up clusters, but can cycle without visiting every slot unless the table size is prime. Double hashing uses a second hash function to set the step size, which spreads entries more evenly but costs a second hash per probe. Python's `dict`, Ruby's `Hash`, and Rust's `std::collections::HashMap` all use open addressing.

The choice between the two policies is a trade between memory locality and degradation behavior. Chaining tolerates high load factors gracefully because extra entries just lengthen lists; open addressing degrades sharply as the array fills, because a nearly full table forces long probe runs before any empty slot appears. But chaining follows a pointer on every collision, which means a cache miss per list node, while open addressing keeps the probe walk inside the array's contiguous memory. For small entries that fit in a cache line, open addressing is faster in practice; for large entries or values that are expensive to move, chaining avoids the resize-time cost of copying them.

One detail separates the two on deletion. In a chained map, removing a key means unlinking its node — the slot is still available to any other key in the list. In an open-addressed map, simply clearing the slot would break probe sequences that jumped past it: a later lookup that hits the cleared slot would stop, concluding the key is absent, when it actually sits further down the probe run. Open-addressed maps solve this with a **tombstone**: the deleted slot is marked as "was occupied, now vacant," so a probe sequence can skip past it while a new insertion can reclaim it. Python's `dict` avoids tombstones by rebuilding on resize rather than marking; linear-probing tables like Go's `map` use tombstones explicitly.

The load factor is the single number that governs all of this. Below it, both policies deliver near-constant lookups. Above it, chaining pays in list walks and open addressing pays in probe lengths, and the map's response is the same in both cases: grow the array and rehash.

A database index is a second data structure stored alongside a table to make reads fast. Without one, finding rows that match a condition requires scanning every row from the first to the last. With one, the database follows a pointer straight to the matching rows. The index is usually a B-tree, which keeps its entries sorted, so the database can binary-search rather than scan.

The cost is storage and write time. Every index is a copy of part of the table, sorted and stored on disk. A table with five indexes holds six sorted copies of its data. An `INSERT` that wrote one row now writes six: one to the table, five to the indexes, each in its sorted position. A `DELETE` or `UPDATE` that touches an indexed column touches every index on that column too. On a table that takes 10,000 writes per second, five indexes can turn that into 60,000 writes per second.

An index hurts when the database cannot use it, or when it serves a query that did not need it. A query like `SELECT * FROM orders` has no filter, so no index helps; the database scans the table, and every index on it sits unused, collecting write overhead for nothing. A query like `WHERE LOWER(name) = 'alice'` wraps the indexed column in a function, and most engines cannot use the index on `name` because the function changes the sort order the index relies on. The index exists, the database pays to maintain it, and the query still scans.

An index also hurts when two of them compete. A query that filters on `last_name` and `first_name` can use one index or the other, but not both in a single pass. The optimizer picks one, filters the rows it returns, and discards the second index's work. A composite index on `(last_name, first_name)` serves the query in one pass; two single-column indexes serve it in one pass plus wasted maintenance.

The decision is a trade between read speed and write cost. An index on a column that appears in a `WHERE` clause on a table with a billion rows turns a full scan into a few disk reads. An index on a column that no query filters on turns every insert into extra work for no return. The first earns its keep. The second is dead weight that slows the writes it was supposed to protect.

TCP sends data as a stream of numbered bytes, not as a sequence of independent messages. The sender attaches a **sequence number** to the first byte in every segment it transmits — a 32-bit counter that identifies that byte's position in the overall stream. Segment 471 carries bytes 1000 through 1099; segment 472 carries bytes 1100 through 1199. The numbers are byte positions, not segment counts.

The network can deliver these segments out of order. Segment 472 can arrive before segment 471 because it took a different route, or because 471 was delayed at a congested router. The receiver's job is to reconstruct the original byte stream despite that disorder, and it uses the sequence numbers to do so.

The receiver holds incoming segments in a buffer and sorts them by sequence number. If segment 472 arrives first, the receiver stores it but does not pass it to the application. It waits for 471. When 471 arrives, the receiver places it ahead of 472, confirms to the sender that it has received all bytes through 1099, and only then delivers the contiguous run to the application. The application never sees a gap.

That confirmation is the **acknowledgment number**. The receiver's reply carries the sequence number of the next byte it expects, which is also the first byte it has not yet received. An ack of 1100 tells the sender: bytes 1000 through 1099 arrived in order and were delivered. An ack of 1000 tells the sender: 471 is still missing, and nothing past it has been delivered, even if 472 and 473 are already sitting in the buffer.

A missing segment stalls the stream at the gap. Segments that arrived early wait in the buffer, held in sequence-number order, until the missing one fills the hole. Once it does, the receiver delivers the entire contiguous block to the application in one pass and advances the acknowledgment number past it. The application receives bytes in the order the sender wrote them, regardless of the order the network delivered them.

A mutex protects one thing: the interleaving of reads and writes across threads that share memory.

Two threads running on separate cores can each touch the same variable at the same instant. Thread A reads `balance`, adds 100, writes it back. Thread B reads `balance` in the gap between A's read and A's write, adds 50, writes it back. A's write is lost. The final balance is 50 short, and neither thread did anything wrong in isolation — the fault is in the overlap.

The mutex makes the read-and-write indivisible. A thread that wants `balance` calls `lock` on the mutex guarding it. Any other thread that calls `lock` on the same mutex blocks — it stops running and waits. The first thread reads, adds, writes, then calls `unlock`. The second thread wakes, acquires the mutex, and performs its own read-and-write against the value the first thread left behind. The two operations no longer overlap; they run one after the other.

What the mutex does not protect against is everything else. It does not make a single read or write atomic on its own — a bare `x = x + 1` on a 64-bit value is already atomic on most architectures, and a mutex around it adds overhead for nothing. It does not protect against reentrancy from the same thread if the mutex is not recursive — a thread that locks twice without unlocking deadlocks against itself. It does not protect data that is reached through a copied pointer or a cloned reference, because the copy lives outside the mutex's scope and another thread can touch it freely.

The mutex also does not compose without care. Thread A locks mutex 1 then mutex 2. Thread B locks mutex 2 then mutex 1. Each holds one and waits for the other. This is deadlock, and it is a property of the locking order, not of the mutex itself. The fix is a global ordering — every thread acquires mutexes in the same sequence — and that ordering is a discipline the programmer imposes, not something the mutex enforces.

A mutex guards the gap between a read and a write on shared memory, and nothing beyond it. It turns overlap into sequence. The cost is a blocked thread and the obligation to get the locking order right.

Garbage collection finds memory the program no longer reaches. The program allocates objects as it runs, holds references to them through variables and fields, and discards those references when it moves on. The collector's job is to find the objects whose references are gone and reclaim their space. It does this by tracing reachability from a fixed set of roots.

The **roots** are the entry points: the CPU's registers, the call stack of every running thread, and the global or static variables the program can name. An object is **reachable** if a path of references leads from a root to it. An object is **unreachable** if no such path exists. The collector walks the reference graph starting at the roots, marks every object it encounters, and treats every unmarked object as garbage. This is **mark-and-sweep**, the baseline algorithm from which the others descend.

The walk is a graph traversal. The collector reads each root, follows the pointer it holds to an object, follows that object's fields to the objects it references, and so on, marking each one. When the walk finishes, every object that survived has a mark. The collector then sweeps the heap: it scans every allocated object, frees the unmarked ones, and clears the marks on the rest for the next cycle. The cost is proportional to the live objects plus the total heap.

Mark-and-sweep fragments the heap over time. Freed objects leave holes of varying size, and new allocations must fit into them or fail. **Compacting** collectors solve this by moving the surviving objects together into one contiguous block after the mark phase, leaving the rest of the heap as a single free range. Moving objects requires updating every reference to them, so the collector maintains a mapping from old addresses to new ones and rewrites the roots and the surviving objects' fields. The JVM's serial and parallel collectors compact; Go's GC does not.

**Copying** collection makes compaction the default. It splits the heap into two halves, **from-space** and **to-space**. The program allocates in from-space. When it fills, the collector copies every reachable object from from-space into to-space, packing them together, then flips the two halves. The new to-space (the old from-space) is now empty and ready for the next cycle. Dead objects never move; they are simply overwritten on the next flip. The cost is proportional to the live objects only, because the collector never touches the garbage. The trade is that half the heap is always unused, waiting to receive the copy.

The pause this work creates is the problem every production collector tries to solve. A stop-the-world collector halts every thread at the start of a cycle, traces and sweeps or copies, then resumes them. The pause length scales with the live set and the heap size. On a heap of several gigabytes, a full mark-and-sweep pause can stop the program for hundreds of milliseconds.

**Concurrent** collectors trace the graph while the program runs, rather than stopping it. The difficulty is that the program mutates the graph during the trace: it can move a reference from an object the collector already marked to one it has not reached, hiding the target from the walk. Concurrent collectors solve this with a **write barrier** — a small piece of code the runtime inserts at every reference write, which records the mutation so the collector can revisit the affected object. Go's collector uses a write barrier to catch pointers stored into already-marked objects during the concurrent mark phase, which lets it run with sub-millisecond pauses on heaps of tens of gigabytes.

**Generational** collectors exploit the observation that most objects die young. A freshly allocated object is far more likely to be unreachable by the next cycle than an object that has survived ten cycles. The collector divides the heap into a **young generation** and an **old generation**, and collects the young one far more often. A young-generation collection scans only the young objects and the roots, which is a small set, so it finishes fast. Objects that survive several young-generation collections are **promoted** to the old generation, which the collector scans less frequently. The JVM's G1 and ZGC are generational; Go's is not.

**Reference counting** is a different approach that does not trace at all. Every object carries a count of the references pointing to it. A new reference increments the count; a dropped reference decrements it. When the count hits zero, the object is unreachable and the collector frees it immediately, no graph walk required. The cost is spread across every pointer assignment rather than concentrated in a pause. The failure mode is **cycles**: two objects that reference each other keep each other's count above zero forever, even if no root reaches either. A reference-counting collector needs a separate cycle detector to find and break these, or it leaks them. CPython uses reference counting plus a cycle detector; Swift and Objective-C use reference counting without one, which is why Swift's documentation forbids strong reference cycles.

The core idea across all of these is the same. The collector distinguishes memory the program can still reach from memory it cannot, and reclaims the latter. The variations trade pause time against throughput, memory overhead against speed, and collection frequency against promptness. The program allocates; the collector reclaims; the heap stays bounded.

A race condition is a bug that appears only when the timing of two operations lands a certain way. Two threads share a variable. Each reads it, changes it, and writes it back. If the reads and writes interleave, one thread's write overwrites the other's, and a value disappears.

A bank account holds 100. Two threads each withdraw 40. Thread A reads the balance: 100. Thread B reads the balance: 100. Thread A subtracts 40, writes 60. Thread B subtracts 40, writes 60. The account lost 40. Both threads followed the correct steps in isolation; the fault is in the overlap. The read-modify-write sequence is not atomic, and nothing forced the two threads to take turns.

The balance is the shared state. The gap between the read and the write is the race window. Any thread that reads the old value inside that window produces a stale write, and the last write wins. The outcome depends on which thread the scheduler ran first, and the scheduler's choice is not something the program controls.

The fix is to close the window. A mutex around the read-modify-write block makes the sequence indivisible: the second thread cannot read until the first unlocks. An atomic instruction like compare-and-swap does the same without a lock, by having the hardware refuse the write if the value changed since the read. Either way, the two operations no longer overlap, and the balance stops depending on timing.

A CPU cache is a small amount of fast memory sitting between the processor and main memory. Main memory holds everything the program needs, but it is slow — a read takes roughly 100 nanoseconds, which is hundreds of clock cycles. The cache holds a copy of the data the processor is most likely to need next, and a read from cache takes one to three nanoseconds, which is a handful of cycles. The cache speeds the program up by serving most reads from that fast copy instead of from main memory.

The cache works because programs do not access memory at random. They access it in patterns, and the two strongest patterns are **temporal locality** and **spatial locality**. Temporal locality is the tendency of a program to touch the same address repeatedly within a short window: a loop counter is read and written on every iteration. Spatial locality is the tendency to touch nearby addresses in sequence: an array processed element by element moves forward through contiguous memory. The cache exploits both. It keeps recently accessed data for temporal locality, and it pulls data in **cache lines** — blocks of 64 bytes on most x86 and ARM processors — so that reading one address also loads the 63 bytes adjacent to it, betting the program will touch those next.

When the processor reads an address, it checks the cache first. A **cache hit** means the address is there, and the read completes in a few cycles. A **cache miss** means it is not, and the processor must fetch the line from main memory, which costs the full hundred-plus cycles. The hit rate is the fraction of reads the cache serves, and it dominates performance: a loop that sums an array of integers with a 99% hit rate runs close to cache speed; the same loop with a 50% hit rate runs at half main-memory speed, which is to say it runs slow.

The cache is not one pool. Most processors split it into levels. The **L1** cache is smallest and fastest — 32 or 48 kilobytes, one to three cycles, one per core. The **L2** cache is larger and slower — 256 kilobytes to 2 megabytes, roughly 10 cycles, one per core. The **L3** cache is largest and slowest — 8 to 64 megabytes, 30 to 50 cycles, shared across all cores. A read that misses L1 checks L2, then L3, then main memory. Each miss adds latency, so the cost of a miss depends on which level served it.

The layout of data in memory determines the hit rate. An array of 64-bit integers stored contiguously is cache-friendly: one cache line holds eight integers, so reading the first pulls the next seven into cache for free. A linked list is cache-hostile: each node is allocated separately, and following a pointer to the next node is a read to an address the cache does not hold, which is a miss. Walking a million-element array is a million reads from a handful of cache lines fetched in sequence. Walking a million-element linked list is a million cache misses, each costing a hundred cycles, and the program spends its time waiting on memory rather than computing.

The cache also speeds up instruction fetch. The processor reads its own program from memory, and the same cache hierarchy holds recently executed code. A tight loop that fits in L1 runs from cache at full speed; a loop that spills out of L1 fetches from L2 or beyond on every iteration. This is why small code is fast code, independent of the algorithm's complexity.

The cache speeds up a program by being close, being fast, and being right about what the program will need next. The hit rate measures how often it is right, and the data layout determines the hit rate. A program that accesses memory in long contiguous runs feeds the cache the patterns it was built for. A program that jumps between scattered addresses defeats it and pays main-memory latency on every access.

Okay — explain idempotency in the context of an HTTP API, plain register, every sentence carrying a fact.

An HTTP request is idempotent when sending it twice produces the same result as sending it once. The server's state after the second request matches its state after the first, and the second response carries the same payload as the first.

`GET` is idempotent by definition. It reads a resource without changing it, so a client that retries a failed `GET` gets the same data the original would have returned, and the server's stored state is untouched either way. `PUT` is idempotent by contract. It replaces a resource wholesale: a `PUT /users/42` with body `{"name":"Ada"}` sets user 42 to that body, and a second identical `PUT` overwrites the first with the same content, leaving the resource unchanged. `DELETE` is idempotent in effect. The first call removes the resource; the second call finds nothing to remove and returns 404 or 204, but the server's state — resource gone — is the same after both.

`POST` is not idempotent. It creates a new resource each time, so two identical `POST /orders` with body `{"item":"book"}` create two orders. The server's state differs after the second request, and the two responses carry different identifiers. This is why a client that retries a `POST` after a network timeout risks duplicating the order: the original request may have succeeded, and the retry creates a second, distinct record.

The distinction matters because networks drop connections after the request reaches the server but before the response reaches the client. The client cannot tell whether the server processed the request or not, so it retries. If the endpoint is idempotent, the retry is safe — the server either applies the same change again to no effect or returns the same result. If the endpoint is not, the retry doubles the side effect.

The contract is about the server's state, not the response's byte-for-byte identity. A `DELETE` that returns 200 on the first call and 404 on the second is still idempotent, because the resource's state — absent — is the same after both. A `GET` whose response body changes between two calls because another client wrote new data in between is still idempotent, because the `GET` itself changed nothing. The property holds when the request's effect, not its observation, is repeatable.

Idempotency lets a client treat the network as unreliable without treating the server as unreliable. A retry is a retransmission of intent, and an idempotent endpoint absorbs it. A non-idempotent endpoint forces the client to distinguish "the request failed before reaching the server" from "the request reached the server and the response was lost," which the client usually cannot do.

Okay — explain DNS resolution from name to address, plain register, every sentence carrying a fact.

A browser types `example.com` into a URL bar, and the operating system needs its IP address before it can open a connection. DNS is the system that returns that address. It is a hierarchy of servers, each answering for a narrower slice of the name space, and the resolution is a walk down that hierarchy from the root to the authoritative server for the specific name.

The walk starts at the **recursive resolver**, which is the server the operating system is configured to query — typically the one run by the ISP, or a public resolver like Cloudflare's 1.1.1.1 or Google's 8.8.8.8. The operating system sends it the name `example.com`, and the recursive resolver takes responsibility for finding the answer by walking the hierarchy on the client's behalf.

The resolver begins at the **root servers**. There are thirteen root server addresses, published in a file called the root hints, which every recursive resolver ships with. The resolver picks one and sends it the query for `example.com`. The root server does not know the address, but it knows who does: the servers for the `.com` **top-level domain**. It returns a list of those servers' names and addresses.

The resolver picks a `.com` TLD server and sends it the same query. The TLD server does not know the address either, but it knows who does: the **authoritative servers** for `example.com`. When the registrar sold the domain `example.com`, it recorded those servers with the `.com` registry, and the TLD server returns their names and addresses.

The resolver picks an authoritative server for `example.com` and sends it the query. This server holds the actual records for the domain. It finds the **A record** for `example.com`, which lists the IPv4 address — say, `93.184.216.34` — and returns it. The resolver caches that answer for the duration specified in the record's **TTL**, then hands the address back to the operating system, which hands it to the browser, which opens a TCP connection to that address.

Three caches shorten this walk in practice. The operating system caches the result so a second lookup for the same name within the TTL returns immediately. The browser caches it for the same reason. And the recursive resolver caches every answer it receives along the way — the root's delegation to `.com`, the TLD's delegation to `example.com`, and the final A record — so the next query for any `.com` domain starts at the TLD, and the next query for `example.com` returns from the resolver's own memory without contacting any server at all. A cold resolution hits root, TLD, and authoritative in sequence. A warm resolution hits one cache or another and stops.

The hierarchy is what makes the system scale. The root servers answer only for the top-level domains and delegate everything else downward. The TLD servers answer only for their registrants and delegate further. The authoritative servers hold the records for the names under their control. No single server holds the entire name space, and no resolver needs to contact more than three or four servers to find any name on the internet.

Okay — explain deadlock and one avoidance method, plain register, every sentence carrying a fact.

Two threads each hold a lock the other needs. Thread A locks mutex 1, then tries to lock mutex 2. Thread B locks mutex 2, then tries to lock mutex 1. A waits for B to release 2. B waits for A to release 1. Neither moves. The program hangs. This is deadlock — a cycle in the wait-for graph where every thread blocks on a resource held by another thread in the cycle.

Four conditions must hold at once for the cycle to form. Resources are held under exclusive locks. A thread holding one resource waits for another without releasing the first. Resources are not preempted — no external force strips a lock from a thread. And the wait order is circular: A waits on B, B waits on A, closing the loop. Break any one condition and the deadlock cannot form.

The simplest way to break the cycle is a global lock ordering. Every thread acquires mutexes in the same sequence. If the rule is "lock 1 before 2," thread A locks 1 then 2, and thread B locks 1 then 2. Thread B cannot hold 2 while waiting for 1, because it must acquire 1 first, and 1 is held by A — so B blocks at the outset, before it ever touches 2. A finishes its work, releases both, and B proceeds. The circular wait never closes because the acquisition order is a total order, and a total order has no cycles.

The discipline is a contract the programmer imposes. The mutexes do not enforce it. A thread that violates the order under a single code path reintroduces the deadlock, and the compiler will not catch it. The cost of the ordering is that a thread may hold a lock longer than its critical section strictly needs, because it must acquire an earlier mutex before a later one even when only the later one guards the data it wants. The benefit is that the wait-for graph stays a directed acyclic graph, and a DAG cannot produce a cycle.

A hash map turns a key into an integer, then uses that integer as an index into an array. Two different keys can produce the same integer. When that happens, the map has a collision, and the design has to say where the second value goes.

The hash function spreads keys across the array's slots, called buckets. A good function distributes keys evenly, but it cannot guarantee that no two keys land in the same bucket, because the array is smaller than the set of possible keys. Collisions are not a bug; they are a mathematical certainty once the number of keys exceeds the number of buckets.

There are two ways to handle them.

**Chaining** stores a linked list at each bucket. When a key hashes to an occupied bucket, the map walks the list, compares keys one by one, and either updates the matching entry or appends a new node. Lookup time is proportional to the list's length. If the hash function is good and the map keeps its load factor — the ratio of stored keys to buckets — below a threshold like 0.75, the lists stay short and lookups stay close to constant time. Java's `HashMap` and C++'s `std::unordered_map` use this approach.

**Open addressing** stores all entries in the array itself. When a key hashes to an occupied bucket, the map applies a probe sequence to find the next open slot. Linear probing checks the next bucket, then the one after that. Quadratic probing jumps by squares of increasing size. Double hashing uses a second hash function to set the jump distance. On lookup, the map follows the same probe path until it finds the key or hits an empty bucket. Deletion is harder than with chaining: removing an entry and leaving a hole would break the probe chain, so the map marks the slot as a tombstone, a value that means "occupied but deleted," and skips it during probes while treating it as empty for inserts. Python's `dict` and Ruby's `Hash` use open addressing.

The tradeoff is memory locality against degradation under load. Chaining allocates a node per entry, which scatters them across the heap, but it degrades gracefully as the load factor climbs — lists get longer, but the map never fills up. Open addressing keeps every entry in one contiguous array, which is cache-friendly and fast when the load factor is low, but performance drops sharply as the array fills, because probe sequences lengthen and collide with each other. Most open-addressing maps resize when the load factor crosses a fixed threshold, copying every entry into a larger array and rehashing each one into its new bucket.

That resizing is the same operation for both designs: allocate a new array, rehash every key, move every entry, free the old array. It is the most expensive thing a hash map does, and it is amortized across all the inserts that happened since the last resize, so any single insert is fast on average and slow on the one that triggers growth.

A database index is a second data structure stored alongside a table to make reads fast. It trades disk space and write speed for lookup speed.

Without an index, finding rows that match a condition requires a full table scan: the database reads every row in the table and checks the condition against each one. A table with ten million rows and no index means ten million disk reads for a single query. With an index on the filtered column, the database navigates a tree structure to the matching rows in a handful of steps, typically three or four page reads for a B-tree on a large table.

The structure is usually a B-tree. The tree keeps its keys sorted, so it can answer range queries — all orders above $500, all users created after March — not just exact-match lookups. Each leaf node holds a key and a pointer back to the full row in the base table. The database traverses from root to leaf, follows the pointer, and reads the row.

That pointer is the cost. An index is a separate copy of part of the data, sorted differently. Every insert, update, or delete that touches an indexed column must update both the table and every index on that column. A table with five indexes takes six writes for one insert: one to the table, five to the indexes. The B-trees must stay balanced, so writes can trigger page splits that rewrite large chunks of the tree. On a write-heavy workload, indexes slow the system down.

Indexes also consume disk space and memory. A B-tree index on a large column can approach the size of the table itself. Database engines cache frequently used index pages in RAM to avoid disk reads, so each index claims a share of a finite buffer pool. Too many indexes evict useful data from cache, which slows the queries the indexes were meant to help.

An index hurts when it serves a query that runs rarely and costs more to maintain than it saves. A column updated every second and queried once a month is a poor index candidate. A column that appears in a `WHERE` clause on a query that runs a thousand times a minute is a good one. The decision rests on the ratio of reads to writes for that specific column, and on whether the index's selectivity — the fraction of rows it eliminates — is high enough to matter. An index on a boolean `is_active` column where 99% of rows are true filters almost nothing; the database may read the index, collect most of the table's row pointers, and then fetch all those rows anyway, which is slower than scanning the table once.

The right index makes a query that scanned millions of rows scan dozens. The wrong one taxes every write and never earns it back.

TCP sends data as a stream of numbered bytes, not as a sequence of independent messages. Each byte gets a sequence number drawn from a 32-bit counter that starts at a random value agreed during the handshake. Every segment the sender transmits carries the sequence number of its first byte and the count of bytes it contains, so the receiver can place that segment at an exact offset in the stream.

The network can deliver segments out of order. Segment 5 can arrive before segment 4 because it took a different path, or because segment 4 was lost and retransmitted. The receiver handles this with a receive buffer. It places each arriving segment at the position its sequence number indicates, not at the end of a queue. Gaps are expected. If bytes 1 through 100 and 201 through 300 are present but 101 through 200 are missing, the buffer holds the two blocks and leaves the middle empty.

The receiver tells the sender what it has. Every acknowledgment segment carries the sequence number of the next byte the receiver expects — the first byte of the lowest gap. This is a cumulative acknowledgment. It does not say "I received 201 through 300." It says "I am waiting for 101." The sender learns two things from that number: everything before it arrived, and something at or after it is missing.

The sender keeps a send buffer for the same reason. Bytes the application writes sit there until acknowledged. The sender starts a retransmission timer for the oldest unacknowledged byte. If the timer expires, the sender retransmits the segment that starts at that byte. It does not retransmit everything sent after it; it retransmits the segment at the acknowledged boundary, then relies on cumulative acknowledgments to discover whether later segments also need retransmission. This is the core of TCP's reliability, and it is built on the sequence number, the receive buffer, and the cumulative acknowledgment.

Once the gap fills, the receiver advances the acknowledgment number past all contiguous bytes it now holds. If 101 through 200 arrive, the acknowledgment jumps from 101 to 301 in one step. The application reads from the contiguous prefix of the buffer, so it never sees bytes out of order. The buffer absorbs the disorder; the sequence numbers resolve it.

A mutex protects one thing: the interleaving of reads and writes on shared state across threads.

Two threads running on separate cores can each execute a read-modify-write sequence on the same memory location. Thread A reads a counter at 5, adds 1, writes 6. Thread B reads the same counter at 5 before A's write lands, adds 1, writes 6. Two increments produced one. The counter should be 7. This is a data race, and the mutex exists to prevent it.

A mutex is a lock with one owner. A thread acquires the mutex before touching the shared data and releases it after. While one thread holds the mutex, every other thread that tries to acquire it blocks — it stops running and waits. The operating system or the runtime places the waiting thread in a queue associated with that mutex and schedules another thread on the core. When the holder releases, the scheduler wakes one waiter and grants it ownership.

The critical section is the code between acquire and release. The mutex guarantees that at most one thread executes that section at a time. If the section reads a counter, increments it, and writes it back, no other thread can interleave a read or a write between those steps. The increment becomes atomic with respect to other threads holding the same mutex.

A mutex does not protect against deadlocks on its own. If thread A holds mutex M1 and waits for M2 while thread B holds M2 and waits for M1, both block forever. The mutex mechanism enforces exclusion; it does not enforce acquisition order. Avoiding deadlock is the programmer's job: acquire mutexes in a fixed order across all threads, or release one before acquiring the next.

A mutex also does not make individual operations atomic by itself. It makes a *sequence* of operations atomic with respect to other threads that acquire the same mutex. A thread that modifies the shared data without acquiring the mutex bypasses the protection entirely. The mutex guards a convention, not the memory. C++ makes this explicit: a `std::mutex` protects nothing unless every access to the shared variable is wrapped in a `std::lock_guard` or equivalent. The compiler does not enforce this. Rust's `Mutex<T>` does — it owns the data, and the type system requires a lock to produce a reference to it.

The cost is contention. If ten threads contend on one mutex, nine wait while one runs. The critical section becomes serial. A mutex held for ten microseconds across a thousand calls per second costs ten seconds of wait time per second of wall clock — the system cannot keep up. Short critical sections and coarse-grained locks trade off against each other: a coarse lock is simple but serializes more work; a fine-grained lock parallelizes more but increases the risk of deadlock and the overhead of acquire and release. The right granularity depends on which data is actually shared and how long each thread needs it.

Garbage collection reclaims memory the program can no longer reach. The question is how it knows what is unreachable.

Every object a program creates has a root. Roots are the references the program can use directly: local variables on the stack, static fields, the CPU registers holding pointers. From those roots, the program follows references to other objects, and from those to still others, forming a graph. An object is reachable if a path exists from some root to it. An object is garbage if no such path exists. The collector's job is to find every object that no root can reach and free its memory.

The tracing collector walks the graph. It starts at the roots, marks each object it finds as live, and follows that object's references to mark the objects they point to. When the walk finishes, every marked object is reachable and every unmarked object is garbage. The collector then sweeps the heap: it scans every object, frees the unmarked ones, and clears the marks on the rest. This is mark-and-sweep, the design behind the JVM's basic collector and the .NET runtime's.

Mark-and-sweep fragments the heap. Freed objects leave holes of varying sizes, and allocating a large object may fail even when enough total free space exists, because that space is scattered. A compacting collector fixes this. After the mark phase, it moves every live object into a contiguous block at one end of the heap, sliding them together and leaving a single unbroken free region behind. Every moved object's references must be updated to point at the new addresses. The JVM's serial and parallel collectors compact this way.

Moving objects while the program runs breaks pointers. If the program holds a reference to an object at address 0x1000 and the collector moves it to 0x2000, the program's reference now points at garbage. Most collectors solve this by stopping the program's threads during the collection. The JVM calls these stop-the-world pauses. Every application thread halts, the collector traces, marks, compacts, and updates references, then the threads resume. The pause is proportional to the heap size and the number of live objects, which is why large heaps produce long pauses.

Concurrent collectors reduce the pause by doing most of the work while the program runs. The JVM's G1 collector divides the heap into regions and collects the regions with the most garbage first, which is where the name comes from — garbage first. It marks live objects concurrently with application threads, then pauses briefly to evacuate live objects out of a region into empty ones. The pause length depends on the number of regions being collected, not the total heap size, so a ten-gigabyte heap can still pause for a few milliseconds if only a handful of regions are evacuated. Shenandoah and ZGC push this further, doing compaction concurrently and keeping pauses under a millisecond on large heaps, at the cost of higher CPU overhead outside the pauses.

A different family avoids tracing entirely. Reference counting stores, with each object, an integer count of how many references point to it. When a reference is created, the count goes up. When a reference is dropped, the count goes down. When the count hits zero, no reference can reach the object, so the collector frees it immediately. C++'s `shared_ptr` and Swift's `ARC` work this way. The cost is two operations on every reference assignment, and the failure mode is cycles: two objects that reference each other keep each other's count at one forever, even when no root can reach either. A tracing collector handles cycles naturally because it starts from roots; a reference counter needs a separate cycle detector or it leaks them.

The generational hypothesis shapes most production collectors. It observes that most objects die young — temporary buffers, intermediate strings, loop variables are created and discarded within one or two allocations. The collector splits the heap into a young generation and an old generation. New objects go into the young generation, which is small and collected frequently. Most objects there are already garbage, so the collection is fast and reclaims a lot of space. Objects that survive several young-generation collections are promoted to the old generation, which is large and collected rarely. This is why the JVM's G1 and .NET's collector both use generations: the young generation is collected in a few milliseconds because it is small, and the old generation is left alone until it actually fills.

What unifies every design is the same two-step logic. Find what is reachable by walking from the roots. Free everything else. The variations — sweeping versus compacting, stop-the-world versus concurrent, tracing versus reference counting, generational versus flat — are different answers to the same engineering question: how to find the garbage fast enough that the program does not stall, and how to reclaim it without fragmenting the heap or wasting CPU on objects that are still alive.

A race condition is a bug that appears only when the timing of two operations lands a certain way. Two threads share a piece of memory. Each reads it, changes it, and writes it back. If the reads and writes interleave, the final value is wrong, and no thread reports an error.

A bank account holds $100. Two threads each withdraw $60. Thread A reads the balance: 100. Thread B reads the balance: 100. Thread A subtracts 60, writes 40. Thread B subtracts 60, writes 40. The account lost $120 and holds $40. One withdrawal vanished. The bank has no record of it.

The sequence that produces the correct result is A reads 100, A writes 40, B reads 40, B writes 0. The account is empty, which is right. The race is that the hardware offers no guarantee about which sequence runs. The operating system can pause A after its read and resume B before A's write. The language runtime can reorder the instructions. A second core can execute B's read before A's write becomes visible to it. Each thread's code is correct in isolation. The bug lives in the gap between the read and the write, where another thread can enter and act on a value that is already stale.

The fix is to make the read-modify-write indivisible. A mutex around the withdrawal serializes the two threads: A acquires the lock, reads, writes, releases; B waits for the lock, then reads the value A wrote. An atomic instruction like compare-and-swap does the same without a lock — the CPU guarantees that no other thread alters the value between the read and the write. Either way, the second thread sees the first thread's result, and the arithmetic is correct.

The defining trait of a race condition is that the program's output depends on the order of events the program did not control. Run it a thousand times and it may pass every time. Run it under load, on a different core count, or after an unrelated timing change, and it fails. The bug is not in the logic. The logic is sound. The bug is in the assumption that the logic runs uninterrupted.

A CPU runs a thousand times faster than the memory it talks to. Fetching a single value from main memory can take two hundred cycles; the processor can do nothing while it waits. A cache fixes this by keeping copies of recently used data in a small, fast memory that sits on the chip itself, where a fetch takes three or four cycles instead of two hundred.

The cache works because programs do not access memory at random. They access it in patterns. A loop that sums an array reads element 0, then 1, then 2, in order. A function that processes a customer record reads the customer's name, then its address, then its balance, all stored near each other in memory. This is called locality of reference, and it comes in two forms. Temporal locality says a value used once will probably be used again soon. Spatial locality says a value near a used value will probably be used soon too.
