The cache exploits both. When the processor requests a byte from main memory, the memory controller does not send just that byte. It sends a block of consecutive bytes, called a cache line, typically sixty-four bytes wide. The cache stores the whole line. If the program then reads the next byte, or the byte sixty-four positions later, the data is already on the chip. No main-memory fetch is needed. This is why iterating through an array in order is fast and why jumping to random positions in a linked list is slow: the array fills each cache line and uses every byte in it, while the linked list scatters its nodes across memory, so each jump misses the cache and pays the full two-hundred-cycle cost.

Caches are organized in levels. The L1 cache is smallest and closest, thirty-two kilobytes per core, with a latency of three or four cycles. The L2 cache is larger, around two hundred fifty-six kilobytes, with a latency of ten to twelve cycles. The L3 cache is shared across all cores, several megabytes, with a latency of thirty to forty cycles. Main memory sits behind all of them at two hundred cycles. A request checks L1, then L2, then L3, then main memory. A hit at any level stops the search. The hit rate — the fraction of requests served by the cache — determines how fast the program runs. An L1 hit rate of ninety-five percent means nineteen out of twenty fetches take four cycles.

The cache also speeds up writes. A store instruction writes to the L1 cache and moves on; the cache line is marked dirty, meaning its contents differ from main memory, and the controller writes it back to main memory later, in bulk. The processor does not wait for main memory on every write.

What makes a program cache-friendly is how it lays out data in memory and how it walks through it. An array of structures, where each element holds a name, an address, and a balance, forces the cache to load the name and the address even when the program only wants the balance. A structure of arrays, where all the balances sit in their own contiguous array, lets the cache load only balances. The second layout runs faster for a scan that sums balances, because every byte the cache loads is a byte the program uses. The first layout wastes cache space on fields the program never touches in that loop.

The cache turns the processor's two-hundred-cycle memory wait into a four-cycle fetch most of the time. The program controls this by how it stores its data and how it walks through it.

Okay, explain idempotency in the context of an HTTP API, in plain register.

An HTTP method is idempotent when a client can send the same request twice and leave the server in the same state as sending it once. The second call does not duplicate the first call's effect. The server's stored data ends up identical either way.

`GET` is idempotent because it reads data without changing it. Two identical reads return the same response, assuming nothing else modified the resource between them. `PUT` is idempotent because it replaces a resource wholesale. A `PUT` to `/users/42` with a given body creates user 42 if it does not exist and overwrites it if it does. Sending that same `PUT` ten times produces the same user 42 with the same fields. The tenth call overwrites the ninth, which overwrote the eighth. The final state is the state the last request carried.

`DELETE` is idempotent in a specific way. The first call removes the resource. The second call finds nothing at that location and returns `404 Not Found`, but the server's state is the same after both calls: the resource is gone. The response status differs. Idempotency is about the resulting state, not the response body.

`POST` is not idempotent. A `POST` to `/users` with the same body creates a new user each time. Ten calls produce ten users. The server's state grows with each request. This is why payment endpoints use `POST` — a second call must not charge the customer a second time without explicit intent.

The distinction matters because networks are unreliable. A client sends a `PUT`, the server processes it, the response is lost to a dropped connection, and the client does not know whether the write landed. If the method is idempotent, the client retries the same request. The server applies it again, the state is unchanged, and the system converges. If the method is not idempotent, a blind retry risks a duplicate charge, a duplicate order, a duplicate record. The client must then use a separate mechanism — an idempotency key, a unique request token the server checks before processing — to make a non-idempotent operation safe to retry.

The HTTP specification defines idempotency as a property of the method, not the implementation. A server that increments a counter inside a `GET` handler has broken the contract. The method declares what repeated calls do; the server must honor it.

Okay, explain how DNS resolves a domain name to an IP address, in plain register.

A browser types `example.com` into a URL bar. The machine needs that name's IP address before it can open a connection, and it has no map of the internet stored locally. DNS is the lookup system that returns the address.

The machine first asks a resolver. Most machines run no resolver of their own; they send queries to one configured by the network or the ISP, often a server inside the router or a public resolver like Google's `8.8.8.8` or Cloudflare's `1.1.1.1`. That resolver does the walking on the machine's behalf and caches the answers it finds.

The resolver does not know `example.com`'s address. No single server does. The name is a hierarchy, and the hierarchy is distributed across thousands of servers. The resolver starts at the top and works down.

It asks a root server for `example.com`. The root server does not know the address either, but it knows which servers handle the `.com` top-level domain. It returns a list of those servers' addresses. There are thirteen root server addresses, labeled A through M, backed by hundreds of physical instances spread across the world. Any one of them answers.

The resolver takes that list and asks a `.com` server for `example.com`. The `.com` server does not know the address. It knows the nameservers authoritative for `example.com` — the servers operated by whoever registered the domain. It returns their addresses.

The resolver asks one of those authoritative servers for `example.com`. This server holds the actual record. It returns an A record containing the IP address, or a CNAME record containing another domain name that the resolver must then resolve from scratch.

The resolver hands the address back to the machine. The machine opens a TCP connection to that address. The whole walk took three round trips — root, TLD, authoritative — plus the original query from the machine. A cold lookup from a London machine to a root server in Frankfurt, a `.com` server in Amsterdam, and an authoritative server in Dublin might take forty milliseconds. A warm lookup, where the resolver already holds the answer in its cache, takes one.

Caching is what makes the system survive. Every server in the chain caches the records it receives, and every record carries a time-to-live — a number of seconds the record may be held before it must be discarded and fetched again. A TTL of 3600 means the resolver keeps the answer for an hour. The root and TLD servers see almost no direct traffic from end users because resolvers cache their delegations aggressively. The authoritative servers for a popular domain see traffic only when a resolver's cached answer expires.

The system works because each layer delegates downward and because the resolvers remember what they learned. The root never answers a query directly. It points. The TLD never answers directly. It points. The authoritative server answers, and the answer spreads outward through the resolvers' caches until the next expiry.

Okay, explain what a deadlock is and one way to avoid it, in plain register.

A deadlock is a state where two threads each hold a resource the other needs and each waits for the other to release it. Neither moves. Both wait forever.

Thread A holds lock M1 and asks for lock M2. Thread B holds lock M2 and asks for lock M1. A cannot proceed until B releases M2. B cannot proceed until A releases M1. The scheduler parks both. The program hangs. No error fires. No exception throws. The threads sit.

Four conditions produce this, all required at once: resources that cannot be shared, threads that hold one resource while waiting for another, resources that cannot be taken away from a holder, and a circular chain of waits. Break any one and the deadlock cannot form.

The simplest fix is a lock ordering rule. Pick a global order for every lock in the program. Every thread acquires locks in that order, always. If the rule says M1 before M2, thread A acquires M1, then M2. Thread B also acquires M1, then M2. Thread B blocks at M1 while A holds it. When A releases both, B acquires M1, then M2. The circular wait never forms, because no thread holding a later lock ever waits for an earlier one.

The rule is cheap to state and hard to enforce. A program with three locks and forty call sites must acquire them in the same order at every site. A lock acquired inside a function call, invisible to the caller, can break the order without warning. Java and C++ offer tools — `std::lock(M1, M2)` in C++, `ReentrantLock.tryLock` with a timeout in Java — that acquire multiple locks atomically or back out on failure. They handle the cases where a fixed order is impractical. The discipline is the same: prevent the circular wait, and the deadlock cannot happen.

A hash map turns a key into an integer, then uses that integer as an index into an array of buckets. Two keys can produce the same integer. When that happens, the map has a collision, and the design has to say where the second entry goes.

The hash function does the first job. It maps a key — a string, a number, a struct — into a fixed-range integer, typically reduced modulo the bucket count. A good function spreads keys across the range so that real-world inputs do not cluster. A bad one makes every collision a self-inflicted wound.

The array of buckets does the second. Each slot holds zero or one entry in the simplest case. When a collision puts a second entry at the same slot, one of two things happens.

**Chaining** stores a linked list at each bucket. The slot points to the first entry; each entry points to the next. A lookup hashes the key, walks the list, and compares keys until it finds a match or reaches the end. Insertion appends to the list. Deletion unlinks the node. The cost of a lookup is the hash plus the list walk, so if every key lands in one bucket, the map degrades to a linked list and a lookup takes linear time. Java's `HashMap` and C++'s `std::unordered_map` both chain.

**Open addressing** stores entries in the array itself. On collision, the map probes another slot according to a fixed sequence. Linear probing checks the next slot, then the next, until it finds an empty one. Quadratic probing jumps by squares of the index. Double hashing uses a second hash function to set the probe step. Lookup follows the same probe path until it finds the key or an empty slot. Deletion is the hard part: removing an entry and leaving a hole would break the probe chain for any key that passed through, so the map marks the slot as a tombstone — occupied for probing, available for insertion. Tombstones accumulate and slow lookups, so the map rehashes to clear them. Python's `dict`, Ruby's `Hash`, and Go's built-in map all use open addressing.

Both designs share a failure mode. As the array fills, collisions multiply, and every operation slows. The map tracks its load factor — the ratio of entries to slots. When the factor crosses a threshold, the map allocates a larger array, re-hashes every entry into its new slot, and frees the old array. Chaining tolerates high load factors because the lists absorb overflow. Open addressing needs a lower threshold — usually around 0.7 — because a full array has nowhere to probe.

The choice between the two turns on three things. Chaining wastes memory on pointers but handles high load and frequent deletion without rehashing. Open addressing keeps entries packed in the array, so cache locality is better and a lookup touches fewer memory lines, but it punishes a full table and makes deletion clumsy. A map that holds a stable set of keys and serves read-heavy traffic benefits from the packed array. A map with churn — constant insert and delete — pays less for the linked lists.

A database index is a second data structure stored alongside a table to make lookups fast without scanning every row.

Without an index, finding the rows where `status = 'shipped'` means reading the whole table and testing each row. A million-row table costs a million reads. With an index on `status`, the database follows a pointer straight to the matching rows. The million reads become a handful.

The structure is usually a B-tree. It sorts the indexed column and stores each value next to a pointer to the full row. Sorted data lets the database binary-search in logarithmic time rather than scan linearly. A lookup in a million-entry B-tree touches about twenty nodes, not a million rows.

Indexes serve reads. They tax writes. Every `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, or `DELETE` that changes an indexed column must update the index too. A table with five indexes pays six writes for one row insertion — one to the table, five to the indexes. A table that absorbs a thousand inserts per second and has five indexes pays six thousand writes per second.

Indexes also cost storage. An index duplicates the column values and adds tree nodes and pointers. An index on a large text column can approach the size of the table itself. Five indexes on a large table can double its footprint on disk.

An index hurts when its maintenance cost exceeds its lookup savings. A table written constantly and read rarely gains nothing from an index the writes maintain. A query that selects most of the table — say, 40% of the rows — gains nothing either; the database reads the index, then chases pointers to the rows, and the pointer-chasing costs more than scanning the table directly. The planner sees this and skips the index, but the writes still pay to keep it current.

A column with few distinct values — a boolean flag, a status field with three states — makes a poor index. The B-tree has three leaves, each pointing to a third of the table. The database still reads most of the rows, plus the index. The index adds work without narrowing the search.

The useful index sits on a column that queries filter by, that holds many distinct values, and that appears in queries returning a small fraction of the table. A primary key meets all three. A foreign key in a join usually meets them. A created-at timestamp queried by range often meets them. Everything else is a guess that needs measuring: the query plan before and after, the write latency, the storage cost. Adding an index without those numbers is gambling with the write path.

TCP sends data as a stream of numbered bytes, not as a sequence of independent messages. The sender attaches a sequence number to every byte it transmits. The receiver uses those numbers to put the bytes back in the order the sender wrote them, regardless of the order they arrive.

The connection starts with a three-way handshake. The sender picks an initial sequence number — not zero, not one, but a random 32-bit value — and sends it in the SYN packet. The receiver replies with its own random initial number in SYN-ACK. Both sides now agree on where the byte stream begins for each direction. The randomness serves a purpose: an attacker who can predict the starting number can forge packets that the receiver would accept as belonging to the stream.

Once the handshake finishes, every data packet carries the sequence number of its first byte. If the initial number was 1000 and the sender transmits 500 bytes, the first packet is numbered 1000, the next is 1500, the next is 2000. The numbers are byte offsets from the starting point, not packet counts.

IP, the protocol that actually carries the packets across the network, makes no delivery guarantee. Packet 3 can arrive before packet 2. A packet can vanish entirely. A packet can arrive twice. TCP's job is to hide all of that and present a clean, ordered byte stream to the application above it.

The receiver does this with a buffer. When packet 3 arrives before packet 2, the receiver stores packet 3 in the buffer and waits. When packet 2 arrives, the receiver writes bytes 2 and 3 to the application in order, then frees that buffer space. The application never sees the gap.

Each acknowledgment the receiver sends back tells the sender the number of the next byte it expects. If the receiver has cleanly received bytes 1000 through 1499, it sends ACK 1500. That single number communicates "I have everything before 1500; send me 1500 and onward." This is a cumulative acknowledgment. It does not say "I got packet 2." It says "I got everything up to 1500, regardless of arrival order."

A lost packet breaks the chain. The sender transmits bytes 1000–1499, 1500–1999, and 2000–2499. The middle packet drops. The receiver gets 1000–1499, sends ACK 1500. It gets 2000–2499, stores it in the buffer, and sends ACK 1500 again — the same number, because 1500 is still the next expected byte. The sender sees a second ACK 1500 and recognizes it as a duplicate. Duplicate acknowledgments signal that something arrived out of order, which means a later packet got through while an earlier one did not.

Three duplicate ACKs trigger fast retransmit. The sender stops waiting for its retransmission timer to expire and resends the missing packet immediately. When the retransmitted 1500–1999 arrives, the receiver releases the buffered 2000–2499 along with it, and sends a single ACK 2500 — the next byte after everything now received in order.

If no duplicate ACKs arrive — say, only one packet was in flight when the loss happened — the sender's retransmission timer is the backstop. The sender starts a timer when it transmits a packet. If the timer expires before an acknowledgment covers those bytes, the sender retransmits. The timer length adapts to measured round-trip time, tightening on fast links and stretching on slow ones.

The sequence numbers also solve a second problem. Packets from an old connection can linger on the network and arrive after the connection closes. A 32-bit sequence space of roughly 4.3 billion bytes, combined with the random initial number, makes it unlikely that a delayed packet from an old connection falls inside the valid window of a new one. The numbers wrap around at 2³², but the windowing logic handles the arithmetic modulo 2³².

What the application receives, then, is a pipe. Bytes go in one end in order, come out the other in order. The numbering, the buffer, the cumulative acknowledgments, and the retransmission machinery together reconstruct that pipe from a network that scrambles and drops packets. The application never opens a buffer or reorders a byte. TCP does all of it, and the sequence number is the thread running through every piece.

A mutex protects one thing: shared memory touched by more than one thread at the same time.

A thread is a sequence of instructions running independently. Two threads in the same process share the process's memory — its global variables, its heap, the buffers it allocates. Sharing is the point of threads; it is also the hazard. A thread reads a variable, does some arithmetic, writes the result back. If a second thread reads the same variable between the first thread's read and its write, it sees a stale value and the computation is wrong. The mutex prevents that interleaving.

The mechanism is a lock with two operations. A thread calls `lock` before touching the shared data and `unlock` after. Between those two calls, the thread holds the mutex. The operating system guarantees that only one thread can hold a given mutex at once. A second thread that calls `lock` on a mutex already held blocks — it stops running and waits — until the holder calls `unlock` and the system wakes one waiting thread and hands it the lock. The result is a serial section: the code between `lock` and `unlock` runs one thread at a time, even when many threads want to run it.

The concrete case is a bank balance. Two threads each read a balance of 100, each add 10, each write 110. One deposit vanished. The fix is a mutex around the read-add-write sequence. The first thread locks, reads 100, writes 110, unlocks. The second thread locks, reads 110, writes 120, unlocks. The balance is correct because the two operations did not overlap.

A mutex protects against data races, which is the specific term for two or more threads accessing the same memory location with at least one of them writing, and no synchronization between them. The C++ and Rust memory models call this undefined behavior. The hardware itself can make it wrong: on a 64-bit machine, writing a 64-bit value is usually atomic, but on a 32-bit machine the same write is two 32-bit stores, and a reader can see the first half updated and the second half stale. The mutex removes that possibility because the writer holds the lock across both stores and the reader holds the lock across the whole read.

A mutex does not protect against everything. It does not protect against deadlocks, which it creates: two threads each holding one mutex and waiting for the other's mutex block forever. It does not protect against reentrancy problems, which it also creates: a thread holding a mutex calls a function that tries to lock the same mutex again, and if the mutex is not recursive, it deadlocks against itself. It does not make code correct by existing — it makes code correct only if every thread that touches the shared data locks the same mutex first. A mutex that guards a balance in one function is useless if another function writes the balance without locking.

The cost is contention. When three threads want the same mutex, two of them wait. The serial section becomes a bottleneck. The longer the section, the longer the wait. A mutex held across a disk read or a network call — operations measured in milliseconds — can stall every thread in the program. The discipline is to hold the lock for the shortest time possible: lock, update the shared variable, unlock, then do the slow work outside the lock.

A mutex is the simplest synchronization primitive that does this job. A spinlock does the same thing but busy-waits instead of blocking, burning CPU while it waits, which is the right choice only when the hold time is shorter than the cost of a context switch. A read-write lock allows many readers or one writer, which helps when reads dominate and writes are rare. A mutex does not distinguish readers from writers; it serializes all access. That is its limitation and its strength — it is cheap to reason about because it makes no exceptions.

Garbage collection reclaims memory the program can no longer reach. The question is how it knows what is unreachable.

A program allocates objects on a heap. Each object holds data and may hold pointers to other objects. The result is a directed graph: objects are nodes, pointers are edges. Some objects are reachable through roots — global variables, local variables on every thread's stack, CPU registers. Anything reachable from a root is live. Anything not reachable is garbage. The collector's job is to draw that line.

The tracing collector walks the graph. It starts at the roots, follows every pointer, and marks each object it reaches. When the walk finishes, every marked object is live. Every unmarked object is garbage. The collector then sweeps the heap: it walks every object, frees the unmarked ones, and clears the marks on the rest. This is mark-and-sweep, the design McCarthy described in 1960 and the ancestor of most collectors in use today.

Mark-and-sweep leaves gaps. Freed objects scatter holes across the heap, and allocating a large object means searching for a hole big enough. The collector can compact the heap instead: after marking, it slides every live object into a contiguous block at one end, updating every pointer to the new address. The heap has no holes after compaction. Allocation is a pointer bump — advance a cursor by the object's size, return the address. The cost is the work of moving objects and fixing their pointers.

Compaction pairs naturally with a copying collector. The heap splits into two halves. Allocation proceeds in one half by pointer bumping. When that half fills, the collector copies every live object from the full half to the empty half, packing them contiguously. The full half becomes empty. Allocation resumes. Copying collectors never touch dead objects — they copy only what survives. When most objects die young, as many programs' do, the collector copies little and reclaims much. The trade is memory: the program uses only half the heap at any time.

That observation — most objects die young — drives generational collection. The heap divides into a young generation and one or more old generations. New objects go in the young generation. The collector scans the young generation frequently and the old generations rarely. Most collections reclaim most of the young generation in a short pause. An object that survives several young-generation collections promotes to an old generation, where it sits through long stretches without being examined.

The hard part of generational collection is the remembered set. An old-to-young pointer — an old object holding a reference to a young one — makes the young object reachable. A young-generation collection that ignores old objects would miss that reference and free a live object. The collector maintains a remembered set: a record of every old-to-young pointer, updated on every write to an old object. A write barrier — a small piece of code the compiler inserts after each pointer store — records the cross-generational reference. The young collection then treats the remembered set as additional roots and preserves the referenced young objects.

Reference counting is a different lineage. Every object carries a count of incoming pointers. Assignment increments the count; overwriting a pointer decrements the old target's count. When the count hits zero, no one references the object, and the collector frees it immediately. No tracing, no pause, no walk. The cost is two arithmetic operations on every pointer assignment, everywhere, always. The failure is cycles: two objects pointing at each other keep each other's count above zero forever. A cycle of dead objects never reaches zero and never frees. Python uses reference counting and runs a cycle collector periodically to break unreachable cycles. Most tracing collectors avoid the problem entirely — a cycle is unreachable if no root reaches it, and tracing detects that directly.

The pause is the visible cost. A stop-the-world collector halts every thread at a safepoint, runs the collection, then resumes them. The pause length grows with the live set, not the heap size — a collector that copies ten megabytes of survivors pauses longer than one that copies one. Concurrent collectors do most of the marking and sweeping while the program runs, shortening the pause to the moments where the collector and the program must agree on state. The trade is complexity: the collector must handle objects the program modifies mid-trace, which requires write barriers and careful ordering. Go's collector marks concurrently and stops the world only to toggle a phase flag and scan a small set of stacks. The JVM's G1 divides the heap into regions and collects the regions with the most garbage first, bounding pause time by capping how many regions it reclaims per cycle.

What every collector shares is the core move: distinguish live from dead by reachability from roots, then reclaim the dead. The variations — sweep versus copy, generational versus flat, stop-the-world versus concurrent — trade pause time against throughput against memory overhead. The program's allocation pattern decides which trade pays off.

A race condition is a bug where the result depends on the order in which two operations run, and that order is not controlled.

Two threads share a counter. Both read 5, both add 1, both write 6. The counter should be 7. It is 6. One increment is gone. The read and the write are separate instructions, and the scheduler can pause one thread between them and run the other. That interleaving is the race.

The name comes from the threads racing for the same memory. Nothing coordinates them. The winner's write clobbers the loser's. Run the program again and the scheduler picks a different order, the writes do not overlap, and the counter reaches 7. The bug is intermittent. It depends on timing, and timing is the one thing a program should never depend on for correctness.

The counter is the simplest case. The pattern is broader. A thread checks a flag, sees it false, and decides to proceed. Another thread sets the flag between the check and the proceed. The first thread acts on a value it read before the change. This is check-then-act: the check and the act are not atomic, and the state can change in the gap. A bank app checks a balance, approves a withdrawal, and a second withdrawal lands in the gap. The balance goes negative. The check was honest when it ran. It was a lie by the time the act ran.

The fix is synchronization. A mutex around the read-modify-write makes the three steps one indivisible operation. The second thread cannot read the counter until the first thread writes it. The interleaving cannot happen. The cost is that the threads serialize on the mutex, and the one waiting blocks. The fix removes the race by removing the concurrency from the section that needs to be correct.

A race condition is not a crash. It is silent corruption. The program produces a wrong answer with no error, no warning, no log line. The counter is 6 instead of 7 and nothing complains. That silence is what makes race conditions hard to find and hard to trust tests against. A test that runs a thousand times and passes has not proven the race is gone. It has proven the scheduler did not pick the losing order on those thousand runs.

Okay: explain how a CPU cache speeds up a program, in the plain register already established.

A CPU cache is a small block of fast memory sitting between the processor and main memory. It speeds up a program by keeping copies of the values main memory holds, so the processor reads from the cache instead of from main memory.

The speed gap is the reason the cache exists. A modern processor can execute several instructions per nanosecond. A read from main memory takes 100 nanoseconds. The processor spends most of that time idle, waiting for the value to arrive. The cache returns a value in 1 to 3 nanoseconds. The wait shrinks by a factor of 30 to 100.

The cache works because programs do not touch memory at random. They touch it in patterns. A loop that sums an array reads element 0, then element 1, then element 2. A function that reads a struct's first field often reads its second field soon after. The cache exploits two such patterns. **Spatial locality** is the tendency to touch nearby addresses in sequence. **Temporal locality** is the tendency to touch the same address again soon. The cache is built around both.

Hardware loads memory in blocks, not single bytes. The block is a cache line, usually 64 bytes. When the processor reads a single int from an array, the hardware fetches the entire 64-byte line containing it and stores it in the cache. The next read — the adjacent int — is already in the cache. That is spatial locality turned into speed. One slow trip to main memory serves 16 reads.

The cache holds the line for future use. When the processor reads the same variable again — a loop counter incremented every iteration — the value is still in the cache from the previous iteration. That is temporal locality. The line stays until the cache needs the space for something else.

Caches sit in levels. The L1 cache is smallest and closest, 32 to 64 kilobytes, a 1-nanosecond hit. The L2 is larger, 256 kilobytes to 1 megabyte, a 3- to 5-nanosecond hit. The L3 is largest and shared across cores, 8 to 64 megabytes, a 10- to 20-nanosecond hit. A miss at L1 checks L2, then L3, then main memory. Each miss costs more time. The hit rate — the fraction of reads the cache satisfies — determines how fast the program runs.

The cache has limited space. It holds a fixed number of lines. When a new line arrives and the cache is full, the hardware evicts an old line to make room. The replacement policy is usually least-recently-used: the line that has gone longest without a read is the one removed. A program that streams through a large array fills the cache with new lines and pushes out the old ones. If the array is larger than the cache, the first elements are evicted before the loop reaches them again. The second pass through the array misses on every read. The cache helped on the first pass, through spatial locality, and helped nothing on the second, because the working set exceeded the cache's capacity.

The cost of a miss is the dominant factor in program speed. A program that runs from L1 cache executes in nanoseconds. A program that misses to main memory on every access spends its time stalled, waiting on the memory bus. Two algorithms with the same instruction count can differ in speed by a factor of 50 if one touches memory sequentially and the other jumps across the address space. The cache turns memory layout into runtime. An array of structs stored contiguously, accessed in order, feeds the cache lines it wants. A linked list of nodes allocated at random heap addresses makes every read a miss, because each node lives in a different cache line and the prefetcher cannot predict the next address.

The prefetcher is a second mechanism. The hardware detects sequential access patterns and fetches cache lines before the processor asks for them. A loop reading an array forward triggers the prefetcher, which pulls the next lines into the cache while the processor works on the current ones. The miss is hidden behind computation. A loop that strides through memory at large intervals — reading every 4096th byte of a large buffer — defeats the prefetcher, because the pattern looks like random access from the hardware's perspective.

A CPU cache speeds up a program by trading capacity for speed. Main memory is vast and slow. The cache is tiny and fast. It works because programs touch memory in patterns the cache can predict: nearby addresses in sequence, the same address repeatedly. The cache loads blocks, keeps them, and serves the next read from fast memory instead of slow. When the pattern holds, the program runs at cache speed. When the working set overflows the cache or the access pattern jumps, the program runs at main-memory speed, and the gap between those two speeds is the gap between a fast program and a slow one.

Okay: explain idempotency for an HTTP API, plain register, every sentence carrying a fact.

An HTTP request is idempotent when sending it twice produces the same result as sending it once. The server's state after the second request matches its state after the first. The client can retry without fear of a double effect.

`GET` is the trivial case. It reads data and changes nothing. A hundred identical GETs return the same response and leave the server untouched. Idempotency costs nothing there.

`PUT` is the interesting case. A PUT sends a full resource representation. The server stores it at the URL the client specified. Sending the same PUT twice overwrites the same resource with the same data. The second request does not create a second copy. The state after the second is identical to the state after the first. The client crashed mid-response, did not receive the 200, and retries. The server applies the same write again. No harm.

`DELETE` is idempotent by the same logic. The first DELETE removes the resource. The second DELETE finds nothing at that URL and returns 404 or 200, depending on the server's convention. Either way, the resource is gone after the first request and stays gone after the second. The server's state does not change between the two.

`POST` is the exception. A POST submits data to a handler, and the server decides what to do with it. A POST to `/orders` with a body describing a purchase creates an order. Sending that POST twice creates two orders. The server's state differs after the second request. POST is not idempotent, and that is why payment endpoints wrapped in POST need a separate mechanism — an idempotency key — to prevent duplicate charges when a client retries after a timeout.

The idempotency key is the pattern Stripe, Square, and Adyen use. The client generates a unique string and sends it in a header on the POST. The server checks whether it has seen that key before. If it has not, it runs the operation, stores the key alongside the result, and returns the response. If it has, it returns the stored result without running the operation again. The second POST becomes a lookup. The key turns a non-idempotent method into an idempotent one by making the server remember what it already did.

The distinction matters because networks are unreliable. A client sends a request, the server processes it, the response is lost on the way back. The client does not know whether the server received the request. It retries. If the endpoint is idempotent, the retry is safe. If it is not, the retry doubles the effect. The HTTP specification marks `GET`, `PUT`, `DELETE`, and `HEAD` as idempotent so that clients and proxies can retry them without special handling. `POST` and `PATCH` carry no such guarantee.

Idempotency is a property of the server's behavior, not of the method name alone. A broken `DELETE` that logs each attempt to an append-only table is not idempotent in effect, even though the method is idempotent by spec. The spec defines what the methods should do. The server decides what they actually do. A client that relies on idempotency trusts the server to honor it.

Okay: explain how DNS resolves a name to an address, plain register, every sentence carrying a fact.

A browser asks for `example.com`. It needs an IP address — a 32-bit number for IPv4, a 128-bit number for IPv6 — because the network routes packets by number, not by name. DNS is the lookup that returns the number.

The asking program does not perform the lookup itself. It hands the name to a resolver, usually a library function called `getaddrinfo`. The resolver checks its own cache first. If it has the answer and the entry has not expired, it returns the address and the lookup is done. No packet leaves the machine.

If the cache is empty, the resolver sends a UDP query to a recursive resolver — the server configured in the operating system's network settings, often run by the ISP or a public provider like Cloudflare at 1.1.1.1 or Google at 8.8.8.8. The recursive resolver's job is to chase the answer across the DNS hierarchy and bring it back.

The hierarchy is a tree. The root is the top. Below it sit the top-level domains — `.com`, `.org`, `.uk`, the 1,500 others. Below each TLD sit the domains registered under it. Each level delegates authority for the level beneath. The root servers know where the `.com` servers are. The `.com` servers know where `example.com`'s servers are. Nobody holds the full map. Each server holds its piece and a pointer to the next.

The recursive resolver starts at the root. It does not know the root servers' addresses by lookup; it carries them as a built-in list of 13 logical addresses, spread across hundreds of physical instances by anycast routing. The resolver asks a root server for `example.com`. The root server does not know the answer. It returns a referral — a list of the `.com` authoritative servers and their addresses. The referral says: I do not have this, but these servers do.

The resolver caches that referral and asks a `.com` server the same question. The `.com` server also does not know the address of `www.example.com`. It returns a referral to the authoritative servers for `example.com` — the name servers the operator of `example.com` configured when registering the domain. The resolver caches that referral too.

The resolver asks `example.com`'s authoritative server for `www.example.com`. This server holds the actual record. It returns an A record containing the IPv4 address, or an AAAA record containing the IPv6 address. The resolver caches the answer with the record's time-to-live — a number of seconds the authoritative server specifies, after which the cache entry expires and the next lookup must repeat the chase.

The resolver returns the address to the asking program. The program opens a TCP connection to that address. The whole chase took three round trips — root, TLD, authoritative — plus the initial query from the machine to the recursive resolver. Each round trip is a few milliseconds on a fast link, more on a slow one. The cache exists because those milliseconds add up, and because the root and TLD servers could not survive every machine on earth asking them on every request.

The records carry types. An A record maps a name to an IPv4 address. An AAAA record maps to an IPv6 address. A CNAME record maps a name to another name, which forces a second lookup at whatever the target resolves to — `www.example.com` as a CNAME pointing to `example.com` means the resolver restarts the chase at `example.com`, though it uses cached referrals for the root and TLD. An MX record names the mail servers for a domain and their priorities. A TXT record holds arbitrary text, used now for domain verification and email authentication flags like SPF and DKIM. The query specifies the type it wants, and the server returns that type or nothing.

The transport is UDP port 53 for queries and responses that fit in 512 bytes. A response that exceeds the limit sets a flag telling the resolver to retry over TCP, which handles the larger payload. DNSSEC, the signed variant, produces responses too large for UDP because it attaches cryptographic signatures, so DNSSEC queries usually fall back to TCP or use a UDP extension called EDNS0 that raises the 512-byte ceiling.

The system's weakness is the unencrypted UDP query. A resolver between the client and the authoritative server can see the name being asked for and forge a response with a wrong address, redirecting the connection. DNS over HTTPS and DNS over TLS wrap the query in an encrypted transport, hiding the name from observers and preventing forgery. Cloudflare's 1.1.1.1 and Google's 8.8.8.8 both support both protocols. The cost is a TCP handshake and TLS negotiation before the first query, adding latency the plain UDP version does not.

DNS turns a name into an address by walking a delegated tree, caching at every step, and returning a typed record. The tree distributes the work so no single server holds every domain. The cache absorbs the repeat traffic so the tree survives the load. The address comes back, the connection opens, and the name never crosses the network again until the cache expires.

Okay: explain what a deadlock is and one way to avoid it, plain register, every sentence carrying a fact.

A deadlock is two threads frozen forever, each holding a lock the other needs.

Thread A locks mutex X, then tries to lock mutex Y. Thread B locks mutex Y, then tries to lock mutex X. A waits for B to release Y. B waits for A to release X. Neither gives. Neither proceeds. The program hangs.

Four conditions produce this. The threads hold locks while waiting for more. The locks are not shared. The locks cannot be taken away. There is a cycle: A waits on B, B waits on A. Break any one and the deadlock cannot form.

The simplest fix breaks the cycle with a lock ordering rule. The program assigns every mutex a rank — an integer, a name, a position in a fixed sequence. Every thread acquires mutexes in ascending rank order. Thread A locks X first because X ranks below Y. Thread B also locks X first. The thread that gets X proceeds to Y. The thread that loses waits at X. It never touches Y until it has X. The cycle cannot close.

The rule works because it removes the circular wait. No thread holds a high-ranked lock while waiting for a low-ranked one. The wait flows in one direction only. The cost is discipline: every lock in the program needs a rank, and every code path that takes two or more locks must follow the order. A single function that locks out of sequence breaks the guarantee and reintroduces the deadlock.

The rule fails when a thread does not know which locks it needs until it holds one. A thread locks a mutex, reads a shared structure, and discovers a second mutex inside it. The second mutex's rank was invisible at the first lock. The thread either violates the order or releases the first lock, re-reads the structure, and acquires both in rank order — a retry that adds complexity and its own races. Lock ordering suits programs whose lock graph is known ahead of time. It does not suit programs that discover the graph at runtime.

A hash map turns a key into an integer with a hash function, then uses that integer as an index into an array of buckets. When two keys hash to the same index, a collision occurs, and the map needs a rule for storing both.

The two rules in common use are separate chaining and open addressing.

**Separate chaining** gives each bucket its own list. A key lands in the bucket at its hashed index, and if that bucket already holds one or more entries, the new entry joins the list. A lookup hashes the key, walks the bucket's list, and compares keys with `equals` until it finds a match or reaches the end. The worst case is every key colliding into one bucket, collapsing the map into a single linked list with O(n) lookups. The average case, with a uniform hash and a load factor kept under 1, is O(1).

**Open addressing** stores all entries in the array itself. On collision, the map probes another slot according to a fixed sequence. Linear probing checks the next slot, then the next, until it finds an empty one. Quadratic probing jumps by squares of the probe count — 1, 4, 9 — to avoid clustering under localized collision patterns. Double hashing uses a second hash function to set the step size, which spreads entries more evenly than a fixed step. Robin Hood hashing, a variant of open addressing, displaces an existing entry if the new entry has probed farther from its home slot, keeping the maximum probe distance short.

Deletion in open addressing cannot simply empty a slot, because a probe sequence might pass through that slot, and emptying it would break the chain for later keys. The standard fix marks the slot as a tombstone — occupied for probing, available for insertion. Tombstones accumulate under heavy churn, lengthening probe sequences, so maps that support frequent deletion either rehash on a tombstone threshold or rebuild periodically.

The load factor — entries divided by slots — governs both schemes. As it rises, collisions multiply and lookups slow. Most implementations keep the load factor below a fixed threshold, commonly 0.75, and allocate a larger array when it is crossed, rehashing every entry into its new bucket. That rehash is O(n) but amortized to O(1) per insertion over a sequence of grows, because it happens rarely relative to the number of insertions between grows.

The choice between the schemes trades memory for locality. Chaining allocates a node per entry and follows pointers on lookup, which costs cache efficiency but tolerates high load factors without severe degradation. Open addressing keeps everything in one contiguous array, which is cache-friendly, but degrades sharply past about 70% full and handles high deletion rates poorly because of tombstone buildup. Java's `HashMap` uses chaining. Python's `dict` uses open addressing with pseudorandom probing. Rust's `HashMap` uses Robin Hood hashing with backshift deletion, which removes tombstones by shifting subsequent entries back on deletion.

A database index is a second data structure stored alongside a table to make reads fast. It trades write speed and disk space for read speed.

The most common form is a B-tree. A B-tree keeps sorted keys in a balanced tree, so a lookup touches a handful of pages instead of scanning every row. A query for `users WHERE email = 'x'` reads perhaps four pages from an index on `email`, then fetches the matching row, instead of reading the whole table. On a million-row table, that is the difference between four disk reads and a million.

An index hurts in four specific situations.

First, every index slows writes. An `INSERT` into a table with five indexes writes the row once, then updates all five index structures. A table with no indexes takes one write per row. A table with six takes seven. Bulk loads into an empty table run faster with indexes dropped and rebuilt after.

Second, an index that a query never uses is pure overhead. It costs writes on every `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, and `DELETE`, and gives nothing back. Indexes added "just in case" or left behind after a query change fit this category. The fix is dropping them, which the query planner confirms is safe if the index appears in no query plan.

Third, an index on a column with low cardinality — few distinct values — rarely helps. An index on a `boolean` `is_active` column splits the table into two large groups. The planner sees that one group is half the table and skips the index, scanning instead, because reading the index plus fetching all those rows costs more than just scanning. The index still pays its write cost on every row change, but earns no read savings.

Fourth, an index can make a query worse when the query needs most of the table. A query selecting 80% of rows through an index does two reads per row: one for the index entry, one for the row. A sequential scan does one read per row in bulk, which is cheaper. Planners estimate this and switch to a scan, but estimates are wrong sometimes, and a forced index hint on a broad query produces the slow two-read path.

The cost is concrete. A B-tree index on a column takes roughly the same space as the table data itself for a narrow key, more for a wide one. Six indexes on a 10 GB table can add 60 GB. Every `INSERT` touches all six. Every `DELETE` removes from all six. Every `UPDATE` to an indexed column updates the index entry.

The rule is narrow. Index the columns that appear in `WHERE`, `JOIN`, and `ORDER BY` clauses on queries that matter. Drop the ones that do not. Measure with `EXPLAIN` before and after, because the planner's choices depend on data distribution, and the only honest answer comes from reading the actual plan.

TCP sends data as a stream of numbered bytes, not as a sequence of independent messages. Every byte gets a sequence number. The first byte's number is chosen randomly during the handshake, and each byte after it counts up by one.

A sender writes 1000 bytes at sequence number 5000. The next segment it sends carries 6000. If the network delivers the second segment first, the receiver holds it in a buffer and waits for 5000. When 5000 arrives, the receiver places both segments in order, hands the reassembled bytes to the application, and sends an acknowledgment for the highest contiguous byte received — in this case, 6000.

The acknowledgment is cumulative. An ACK of 6000 means every byte up to 5999 has arrived in order and been delivered. It does not confirm any individual segment. If 5000 arrives but 5500 is lost, the receiver delivers 5000 through 5499, buffers 6000 onward, and keeps sending ACK 5500. Each repeated ACK tells the sender that 5500 is still missing.

The receiver's buffer is finite. TCP advertises a window size in every segment, telling the sender how many bytes it can accept beyond the last acknowledged byte. If the application reads slowly, the window shrinks. If it reads nothing, the window reaches zero, and the sender stops until a new window advertisement arrives. This is flow control: the receiver governs the rate, and the sender cannot overrun it.

The sender keeps every unacknowledged byte in its own buffer. When an ACK arrives, the sender discards the covered bytes and slides its window forward. If an ACK does not arrive within a timeout, or if three duplicate ACKs arrive for the same sequence number, the sender retransmits the missing segment. The timeout is the retransmission timer, and the three-duplicate-ACK rule is fast retransmit, which fires before the timer expires under steady traffic.

Order is not a property the network provides. IP delivers packets independently, and packets can take different routes, arrive out of order, or vanish. TCP imposes order on top of that by numbering every byte, buffering gaps at the receiver, retransmitting losses, and acknowledging only the contiguous prefix. The application sees a byte stream in the order it was sent.

A mutex protects one thing: the interleaving of reads and writes on shared state across two or more threads.

A thread that wants a resource calls `lock`. If no other thread holds it, the caller gets it. If another thread already holds it, the caller blocks — the operating system parks it until the holder calls `unlock`. Only one thread holds the lock at a time. That is the entire mechanism.

The problem it solves is lost updates and torn reads. Thread A reads a balance of 100. Thread B reads 100. Both add 50. Both write 150. The correct result is 200. Without a mutex around the read-modify-write, the second write clobbers the first. A torn read is the same shape on a single variable: a 64-bit counter on a 32-bit machine takes two memory writes. A second thread reading between those two writes sees a value that was never written — half of the old value stitched to half of the new one.

Wrapping the critical section in a mutex makes the section atomic with respect to other threads holding the same mutex. Thread A's full read-modify-write completes before Thread B's begins, or vice versa. The order is not determined, but the interleaving is gone.

A mutex does not protect against everything. It does not make a data structure thread-safe by existing near it — it protects only the sections that actually acquire it. A thread that bypasses the lock and touches the shared variable directly races against the threads that did not. It does not prevent deadlock: two threads each holding one mutex and waiting for the other's will block forever. It does not compose without care: a function that locks and calls another function that locks the same mutex will deadlock on a non-reentrant lock, or silently extend the critical section on a reentrant one.

The cost is contention. Every lock call is a kernel transition when the lock is contended, which is orders of magnitude slower than the work it protects in the worst case. An uncontended lock on modern hardware is a single atomic instruction, cheap but not free. Holding a lock across a network call, a disk read, or a long computation serializes every thread that needs the resource behind the slowest one.

The discipline is narrow. Identify the shared mutable state. Wrap every access to it in the same mutex. Hold the lock for the shortest section that preserves the invariant. Never hold a lock across a blocking call. Acquire multiple locks in a fixed global order, or acquire them together, to avoid deadlock.

Garbage collection finds memory that no live object can reach, then reclaims it.

The root set is the starting point. It is the collection of references the program can reach directly: local variables on every thread's stack, static fields, and the references held by the runtime itself, such as the global object table. Every object pointed to by a root is live. Every object pointed to by a field of a live object is also live. Reachability is transitive.

**Tracing** walks that graph. The collector marks every root, then follows each root's references to the objects it points to, marks those, follows their references, and so on until it has visited every reachable object. The mark bit on each object says the collector reached it. When the trace finishes, any object without a mark bit is garbage — no path from any root leads to it. The collector sweeps the heap, frees every unmarked object, and clears the marks for the next cycle. This is mark-and-sweep, the scheme used by the JVM's basic collectors and the .NET CLR.

**Reference counting** takes a different route. Every object carries a count of how many references point to it. A new reference increments the count. A dropped reference decrements it. When the count hits zero, no one can reach the object, and the collector frees it immediately. The count is local, so the decision is fast. The failure mode is cycles: object A points to B, B points to A, and both have a count of one, but neither is reachable from any root. The count never reaches zero, and the memory leaks. CPython uses reference counting and runs a separate cycle detector to catch this case. Most tracing collectors do not count references at all.

The hard part is not finding garbage. It is finding it while the program keeps running.

A **stop-the-world** collector pauses every thread, traces, sweeps, and resumes. The pause is correct and simple, and it blocks the program for as long as the heap is large. A 4 GB heap with a million objects can pause for hundreds of milliseconds. The program appears frozen.

**Concurrent** collectors trace while the program runs. The collector and the program's threads share the heap, and the program can mutate the object graph mid-trace. The collector must handle a thread that redirects a reference the collector has already visited: without care, the collector misses the new target and frees a live object. The standard fix is a write barrier — a small piece of code the runtime inserts after every reference write, recording the change so the collector can revisit it. The JVM's G1 and Shenandoah use this approach. The write barrier is the tax concurrent collection pays for not stopping the world.

**Generational** collectors exploit the observation that most objects die young. A web request allocates a buffer, a list, a few strings, and they become garbage the moment the response is sent. The collector splits the heap into a young generation and an old generation. It collects the young generation frequently — it is small, so the pause is short — and promotes objects that survive a few young-gen cycles to the old generation. The old generation is collected rarely. This cuts the average pause from a full-heap scan to a small-fraction scan. The cost is a write barrier on writes from old objects to young objects, so the collector can find young objects referenced by old ones during a young-gen collection.

**Copying** collectors turn sweep into a move. They divide the heap into two halves. During collection, they trace from the roots, and for each live object, they copy it to the empty half and update every reference to point at the new location. When the trace finishes, the old half is pure garbage — no sweep needed, the whole half is free. The live objects are packed together in the new half, which eliminates fragmentation. The cost is half the heap is always unused, and copying long-lived objects every cycle wastes work. Generational collectors use copying for the young generation, where most objects are dead and the copy is cheap, and mark-and-sweep for the old generation, where objects live long and copying them repeatedly would cost too much.

The collector's job is to reclaim memory the program cannot reach. It does that by tracing from the roots, or by counting references, or by some mix of the two. The rest — pauses, barriers, generations, copying — is the engineering of doing it fast enough that the program does not notice.

A race condition is a bug where the result depends on the order in which two threads execute, and that order is not controlled.

Two threads withdraw from a shared bank balance of 100. Thread A reads 100, subtracts 20, and prepares to write 80. Thread B reads 100 before A writes, subtracts 30, and prepares to write 70. One write lands, then the other overwrites it. The final balance is 70 or 80, not 50. The bank lost 20 or 30.

The reads and writes interleaved because nothing forced them apart. The operating system can pause Thread A after its read and resume Thread B, and A cannot tell. The schedule is not deterministic, so the program's output is not deterministic either. Run it twice and the balance can differ.

The fix is a mutex around the read-modify-write. A thread that locks before reading blocks the other thread until it unlocks. The subtraction completes as one indivisible step. The order is still not determined — A may go first or B may — but the interleaving is gone, so the result is always 50.

A CPU cache is a small, fast memory that sits between the processor and main memory. It speeds up a program by keeping the data the processor is most likely to need next.

Main memory is slow. A modern processor can execute hundreds of instructions in the time it takes to fetch one value from DRAM. The cache closes that gap. It is built from SRAM, which is faster than DRAM but smaller, more expensive, and more power-hungry. A typical desktop chip has 32 to 64 KB of L1 cache per core, 256 KB to 1 MB of L2, and 8 to 32 MB of L3 shared across cores.

The cache works because of locality. A program that reads `array[0]` almost always reads `array[1]` next. That is spatial locality: nearby memory gets used together. A program that loops over the same variable hits that variable every iteration. That is temporal locality: recently used memory gets used again soon. The cache exploits both. When the processor requests a byte from memory, the cache pulls in a whole block — 64 bytes on most x86 chips — on the assumption that the next few accesses fall in that block. If the program then reads the adjacent bytes, they are already in the cache.

A cache hit returns the data in one or two cycles for L1, around ten for L2, around forty for L3. A cache miss goes to main memory and costs two to three hundred cycles. The hit rate determines the speedup. A program that reads a 4 KB array in a tight loop hits L1 on every access after the first block, and the loop runs at full speed. The same loop over a 16 MB array larger than L3 misses on most accesses, and the processor stalls waiting for DRAM.

The cache is hardware-managed but software-influenced. The processor decides what to load and what to evict using a replacement policy, typically least-recently-used. The program decides the access pattern. An array traversed in order touches each cache line once and moves on. A linked list traversed by pointer chase touches one node per cache line and pays a miss per node, because the next node's address is not predictable. Two arrays of a million integers processed together in separate loops thrash the cache: the first loop fills it with array A, the second loop fills it with array B, the third loop refetches A. Fusing the three loops into one keeps both arrays resident and cuts misses by a factor of three.

Cache layout matters for writes too. A cache line is the unit of transfer, and a write to any byte in a line marks the whole line dirty. Two threads writing to different fields of the same struct hit the same cache line. On a multicore chip, each core has its own L1, and a write by one core invalidates that line in every other core's cache. The other cores reload it from L3 or memory. This is false sharing. The struct fits in one line, the threads never touch the same field, and the cache coherence traffic still serializes them. Padding the struct so each thread's field lands in its own line removes the contention.

The cache speeds up a program by being right about what comes next. When the access pattern matches the block-fetch and eviction assumptions, the program runs at cache speed. When it does not, the program runs at memory speed, and the processor spends its time waiting.

Idempotency means a client can send the same request twice and the server ends up in the same state as if it received it once.

`PUT /users/42` with body `{"name": "Ada"}` is idempotent. The first request sets the name. The second request sets the name to the same value. The stored result is identical. A hundred retries produce the same row as one.

`POST /users` with body `{"name": "Ada"}` is not. The first request creates user 43. The second request creates user 44. Each call appends a new row, and the server's state diverges with every retry.

The HTTP specification declares `GET`, `PUT`, `DELETE`, and `HEAD` idempotent. It declares `POST` and `PATCH` not idempotent. The declaration describes the method's intent, not the server's implementation. A `DELETE /users/42` that decrements a counter on every call is not idempotent in effect, even though the method is idempotent by spec. The first call deletes the user and drops the counter to zero. The second call finds no user, but the handler still decrements, and the counter goes negative.

The property matters because networks retry. A client sends `PUT /items/7`, the server applies it, the response vanishes in transit, and the client times out and sends it again. If the operation is idempotent, the retry is harmless. The server applies the same write, produces the same state, and returns. If the operation is not idempotent, the retry doubles the work — a second charge, a second order, a second row.

`POST` is not idempotent because it has no way to distinguish a first request from a retry. The fix is an idempotency key. The client generates a unique token, sends it in an `Idempotency-Key` header, and reuses the same token on every retry of that request. The server stores the key with the response. On the second arrival, the server recognizes the key and returns the stored response without reprocessing. Stripe's API uses this pattern: a duplicate charge request with the same key returns the original charge object instead of creating a second one.

Idempotency is a contract about state, not about the response. The second `PUT` may return `200 OK` or `204 No Content` depending on whether the server treats it as an update or a no-op, but the resource on disk is the same either way.

DNS resolves a hostname through a hierarchy of servers, each answering only the part it knows.

A program asks the operating system's resolver for `www.example.com`. The resolver is a stub — it knows nothing about the domain itself, only the address of a recursive resolver, usually the ISP's or a configured one like 8.8.8.8. The stub hands off the name and waits.

The recursive resolver does the walking. It starts at the root. The root servers do not know `www.example.com`, but they know which servers are authoritative for `.com`. The resolver asks a root server, gets a referral to the `.com` servers, and follows it.

The `.com` servers know about every registered `.com` domain, but not the records inside them. They return a referral to the authoritative servers for `example.com` — the name servers the domain owner configured at the registrar. The resolver asks those servers.

The authoritative server for `example.com` holds the actual records. It reads `www.example.com` from its zone file and returns an A record with an address, say `93.184.216.34`. The recursive resolver caches that answer for the time-to-live the record specifies, then returns it to the stub, which returns it to the program.

The whole walk is four network round trips: stub to recursive, recursive to root, recursive to `.com`, recursive to authoritative. In practice the first three are usually warm. The root and `.com` referrals are cached for days, so a typical resolution is one round trip — the recursive resolver already knows where `.com` lives, and often already knows `example.com`'s authoritative servers from a recent query by someone else. A cold resolution, the first lookup of a name nobody has asked for, pays the full cost.

Caching is what makes the system survive. Every server in the chain caches what it learns, for a duration set by the record's TTL. A TTL of 3600 means the answer is good for one hour. After that, the cache entry expires and the next query walks the chain again. Short TTLs let operators move services quickly — change the authoritative record and traffic shifts within minutes. Long TTLs reduce load on the root and TLD servers, which answer billions of referrals a day from a few hundred machines.

The address that comes back is not always the one the authoritative server published. A resolver in London asking for a CDN-backed name gets a different address than one in Tokyo, because the CDN's authoritative server inspects the source of the query and returns an address near that resolver. This is how CDNs route traffic to nearby edge nodes — the DNS answer changes based on who is asking.

Okay — explain deadlock and one avoidance strategy, in plain register.

A deadlock is two threads frozen, each holding a lock the other needs.

Thread A locks mutex X, then tries to lock mutex Y. Thread B locks mutex Y, then tries to lock mutex X. A waits for B to release Y. B waits for A to release X. Neither yields. The program halts at those two threads and nothing in the locked sections ever runs again.

Four conditions produce this: mutual exclusion (only one thread holds a lock), hold and wait (a thread holds one lock while requesting another), no preemption (a thread cannot force another to release), and circular wait (A waits on B, B waits on A). Break any one and deadlocks become impossible.

The cleanest to break is circular wait. Assign every mutex in the program a fixed global order. Every thread acquires locks in ascending order and releases them in reverse. If X comes before Y in the order, a thread that needs both locks X first, then Y. A thread holding Y that decides it also needs X must release Y, acquire X, then reacquire Y. The cycle cannot form because no thread ever holds a higher-numbered lock while waiting for a lower-numbered one.

The discipline costs one thing: every function that locks must know the order, and every caller must respect it. A function that locks Y and calls a function that locks X inverts the order and reintroduces the deadlock. The order is a project-wide invariant, not a local one.

A hash map turns a key into an integer, then uses that integer as an index into an array. The hash function does the turning; the array holds the values. Two keys that hash to the same index collide, and every hash map has to decide what happens then.

The oldest fix is a bucket at each index. Instead of storing one value, the slot stores a pointer to a linked list. On insert, the map hashes the key, walks the list, and appends a new node if the key is absent. On lookup, it walks the same list and compares keys one by one. The cost is linear in the list length. If ten thousand keys land in one bucket, a lookup becomes ten thousand comparisons, and the map's promised constant-time access collapses into a linear scan. Java's `HashMap` worked this way until Java 8, when it began converting long lists into red-black trees to bound the worst case at logarithmic rather than linear.

The second fix avoids lists entirely. Each slot holds exactly one entry, and a collision sends the new entry elsewhere in the same array. Open addressing, as this is called, needs a rule for picking the elsewhere. Linear probing steps forward one slot at a time until it finds an empty one. Quadratic probing jumps by growing intervals — one, four, nine — to spread entries out. Double hashing computes a second hash from the key and uses that as the step size, so different keys take different paths through the table. Python's `dict` uses a variant called open addressing with perturbation, combining the hash with a shifting probe sequence to avoid clustering.

Probing has a weakness the bucket approach does not. If a key is deleted and its slot is simply emptied, a later lookup for a key that probed past it will stop early and miss. The slot must be marked as deleted rather than empty, so probes know to continue through it. These tombstones accumulate, slowing lookups, until the table is rebuilt.

Both schemes share a final mechanism. When the array fills past a threshold — typically around seventy percent for open addressing, lower for chaining — the map allocates a larger array, rehashes every key, and moves each entry to its new position. This is the moment the map pays back the collisions it has been absorbing. A map that never resized would drown in its own buckets; one that resizes too often wastes memory on half-empty arrays. The load factor, the ratio of entries to slots, is the dial that controls the trade.

A database index is a second data structure stored alongside the table. The table holds the rows in the order they were written. The index holds pointers to those rows, sorted by some column.

Without an index, finding the rows where `last_name = 'Smith'` means reading every row in the table and checking each one. With an index on `last_name`, the database finds the sorted `'Smith'` entries in the index, follows their pointers directly to the rows, and reads only those. A table of ten million rows becomes a handful of disk reads instead of ten million comparisons.

The index is a copy of part of the table, kept in sorted order. Sorting is what makes lookup fast, and sorting is also what makes insertion slow. Every `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, or `DELETE` that touches an indexed column must update the index too, shuffling entries to keep the sort intact. A table with six indexes pays six times the maintenance cost on every write. The database does not get the reads for free; it trades write speed and storage space for them.

An index hurts when the database cannot use it. A query like `WHERE LOWER(last_name) = 'smith'` applies a function to the column, and the sorted index on the raw `last_name` values is useless. The database falls back to scanning the whole table, and the index sits on disk consuming space and write bandwidth for nothing. The same happens with `WHERE last_name LIKE '%mith'`, because a leading wildcard destroys the sort advantage. The index works only when the query's condition preserves the column's order.

An index hurts when it is redundant. A composite index on `(last_name, first_name)` can serve queries that filter on `last_name` alone, because `last_name` is the leftmost column and the index is sorted by it first. A separate single-column index on `last_name` adds write overhead without adding any lookup the composite index cannot already do.

An index hurts when the table is small. Scanning a thousand rows in memory is faster than the bookkeeping of traversing an index structure, following pointers, and then fetching the rows. On a small table the index is pure overhead.

The cost is always the same trade. Reads get faster because the index avoids a full scan. Writes get slower because every index must stay sorted. Storage grows because the index is a second structure on disk. An index earns its place when it speeds up queries that actually run, with conditions the index can serve, on a table large enough that the scan matters. Every index that does not meet that test is dead weight.

TCP sends data as a stream of numbered bytes, not as a single block. Each byte gets a position in that stream, and every segment TCP puts on the wire carries the starting position of the bytes inside it. The receiver reads that number, places the bytes at the right offset in its receive buffer, and hands the contiguous, in-order bytes to the application above it.

Segments arrive out of order because IP routes each packet independently. Two packets from the same connection can take different paths through the network and arrive in reverse order. A packet can be duplicated by a link-layer retransmission. A packet can be lost entirely when a queue fills and a router drops it. The sequence number is what lets TCP sort this out.

When a segment arrives, the receiver checks its sequence number against the next byte it expects. If the number matches, the bytes are contiguous and the receiver delivers them upward, then advances its expected position. If a later segment arrives first, the receiver stores it in the buffer but does not deliver it, because a gap separates it from the last delivered byte. When the missing segment finally arrives, the receiver fills the gap, delivers the whole contiguous run, and advances. This is why the buffer exists: it holds bytes that arrived early so they are not lost, and it holds them until the gap closes.

The receiver tells the sender what it has. Every acknowledgment segment carries the sequence number of the next byte the receiver expects, which is the first byte after the contiguous block it has received. An acknowledgment of byte 1001 tells the sender that bytes 1 through 1000 arrived in order and are deliverable. If bytes 1001 through 2000 arrived but byte 1001 did not, the receiver keeps acknowledging 1001, because the contiguous run has not advanced. The sender sees the same number repeated and infers that something after that point arrived but the point itself did not.

The sender retransmits what the receiver has not confirmed. It starts a timer when it sends a segment. If the timer expires before an acknowledgment arrives for those bytes, the sender sends them again. The sequence numbers are unchanged on retransmission; the receiver gets a second copy of bytes it may already have, discards the duplicates by checking their numbers against what it has already placed, and acknowledges the next expected byte. Duplicates are harmless because the sequence number makes every byte's position explicit.

The connection opens with a handshake that sets the starting number. Each side picks an initial sequence number for its direction of the stream, not zero, and announces it in the first segment. The other side acknowledges that number plus one, and data begins from there. Starting at a random point rather than zero prevents a delayed segment from an old, closed connection from landing in a new connection with the same port numbers and being accepted as valid data. The sequence space is large enough that a wandering segment from a previous incarnation will fall outside the current window and be rejected.

Order is not a property of the network underneath TCP. IP delivers packets however it can, in whatever order they arrive, and makes no promise about sequence. TCP imposes order on top of that by numbering every byte, buffering what arrives early, holding back what is not yet contiguous, and retransmitting what never arrived. The application sees a stream in the order it was sent because TCP reconstructs that order one gap at a time.

A mutex protects one thing: the interleaving of reads and writes on shared data.

Two threads running on separate cores can touch the same variable at the same time. Thread A reads `count`, adds one, and writes it back. Thread B does the same. If both read before either writes, both read the same value, both add one, and both write the same result. Two increments produced one. The count is wrong, and no thread notices. The memory is sound; the timing broke the arithmetic.
