The mutex fixes this by making the read-modify-write indivisible. A thread acquires the mutex before touching `count` and releases it after. While one thread holds the mutex, every other thread that tries to acquire it blocks — the operating system parks the thread off the CPU until the mutex is free. Only one thread at a time enters the critical section. The second thread's read cannot slip between the first thread's read and its write, because the second thread is not running.

The mutex protects against lost updates, torn writes, and invariant violations. A lost update is the `count` example: two writes, one result. A torn write happens when one thread writes a 64-bit value in two 32-bit memory operations and a second thread reads between the two halves, seeing a value that was never written. An invariant violation happens when one thread reads a linked list while another thread is halfway through removing a node — the reader follows a pointer to a node that no longer belongs to the list.

The mutex protects only what is reached while it is held. A thread that acquires the mutex, copies a pointer to the shared structure, releases the mutex, and then dereferences the pointer is unprotected. Another thread can free the structure in the gap between release and dereference. The mutex guarded the pointer read, not the pointer's target. The scope of the protection is the scope of the hold.

The mutex does not protect against deadlock. Two threads, each holding a different mutex, each waiting for the other's mutex, will wait forever. The mutex created the deadlock; it did not prevent it. Ordering mutex acquisitions in a fixed sequence across all threads breaks the cycle, but that discipline lives in the code that uses the mutex, not in the mutex itself.

The mutex does not protect against reentrancy from the same thread. A thread that acquires a mutex and then calls a function that acquires the same mutex will deadlock on a plain mutex, because the mutex is already held and the thread blocks waiting for itself. A recursive mutex permits this by tracking ownership and acquisition count, releasing only when the count returns to zero. The plain mutex assumes the caller has structured the code so a thread never asks for what it already holds.

The mutex is a serialization point. Every thread that wants the protected data passes through the same gate, one at a time. Under contention, threads queue and wait, and the protected section becomes the bottleneck on throughput. The shorter the section, the less time threads spend waiting and the more concurrency the system sustains. A mutex held across a disk read or a network call serializes every thread behind that one slow operation. The rule is to hold the mutex for the shortest distance that still covers the shared access, and no longer.

Okay — explain how garbage collection finds unused memory, in the plain register already established.

A program allocates memory it cannot always free by hand. It asks the runtime for an object, uses it, and at some point loses the last pointer to it. The object still sits in memory, but nothing in the program can reach it. Garbage collection is the mechanism that finds these unreachable objects and reclaims their space.

The collector's information is the set of references the program can still see. Every local variable, every field of every live object, every entry on the call stack is a root. The roots are the starting points. An object is reachable if a path of references leads from a root to it; otherwise it is garbage. The collector does not inspect the program's logic or guess whether an object is still wanted. It traces references, and what the references cannot touch is dead.

The trace works like a flood fill. The collector begins at the roots, reads each root's reference, and marks the object it points to. It reads that object's fields, finds the objects those fields point to, and marks them. It repeats this for every newly marked object, walking outward through the reference graph until no new object appears. Every object the walk reached is live. Every object it did not reach is unreachable, and no amount of later computation will ever touch it, because no reference path connects it to the running program.

After the trace, the collector sweeps the heap. It walks every allocated object and asks whether the mark is set. If it is, the collector clears the mark and leaves the object in place for the next cycle. If it is not, the collector adds the object's memory to the free list. That space becomes available for the next allocation. This is mark-and-sweep, the scheme used by the original Lisp collectors and by the JVM's basic modes.

Mark-and-sweep leaves gaps. Live objects are scattered through the heap, and the freed space between them is fragmented into small, non-contiguous pieces. A request for a large block fails even when the total free space is sufficient, because no single gap is large enough. Moving collectors solve this by relocating live objects into a compact region, leaving the rest of the heap as one contiguous free range. The collector must update every reference it moves, since the object's address has changed. This is mark-and-compact, and it trades the cost of moving objects for the elimination of fragmentation.

A third scheme avoids the separation between marking and sweeping entirely. A copying collector divides the heap into two halves. The program allocates only in one half. When that half fills, the collector traces from the roots, copies every reachable object into the other half, and leaves the dead objects behind. The old half becomes the next free space in a single stroke. No sweep is needed, because anything not copied is garbage by definition. The cost is that half the heap is always unused, reserved for the next copy.

The trace must see a consistent picture of the reference graph. If the program mutates the heap while the collector is walking it, the collector can miss an object. The program moves a reference from a field the collector already visited to a field it has not yet reached, and the referenced object becomes invisible to the trace — reachable in reality, unmarked in the collector's view, and wrongly freed. The simplest defense is to stop the program's threads for the duration of the trace. This is a stop-the-world pause, and it is the reason garbage collection has a reputation for latency. The program freezes, the collector traces, the program resumes. For small heaps the pause is short. For large heaps it grows with the number of live objects, and a ten-gigabyte heap can mean a pause of hundreds of milliseconds.

Generational collection attacks the pause by exploiting a pattern the collectors observed in real programs. Most objects die young. A local variable allocated inside a function call is unreachable the moment the function returns, which is often within milliseconds of its birth. The collector splits the heap into generations: a young region for new allocations and an old region for objects that have survived several collection cycles. It collects the young region frequently and the old region rarely. A young-generation collection traces only the references that point into the young region, which is a small subset of the full root set, and it finishes in a fraction of the time a full heap trace would take. Objects that survive a few young collections are promoted to the old generation, where the collector leaves them alone until a major cycle runs.

The collector still has to know when the old generation references the young one, or a young collection would miss those references and free a live object. The runtime records every write of a reference from an old object to a young object in a remembered set, a card table, or a write barrier — the names differ, the mechanism is the same. The store instruction that writes the reference also records that the old object's card now points into the young generation. When the young collector traces, it treats those cards as additional roots and follows them into the young region. The old generation is not traced, but its references into the young one are accounted for.

Concurrent collectors push the pause lower by doing most of the work while the program runs. The collector starts a trace, the program continues mutating the heap, and the collector reconciles the changes the program made against the picture it has already built. This requires barriers at read or write sites so the collector can re-examine objects the program touched after the collector passed them. The trade is throughput: the barriers add overhead to every reference operation, and the collector does more work to correct for mutations it observed mid-trace. The JVM's G1 and ZGC, and .NET's server GC, work this way, trading a small constant cost on every allocation and reference access for pauses measured in single-digit milliseconds or less.

The collector finds unused memory by a single principle: what the roots cannot reach is dead. Every scheme — mark-and-sweep, compaction, copying, generational, concurrent — is a strategy for applying that principle within a constraint the program imposes. The constraint is pause time, throughput, or memory footprint, and each scheme picks a different point on that trade. The trace is the same flood fill in all of them. What differs is when it runs, how much of the heap it covers, and whether the program is running while it walks.

A race condition is a bug where the result depends on the order in which two operations happen, and that order is not controlled.

A bank account holds a balance of 100. Two threads each withdraw 40 at the same time. The first thread reads the balance, sees 100, subtracts 40, and prepares to write 60. The second thread reads the balance before the first thread writes. It also sees 100, subtracts 40, and prepares to write 60. Both threads write 60. The account lost 80 and its balance dropped by 40. The math is correct in each thread; the interleaving broke it.

The word "race" names the cause. The two threads race to read the balance before either writes it back. Whichever thread reads first does not matter to the bug — what matters is that both read before either writes. The outcome depends on timing the program never fixed.

The fix is to make the read and the write one indivisible operation. A mutex around the withdrawal forces the second thread to wait until the first finishes. The second thread then reads 60, not 100, and writes 20. The balance is correct. The race disappears because the mutex removed the overlap that caused it.

Race conditions are hard to find because they do not reproduce on every run. The scheduler decides when each thread runs, and two executions of the same program can interleave differently. A test passes a thousand times, then fails once on a slower machine or under heavier load. The bug was always there. The timing changed.

A CPU cache is a small block of fast memory sitting between the processor and main memory. Main memory holds everything the program needs, but it is slow — a read takes roughly a hundred cycles to come back. The cache holds a copy of the data the processor used most recently, and a read that hits the cache returns in three or four cycles.

The cache works because programs do not touch memory at random. A loop that sums an array reads element 5, then 6, then 7, one after another. A function that reads a field of a struct usually reads the next field soon after. This pattern — touching addresses near ones touched before — is called locality of reference, and it is what makes a cache effective. If memory access were random, a four-kilobyte cache holding a fraction of a gigabyte of memory would miss on almost every read and do nothing useful.

The cache is organized into lines, not single bytes. A line is the unit of transfer between main memory and the cache, typically sixty-four bytes. When the processor reads a single byte from an address not in the cache, the memory controller fetches the entire sixty-four-byte line containing that byte and stores it in the cache. The next read from an address within that line — the next array element, the next struct field — hits the cache and returns immediately. The line was going to be fetched anyway; the prefetch turns one expensive memory access into one expensive access plus several cheap ones.

Modern processors have three levels of cache, each larger and slower than the one before. The L1 cache is smallest, around thirty-two kilobytes, split into one block for data and one for instructions, and it answers the processor in three or four cycles. The L2 cache is a few hundred kilobytes and takes roughly a dozen cycles. The L3 cache is several megabytes, shared among all the cores on the chip, and takes thirty to forty cycles. Main memory is the fallback when all three miss, and it costs the full hundred-plus cycles. A cache miss cascades: L1 misses, L2 is checked, L3 is checked, main memory is read, and the line is installed in all three levels on its way back to the processor.

The cache speeds up a program by turning most memory reads into cache reads. A program whose working set — the data it touches in a tight loop — fits in the L1 cache runs almost as if main memory did not exist. The same program whose working set spills past L3 spends a large fraction of its time stalled, waiting for data to come back from memory. The processor can do nothing while it waits. A loop that multiplies two matrices can run ten times faster when the matrices are traversed in the order the cache expects, and ten times slower when they are traversed in the order that evicts lines before they are reused.

Eviction is the cache's limit. A cache holds a fixed number of lines. When a new line arrives and the cache is full, an old line must leave to make room. The processor picks the line that was least recently used, on the assumption that data touched recently will be touched again soon and data untouched for a long time will not. This assumption holds for most programs, but it fails when the working set is larger than the cache. Each new read evicts a line that the program still needs, and the next access to that line misses again. The cache thrashes, fetching and evicting the same lines in a cycle, and the program runs at the speed of main memory.

The cache does not change what the program computes. It changes how long the computation takes. A program that respects the cache — touching data in contiguous runs, keeping working sets small, ordering nested loops so the innermost loop walks memory sequentially — runs fast because the cache turns most reads into three-cycle operations. A program that fights the cache — jumping across memory, evicting lines before reuse, reading data in an order that defeats the line prefetch — runs slow because the processor stalls on every access. The arithmetic is the same in both cases. The memory traffic is not.

Idempotency means a client can send the same request twice and the server ends up in the same state as if it had been sent once.

`GET /users/42` is idempotent by nature. It reads a row and returns it. A hundred identical requests leave the database unchanged. `PUT /users/42` with the same body is idempotent by contract. The first request sets the name to Alice. The second request sets the name to Alice again. The row holds Alice either way. `DELETE /users/42` is idempotent by exhaustion. The first request deletes the row. The second request finds nothing to delete. The row is gone before and after.

`POST /users` is not idempotent. The first request creates Alice. The second request creates Alice again. Two rows now hold the same name, and the server has doubled what the client asked for. The state after two requests differs from the state after one.

The distinction matters when the network breaks between server and client. The server processes the request, but the response never arrives. The client does not know whether the request landed or died in transit, so it sends the request again. If the operation is idempotent, the retry is safe. The second `PUT` writes the same value over itself. The second `DELETE` deletes nothing. If the operation is not idempotent, the retry creates a second booking, charges the card twice, or sends the email a second time.

A server can make `POST` safe against retries without making it idempotent. The client sends a unique key with each request — a UUID it generates once and reuses on every retry of that same request. The server stores the key. On the first request it processes the payment and records the key. On the second request it finds the key already stored and returns the cached result instead of processing again. The operation is not idempotent in the strict sense, because a second request with a different key would create a second payment. It is safe against duplication because the key lets the server recognize the retry and skip the work.

HTTP's standard methods name idempotency as a property of the method, not the implementation. `GET`, `PUT`, and `DELETE` are idempotent in the specification. `POST` and `PATCH` are not. A server that implements `PUT` to append a row instead of replace one has broken the contract, and a client relying on the specification's promise will send duplicates that the server dutifully creates. The property is a promise the method makes. The code has to keep it.

Okay — explain how DNS resolves a hostname to an IP address, in the plain register already established.

A program asks the operating system to connect to `www.example.com`. The operating system does not know where that is. It knows IP addresses, not names, and the name is a label a human can remember, not a route a router can follow. DNS is the system that trades the name for the address.

The resolver is the first stop. It is a library inside the operating system, and its job is to run the lookup on behalf of the program. The resolver checks its own cache first, a small table of names and addresses it has looked up recently. If `www.example.com` is there, the resolver returns the address and the lookup is over. The network was never touched.

If the cache misses, the resolver sends a query to a recursive resolver, usually the one configured by the network or provided by the ISP. The recursive resolver does the walking. It is the agent that chases the name through the hierarchy until it finds the answer, then hands the answer back to the operating system, which hands it to the program.

The recursive resolver starts at the root. The root nameservers are thirteen clusters of servers, identified by the letters A through M, operated by twelve different organizations. They do not know `www.example.com`. They know only which servers hold the top-level domains — `.com`, `.org`, `.net`, the country codes, the rest. The recursive resolver sends the full name to a root server, and the root server answers with a list of the `.com` nameservers' addresses.

The recursive resolver sends the same query to one of those `.com` servers. The `.com` server does not know `www.example.com` either. It knows which nameservers are authoritative for `example.com`, because the operator of `example.com` registered the domain with a registrar, and the registrar told the `.com` registry to delegate the name. The `.com` server returns the addresses of those authoritative servers.

The recursive resolver sends the query one more time, now to an authoritative server for `example.com`. This server holds the actual records for the domain. It finds a record for `www` — an A record containing an IPv4 address, or a CNAME record pointing to another name that must then be resolved in the same fashion. It returns the address. The recursive resolver passes it to the operating system, caches it for the time the record's TTL specifies, and the program connects.

The hierarchy mirrors the name. The root handles the empty label after the final dot. The top-level server handles `.com`. The authoritative server handles `example.com`. Each level delegates the next label down, and the recursive resolver walks the chain from least specific to most specific, asking one question at each stop: who holds the next piece of this name?

The answer can be shorter than the full walk. The recursive resolver's cache, or the operating system's cache, may already hold the `.com` nameserver addresses from a previous lookup of a different `.com` domain. The resolver skips the root and goes straight to `.com`. If the authoritative server for `example.com` was queried recently for another host in the same domain, its address is cached too, and the resolver skips both the root and `.com` and asks the authoritative server directly. The TTL on each cached record controls how long the shortcut holds. A TTL of 3600 means the cached answer is good for an hour; after that, the resolver asks again, because the record might have changed.

The system is brittle in one place and robust everywhere else. The root is the single point from which all delegation flows, and its thirteen clusters are the most attacked infrastructure on the internet. They survive because they are anycast — each cluster advertises the same IP addresses from dozens of physical locations, so a query to a root server lands at the nearest instance, and an attack on one location diverts traffic to the others. The rest of the system is distributed by design. A domain's authoritative servers are run by the domain's operator, often across multiple providers, and the failure of one leaves the others answering. The recursive resolver is the only piece a single user controls, and its failure breaks every lookup on the network it serves.

A deadlock is a state where two threads each hold a resource the other needs, and both wait forever for the other to release it.

Thread A acquires mutex X. Thread B acquires mutex Y. Thread A now tries to acquire mutex Y, and blocks, because B holds it. Thread B tries to acquire mutex X, and blocks, because A holds it. Neither thread will ever move. Each holds what the other wants, and each waits for what the other has. The program hangs. No error fires. No exception propagates. The threads sit parked off the CPU until the process is killed.

The deadlock needs four conditions, all present at once. Mutual exclusion: a mutex is held by one thread at a time. Hold and wait: a thread holding one mutex asks for another. No preemption: a held mutex cannot be forced from its owner; it must be released voluntarily. Circular wait: a cycle of threads exists, each waiting for a resource held by the next. Break any one condition and the deadlock cannot form.

The simplest way to break it is to destroy circular wait. Order every mutex in the program and require all threads to acquire them in that same order. Thread A acquires X, then Y. Thread B acquires X, then Y. B cannot hold Y while waiting for X, because it must acquire X first, and X is held by A, so B blocks at the start before it holds anything. The cycle never closes. A finishes, releases both, and B proceeds.

The fix costs nothing at runtime. It costs discipline in the code. Every function that takes two or more mutexes must know the order and follow it, and every later change to that code must preserve it. A single function that grabs mutex Y before X breaks the ordering and reintroduces the deadlock the rule was written to prevent.

Okay — explain hash map collisions, plain register, every sentence carrying a fact.

A hash map stores values at positions chosen by a hash function. The function maps a key to an integer, which the map reduces modulo the bucket count to pick a slot. Two keys can land in the same slot. That is a collision, and every hash map has a policy for it.

**Separate chaining** keeps a linked list at each slot. On insert, the map hashes the key, finds the slot, and appends the entry to that list. On lookup, it walks the list and compares keys until it finds a match or reaches the end. The list grows with collisions, so a slot hit by ten keys holds ten nodes. Java's `HashMap` and C++'s `std::unordered_map` both use this approach. The cost is one extra pointer per entry and, in the worst case, a lookup that touches every key in the slot.

**Open addressing** stores entries in the bucket array itself. When a key's slot is already occupied, the map probes another slot by a fixed rule and places the entry there. Three rules are common. Linear probing checks the next slot, then the next, stepping by one. Quadratic probing steps by 1, 4, 9, 16 — the square of the attempt number — which spreads entries out but can miss empty slots if the table size is poorly chosen. Double hashing computes a second hash of the key and uses it as the step size, so different keys take different paths through the table. Python's `dict` and Ruby's `Hash` use open addressing.

Open addressing has no pointers to follow, so it is cache-friendly: the CPU prefetches nearby slots because they sit contiguously in memory. The tradeoff is clustering. Linear probing produces long runs of occupied slots that slow every insert and lookup passing through them. Deleting an entry is delicate: removing a node from the middle of a probe sequence breaks the chain, so the map writes a tombstone marker instead and skips it during lookup but reuses it during insert.

Both policies degrade as the table fills. The **load factor** — entries divided by slots — measures how full the table is. Separate chaining tolerates a load factor above 1.0 because lists can grow past the slot count. Open addressing cannot exceed 1.0 because there are no lists, only slots, and every slot holds at most one entry. When the load factor crosses a threshold (0.75 in Java, 2/3 in Python), the map allocates a larger array, rehashes every entry into its new slot, and discards the old array. That rehash is O(n) but amortized across inserts, so any single insert is O(1) on average.

The worst case for both is one bucket holding every key. This happens when an attacker crafts keys that all hash to the same slot, turning lookups into O(n) scans. Hash flooding. Modern maps defend by randomizing the hash function per process — Python seeds its hash with a random value at startup, and SipHash, used by Rust and Swift, is a keyed hash function designed to resist collision attacks. Separate chaining can also switch a slot's list to a balanced tree past a threshold; Java converts a bucket's linked list to a red-black tree at eight entries, turning the worst case from O(n) to O(log n).

Okay — explain database indexes, what they cost, and when those costs outweigh the benefit, in plain register with every sentence carrying a fact.

A database index is a separate data structure stored alongside a table. It holds a copy of one or more columns plus a pointer back to the matching row. The structure is usually a B-tree: a balanced tree where each interior node splits its children by key range, and each leaf holds a sorted run of values. B-tree depth grows logarithmically, so a lookup in a ten-million-row index touches about four nodes — log₂ of 10⁷ rounded up — and each node is a disk page read. Without the index, the database scans every row in the table to find the ones matching a filter. With it, the database traverses the tree, lands on the first matching leaf, and reads only the rows the leaf entries point to.

A query against a million-row table with a WHERE clause on an unindexed column reads a million rows. The same query with an index on that column reads four tree pages plus the matching data pages. That is the case for indexing: turn a full scan into a tree walk.

The index is not free. It costs storage — a B-tree on a 50-column table holding 10 million rows can run hundreds of megabytes, because it duplicates the indexed columns and adds tree overhead. It costs writes. Every INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE that touches an indexed column must update the index too, writing the new leaf page and possibly splitting a node. A table with five indexes takes six writes per insert: one for the row, five for the trees. On a read-heavy analytics database that batch-loads once a night, that cost is invisible. On a transactional system writing thousands of rows per second, it is the dominant constraint.

An index hurts when the database cannot use it, or when it serves a query that does not need it. A B-tree index on a column is useless for a query that does not filter on that column — the database still scans the table, and the index sits on disk consuming space and write bandwidth for nothing. An index on a low-cardinality column — a boolean flag, a status field with three values — rarely helps, because the tree points to a large fraction of the table anyway. A query filtering a million-row orders table on `status = 'shipped'` where 90% of rows are shipped returns 900,000 rows; the index lets the database skip 100,000 rows, and the 900,000 pointer-follows cost more than a sequential scan would have. PostgreSQL tracks this and will choose a sequential scan over an index scan when the index covers too much of the table.

A composite index on `(last_name, first_name)` serves queries filtering on last name, or on both columns. It does not serve a query filtering on first name alone, because the B-tree sorts by last name first and the first names are scattered across every leaf. The index exists, the database reads it, and the read is wasted — the tree cannot prune by the second column without the first. This is the most common way an index hurts: it was built for a query pattern that moved on, and now it taxes every write while serving no read.

Indexes also hurt when two of them compete. A query filtering on `date` and `customer_id`, where each column has its own index, forces the database to pick one, traverse its tree, fetch a set of row pointers, then filter the fetched rows by the other column. If both columns are selective, a composite index on `(date, customer_id)` serves the query in one tree walk. Two single-column indexes in that case are write cost with no read benefit — the database uses one and ignores the other.

The rule is arithmetic, not aesthetic. An index pays for itself when the queries it accelerates run often enough and touch few enough rows that the saved scans outweigh the write overhead and storage cost across every insert and update for the life of the index. It hurts when that inequality runs the other way: the writes are frequent, the queries are rare or unselective, and the index is a tax funding nothing.

Okay — explain how TCP keeps data in order, plain register, every sentence carrying a fact.

TCP gives each byte a number. The sender picks an initial sequence number at connection setup — a 32-bit value chosen randomly, not zero, to keep old packets from a previous connection on the same port from landing in a new stream. The first data byte the sender transmits carries that number, and every byte after it increments by one.

The receiver acknowledges what it has. Every TCP segment the receiver sends back carries an acknowledgment number: the sequence number of the next byte it expects. If the receiver has seen bytes 1 through 500, it sends ACK 501. The sender reads that number and knows 500 bytes arrived.

Gaps are where ordering matters. If bytes 1 through 500 arrive, then bytes 1001 through 1500, the receiver stores the second segment in a buffer and sends ACK 501 again. It will not advance the acknowledgment past 501 until byte 501 arrives. This is cumulative acknowledgment: the receiver tells the sender the lowest contiguous byte it has not yet received, and everything below that number is in order and complete.

The receiver holds out-of-order segments in a memory buffer sized by the receive window, a value it advertises in every segment. The window tells the sender how many bytes it may transmit before waiting for an acknowledgment. When the missing bytes arrive — say 501 through 1000 — the receiver places them in the buffer ahead of the already-stored 1001 through 1500, delivers the full 1-through-1500 run to the application in sequence, and sends ACK 1501.

The sender retransmits what the receiver did not get. It starts a timer when it sends a segment. If the timer expires before an acknowledgment covers those bytes, the sender sends them again. TCP also uses duplicate ACKs as a faster signal: if the receiver sends ACK 501 three times because it received three later segments but not 501, the sender infers a loss and retransmits 501 without waiting for the timer. This is fast retransmit, and it avoids the round-trip delay the timer would impose.

The sequence number is 32 bits, so it wraps after 4,294,967,296 bytes. TCP handles this with modular arithmetic — the comparison "is this sequence number before or after that one" accounts for wraparound, so a segment with a low number near 2³² is treated as later than one near zero if the connection has wrapped. The math is defined in RFC 1323, which also adds timestamp options to disambiguate wrapped numbers on high-bandwidth links where the same sequence space is reused quickly.

What TCP does not do is guarantee delivery to the application in a single read. The application may call `recv` and get 500 bytes, then call again and get 1,500. TCP guarantees the bytes arrive in the order the sender wrote them, not that the application receives them in the same chunking the sender used. A sender that writes 2,000 bytes in one call may see the receiver deliver them as two 1,000-byte reads, or four 500-byte reads, depending on segment size, window, and buffer state. The byte order is preserved; the message boundary is not.

Okay — explain what a mutex protects against, plain register, every sentence carrying a fact.

A mutex protects one thing: shared state touched by more than one thread at the same time. Two threads running on separate cores can both read a variable, both compute a new value from it, and both write back. One write overwrites the other. The losing thread's update is gone. This is a data race, and the result is a variable holding a value that neither thread intended.

The mutex is a lock with two operations. A thread calls `lock` before touching the shared data and `unlock` after. Between those two calls, the mutex guarantees that no other thread holding the same mutex can proceed. The operating system or runtime suspends the second thread at its `lock` call until the first thread calls `unlock`. The protected region — the code between `lock` and `unlock` — is the critical section. Only one thread is inside it at a time.

What the mutex does not protect is everything outside the critical section. A thread that reads a shared counter without locking the mutex sees whatever value the counter holds, including values mid-write from a thread that did lock. The mutex is a contract: every thread accessing the shared state must acquire the lock first. One thread that skips the lock makes the mutex useless for that state. The protection is voluntary and must be universal.

A mutex protects against interleaved access, not against reentrancy from the same thread. A thread that calls `lock`, then calls a function that calls `lock` again on the same mutex deadlocks — it holds the lock and waits for itself to release it. Some implementations offer a recursive mutex that permits this, tracking the lock count and requiring a matching number of unlocks. A plain mutex does not. The deadlock is the thread's own doing; the mutex did what it was told.

The mutex also does not protect against deadlocks between two locks. Thread A locks mutex 1 then mutex 2. Thread B locks mutex 2 then mutex 1. Each holds one and waits for the other. The fix is ordering: every thread acquires the mutexes in the same sequence, so the second thread blocks on mutex 1 before touching mutex 2, and the cycle never closes. The mutex provides mutual exclusion; it does not provide a discipline for combining exclusions. That discipline is the programmer's.

A mutex is not a memory barrier by intent, but on modern hardware acquiring one has the effect of one. The CPU can reorder a thread's reads and writes for efficiency, so a write to a shared variable made before `unlock` could appear to another thread as happening after it. Acquiring and releasing a mutex issue memory fences that prevent this: writes before `unlock` are visible to a thread that next acquires the lock. Without that guarantee, the mutex would exclude concurrent access but still deliver stale or reordered data to the thread entering the critical section. The fence is what makes the lock meaningful, not just the exclusion.

The cost is contention. When two threads want the same mutex, one waits. The waiting thread is not doing work; it is blocked in the kernel scheduler or spinning in a userspace loop, depending on the implementation. A mutex held for ten microseconds across a thousand threads serializes ten milliseconds of work that could have run in parallel. The lock is only worth acquiring when the work inside the critical section is short and the shared state genuinely needs exclusion. A mutex around a counter increment is cheap. A mutex around a network call is a bottleneck — every thread waits for the slowest I/O to finish before any of them can proceed.

Okay — explain how garbage collection finds unused memory, plain register, every sentence carrying a fact.

A program allocates memory on the heap when it creates an object. The runtime hands back a pointer to that block and records that the block is in use. The program stores that pointer in a variable, passes it to functions, builds data structures from it. As the program runs, variables go out of scope, get reassigned, and the pointers that once reached the block disappear. The block is still on the heap. The program no longer has a way to reach it. That is garbage: memory the runtime allocated, the program cannot access, and nothing will ever free.

Garbage collection finds those blocks and returns them to the heap. The core question is reachability: can the program, starting from the pointers it still holds, follow a chain of references to this block? If yes, the block is live. If no, it is garbage. The collector answers that question by tracing the graph of references from a fixed set of starting points.

Those starting points are the roots. The roots are the pointers the program can reach without following any other pointer: the CPU registers, the call stack of every thread, and the global variables. The stack holds the local variables of every function currently executing. The registers hold values the CPU is working on right now. The globals hold references that persist for the program's lifetime. Every live object is reachable from one of these, through some chain of pointers stored in other live objects.

**Mark-and-sweep** is the simplest tracing collector. It runs in two phases. In the mark phase, the collector takes every root pointer, follows it to the object it points to, and marks that object. Then it follows every pointer inside that marked object to the objects it references, and marks those. It repeats this until it has followed every reachable pointer. In the sweep phase, the collector walks the entire heap. Every block it finds that is not marked is garbage. It frees those blocks and clears the marks on the rest. The heap is now clean: every remaining block is reachable, every freed block is available for new allocation.

Mark-and-sweep pauses the program for the entire trace. A heap with ten million objects stops the world while the collector walks the graph. The pause grows with the heap. A program that needs fifty-millisecond response times cannot tolerate a collector that pauses for two seconds on a four-gigabyte heap.

**Copying collection** cuts the pause by compacting the heap at the same time. It splits the heap into two halves: from-space and to-space. The program allocates in from-space until it fills up. Then the collector copies every reachable object from from-space into to-space, packing them contiguously. It updates every pointer to point at the new location. When the copy is done, from-space is empty — everything in it was garbage or has been moved — and the collector swaps the two halves. The program allocates in the new from-space, which was the old to-space, until it fills again.

Copying collection pays no cost for garbage. The collector touches only live objects; dead ones are never examined, just overwritten when the half is reused. A heap that is 90% garbage traces 10% of its objects and declares the rest free by flipping a pointer. The tradeoff is memory: the program uses only half the heap at any time, because the other half sits empty waiting for the next copy. A four-gigabyte heap gives the program two gigabytes of usable space.

Most production collectors combine both. The JVM's generational collector divides the heap into a young generation and an old generation. The young generation is small and collected often with a copying collector. Most objects die young — temporary buffers, loop variables, intermediate strings — so the young-gen collection reclaims a lot of memory by copying the few survivors. Objects that survive several young-gen collections get promoted to the old generation, which is larger and collected less often with mark-and-sweep. The old generation holds long-lived objects: caches, singletons, connection pools. Collecting it is expensive because most of it is live, so the collector runs that trace rarely.

**Concurrent collectors** try to do the tracing while the program runs, not while it is paused. The collector and the program's threads run at the same time, which means the program can move a pointer while the collector is following it. The collector handles this with write barriers: every time the program writes a pointer, the runtime records that write so the collector knows which objects changed during the trace. The collector re-examines those objects at the end to catch references the program added mid-trace. This shrinks the pause but adds overhead to every pointer write. The JVM's G1 collector and Go's runtime both work this way. G1 divides the heap into regions and collects the regions with the most garbage first, pausing only to evacuate objects between regions. Go's collector runs a concurrent mark phase and short stop-the-world pauses at the start and end to flip the mark bit and clean up.

Reference counting is a different approach that does not trace at all. Every object carries a count of how many pointers reference it. When the program creates a pointer to the object, the count goes up. When a pointer is overwritten or goes out of scope, the count goes down. When the count hits zero, no pointer reaches the object, and the runtime frees it immediately. CPython uses this for its memory management. The cost is paid on every pointer assignment, not in batch pauses. The failure mode is cycles: two objects that point at each other have a count of one each, but neither is reachable from the roots. The count never reaches zero, and the memory leaks. CPython runs a separate cycle detector periodically to find and break these. A tracing collector finds cycles for free, because the cycle is unreachable from the roots and the trace never visits it.

The collector's job is to answer one question for every block on the heap: is there a path from a root to this block? The mechanisms differ in when they ask, how much they pause to ask, and whether they compact the heap while they work. The answer is the same. No path, no pointer, no use. Free it.

Okay — explain a race condition with a concrete example, plain register, every sentence carrying a fact.

A race condition happens when two threads read and write the same memory, and the outcome depends on which thread runs first. The program has no control over that ordering. The scheduler decides.

Consider a bank balance stored as an integer, starting at 100. Two threads each deposit 50. Each thread runs the same three instructions: read the balance into a local variable, add 50 to that variable, write the variable back. Thread A reads 100. Thread B reads 100 before A writes. A computes 150 and writes it. B computes 150 and writes it. The balance is 150. It should be 200. Fifty is gone.

The lost update is not a bug in the arithmetic. Both threads added correctly. The bug is that the read and the write are not atomic. Between A's read and A's write, B sneaked its own read. B saw the pre-deposit value and computed from stale data. The window is narrow — a few CPU cycles — but the scheduler can pause a thread at any instruction boundary, and that pause opens it.

The fix is mutual exclusion. A mutex around the read-modify-write block forces the threads to take turns. A locks, reads 100, adds, writes 150, unlocks. B locks, reads 150, adds, writes 200, unlocks. The balance is correct. The mutex made the three instructions atomic with respect to other threads holding the same lock.

Race conditions are hard to reproduce because they depend on timing. A test that runs the two deposits a million times may pass every time on a single-core machine where the scheduler interleaves predictably. The same test on an eight-core chip, where both threads run simultaneously on separate cores, fails on the third run. The bug is real every run; the timing just does not expose it every time. This is why concurrency bugs are the worst class to diagnose: the program is wrong, the test is green, and the failure arrives in production at 3 a.m. when load patterns shift.

Okay — explain how a CPU cache speeds up a program, plain register, every sentence carrying a fact.

A CPU runs at four gigahertz. Main memory runs at about three hundred megahertz. The processor can execute several instructions per cycle, so it needs data faster than memory can deliver it. A request to DRAM takes roughly one hundred nanoseconds to return. In that span the CPU could have completed four hundred instructions. It sits idle instead, waiting for the data.

The cache closes that gap. It is a small block of SRAM built into the processor die, sitting between the execution units and the memory controller. SRAM is faster than DRAM because it uses six transistors per bit instead of a capacitor, and it does not need to refresh. It is also more expensive — a megabyte of SRAM takes more silicon than a megabyte of DRAM, which is why caches are small. A modern desktop chip has 64 kilobytes of L1 cache per core, 512 kilobytes of L2, and 16 megabytes of L3 shared across all cores.

L1 responds in one or two nanoseconds. L2 takes four to ten. L3 takes thirty to forty. DRAM takes one hundred. The cache hierarchy catches the data the CPU needs most often and holds it at the fastest level.

It works because programs do not access memory at random. They access it in patterns, and those patterns repeat. A loop that sums an array reads element 0, then 1, then 2, then 3. Once the CPU reads address 0, it will almost certainly read address 1 next. This is spatial locality: nearby memory gets accessed close together in time. The cache exploits it by fetching in chunks, not one word at a time. A cache line is 64 bytes on most x86 and ARM processors. When the CPU requests a four-byte integer at address 1000, the memory controller pulls the full 64-byte line containing addresses 976 through 1039 and loads it into the cache. The next three integers the loop reads are already there.

The other pattern is temporal locality: a memory location accessed once is likely to be accessed again soon. A variable used inside a loop is read and written on every iteration. The first read misses the cache and fetches from DRAM. Every subsequent read hits the cache and returns in one nanosecond. The loop runs fast because the data stays in the cache across iterations.

A cache hit is a request the cache satisfies. A cache miss is one it cannot, which forces the CPU to fetch from the next level down. The hit rate determines the speedup. A program with a 95% L1 hit rate serves most reads in one nanosecond and the remaining 5% from L2 at five nanoseconds, averaging 1.2 nanoseconds per access. The same program running from DRAM averages one hundred. The cache makes memory access eighty times faster for that program.

The hit rate depends on the working set — the bytes the program touches in a tight loop. A loop that walks a 32-kilobyte array fits entirely in L1 and hits on every access after the first pass. A loop that walks an eight-megabyte array exceeds L1 and L2 but fits in L3, hitting at thirty nanoseconds. A loop that walks a 200-megabyte array exceeds every cache level and hits DRAM on every access, and the cache provides no speedup at all. The array size determines the speed, because it determines which level of the hierarchy holds the data.

Cache misses come in three kinds, and the distinction matters for why a program is slow. A compulsory miss is the first access to a line — the data was never in the cache, so the CPU must fetch it. Nothing avoids these; the data has to arrive once. A capacity miss happens when the working set is larger than the cache. The CPU loads a line, uses it, loads more lines that evict it, then needs the first line again. The cache was full, so the old data was discarded to make room. A conflict miss happens when two memory addresses map to the same cache slot. L1 caches are typically set-associative with eight ways, meaning eight lines can occupy each set. If a loop alternates between nine addresses that all hash to the same set, the cache evicts one on every access even though the other seven ways are empty. The cache has room, but the mapping collides.

The eviction policy is least-recently-used. When the cache needs to discard a line to make room for a new one, it picks the line that was accessed longest ago. This works because of temporal locality: a line not touched in a while is unlikely to be touched soon. The hardware tracks access order per set using a small recency table, not a timestamp — there is no room for that — but the effect is the same. The lines the program is actively using stay; the ones it abandoned leave.

The cache also speeds up writes. A store instruction writes to L1 and returns immediately. The cache line is now dirty: it holds data newer than DRAM. The CPU writes it back to memory later, either when the line is evicted or when another core requests it. This lets the program continue executing without waiting for the DRAM write to finish. A program that writes a thousand values to an array in a loop touches L1 on every store, not DRAM. The writes complete in one nanosecond each, and the cache flushes them to memory in the background.

What makes a program cache-friendly is accessing memory in the order it is laid out. C stores a two-dimensional array in row-major order: row 0's elements are contiguous, then row 1's, then row 2's. A loop that walks the array row by row reads consecutive addresses and hits the cache on every element after the first in each line. A loop that walks it column by column jumps by the row length on every access — 64 bytes for a 64-element row of integers — and every access lands in a different cache line. The column-wise loop misses on every element. The row-wise loop misses once per 16 elements. Same array, same work, sixteen times the memory traffic. The cache made the row-wise loop fast and did nothing for the column-wise one, because the access pattern matched or fought the way the cache fetches data.

Okay — explain idempotency for an HTTP API, plain register, every sentence carrying a fact.

An operation is idempotent when calling it once has the same effect as calling it a hundred times. The result is not that nothing happens. The result is that the second through hundredth calls do not change anything the first call did not already change.

For an HTTP API, this means a client can retry a request without fear. Networks drop connections. Proxies time out. The client never saw a response and does not know whether the server processed the request. It sends it again. If the operation is idempotent, the retry is safe. The server's state after the retry matches its state after the first attempt.

`GET` is idempotent by definition. It reads a resource and returns a representation. It does not modify server state, so a retry changes nothing. `PUT` is idempotent by contract. A `PUT` to `/users/42` replaces the resource at that path with the body the client sent. The first request creates or overwrites the user. The second request overwrites it with the same body. The resource ends in the same state. `DELETE` is idempotent in the same way. The first call removes the resource. The second call finds nothing to remove and returns 404, or returns 204 depending on the implementation. The resource is gone either way. The state is the same.

`POST` is not idempotent. A `POST` to `/users` creates a new user. The server assigns it an ID, writes it to the database, and returns 201. The client's connection drops before it reads the response. The client retries. The server creates a second user with a second ID and a second row. The database now holds two users where the client wanted one. This is the classic duplicate-submission problem, and it is why payment forms say "do not click twice."

The HTTP specification defines idempotency as a property of the method, not the implementation. A server that makes `GET` increment a counter in a database has broken the contract. The method promises safety; the code violates it. A client relying on that promise retries the `GET` and inflates the counter. The spec is clear about this: the property belongs to the method's semantics, and a server that ignores it does so at the cost of every client that follows the spec.

The harder case is idempotency across failures. A `PUT` that arrives at the server, writes the resource, and then crashes before sending a response leaves the client blind. The client retries. The server processes the `PUT` again and overwrites the resource with the same body. The state is correct. But if the server had crashed mid-write — after updating the database row but before flushing the transaction log — the retry completes the write. The first attempt was partial; the second made it whole. Idempotency held because the operation was a full replacement, not a delta.

`PATCH` is the method that breaks idempotency in practice. A `PATCH` sending a JSON merge document that sets `{"status": "active"}` is idempotent: applying it twice leaves the status at `active`. A `PATCH` sending a JSON Patch document that adds an element to an array is not: applying it twice adds two elements. The method's idempotency depends on the body's semantics, which is why `PATCH` is listed as non-idempotent in the spec. The client cannot assume it.

The practical fix for non-idempotent operations is an idempotency key. The client generates a unique token — a UUID — and sends it in an `Idempotency-Key` header. The server stores the key with the response. On a retry with the same key, the server returns the stored response instead of processing the request again. Stripe's API uses this pattern. The first `POST /v1/charges` with a given key creates the charge and returns the result. The second call with the same key returns the cached result without creating a second charge. The operation becomes idempotent by contract, enforced by the server, keyed by the client. This is how a non-idempotent method gets idempotent behavior: the server remembers what it did and refuses to do it twice.

Okay — explain DNS resolution from name to IP, plain register, every sentence carrying a fact.

A browser types `example.com` into a URL bar. The operating system needs its address — 93.184.216.34 — before it can open a TCP connection. DNS is the system that returns that address. It is a distributed database with no single server holding every name, and the resolution walks it in stages.

The walk starts at the **stub resolver**, a library inside the operating system. The resolver reads `/etc/resolv.conf` on Linux or the network control panel on Windows, finds the address of a **recursive resolver**, and sends it a query: "What is the A record for `example.com`?" The stub resolver does no walking itself. It hands the question to the recursive resolver and waits.

The recursive resolver is the agent that does the walking. It is usually operated by the ISP or a public provider like Cloudflare at 1.1.1.1 or Google at 8.8.8.8. It receives the query and checks its cache first. If it has answered this question recently, it returns the cached address and the walk stops here. If not, it begins at the root.

The root zone is the top of the DNS hierarchy. Its servers — the thirteen logical root instances, labeled A through M, replicated across more than a thousand physical locations via anycast — hold the addresses of the **top-level domain** servers. The recursive resolver picks one root server from a built-in list, sends the query for `example.com`, and the root server replies with a referral: "I do not know `example.com`, but here are the addresses of the `.com` TLD servers." The root never answers with an IP for a name. It answers with the next server down.

The resolver sends the same query to a `.com` TLD server. Verisign operates the `.com` registry and runs those servers. The TLD server holds the **delegation** for every domain under `.com`: the addresses of the authoritative name servers that each domain's owner has registered. The TLD server replies with a referral: "I do not know `example.com`, but here are the addresses of `a.iana-servers.net` and `b.iana-servers.net`, the authoritative servers for `example.com`."

The resolver sends the query to one of those authoritative servers. The authoritative server holds the actual records for the domain — the zone file the domain owner configured. It reads the file, finds the A record for `example.com`, and returns `93.184.216.34`. This is the answer. The resolver caches it for the **time to live** — the number of seconds the authoritative server specified, often 3600 — and returns it to the stub resolver. The operating system hands the address to the browser, and the TCP handshake begins.

Each step trims the question. The root answers for the top-level domain. The TLD answers for the domain. The authoritative server answers for the record. The resolver caches every referral and every answer along the way, so the next lookup for any `.com` domain skips the root and starts at the TLD, and the next lookup for `example.com` returns from cache without walking at all.

The system handles names with more labels the same way. `api.staging.example.com` sends the resolver to the root, then `.com`, then `example.com`'s authoritative servers. Those servers hold the delegation for `staging.example.com` and return its name servers. The resolver queries those, gets the delegation for `api.staging`, queries those servers, and receives the A record. Each zone delegates the next subdomain down, and the resolver follows the chain until a server answers with a record instead of a referral.

DNS runs over UDP port 53. A query and its response fit in a single 512-byte UDP packet for most lookups, which keeps the round-trip count at one per step. Responses larger than 512 bytes — DNSSEC signatures, large TXT records — trigger a fallback to TCP, where the resolver reopens on port 53 and reissues the query. The fallback is rare for A-record lookups but common for DNSKEY and RRSIG queries.

The whole walk takes four round trips in the cold-cache case: resolver to root, resolver to TLD, resolver to authoritative, resolver to stub. At thirty milliseconds per round trip to each server, that is one hundred twenty milliseconds before the browser opens its connection. A warm cache collapses it to one round trip — the stub resolver to the recursive resolver, which returns the cached answer in a single packet.

Okay — explain a deadlock with a concrete example and one avoidance method, plain register, every sentence carrying a fact.

A deadlock is two threads stopped forever, each waiting for a lock the other holds. Neither moves. Neither times out. The program hangs.

Two threads, two mutexes. Thread A locks mutex 1, then tries to lock mutex 2. Thread B locks mutex 2, then tries to lock mutex 1. A holds what B wants. B holds what A wants. The scheduler runs A until it blocks on mutex 2, then runs B until it blocks on mutex 1. Both threads are now sleeping. Neither will wake. The locks are never released.

The deadlock needs four conditions, identified by Coffman in 1971. Mutual exclusion: each mutex is held by one thread at a time. Hold and wait: a thread holding one lock requests another. No preemption: a thread cannot force another to release a lock. Circular wait: a cycle of threads where each holds a lock the next one needs. Break any condition and the deadlock cannot form.

The simplest break is lock ordering. Every thread acquires the mutexes in the same sequence. Thread A locks mutex 1, then mutex 2. Thread B locks mutex 1, then mutex 2. B blocks on mutex 1 before it touches mutex 2. A finishes its work, releases both, and B proceeds. The cycle never closes because no thread holds a lock that an earlier-ordered thread needs.

Lock ordering works when the set of locks is known and the order is fixed. It fails when a thread acquires locks dynamically — a function that locks a row in a database table, then calls another function that locks a different row, and the second row's order depends on data the first query returned. Two transactions running that code can still deadlock if they pick rows in opposite orders. The fix there is sorting: the transaction acquires row locks in a sorted order — by primary key, for instance — so two transactions touching rows 5 and 12 both lock 5 first, then 12. The order is not hardcoded in the code. It is derived from the data at runtime, and the sort guarantees every transaction picks the same sequence.

The cost of lock ordering is a constraint on how code is written. A function that needs mutex 2 cannot lock it if the caller already holds mutex 1 and the order is 1-then-2 — the function must release mutex 1 first, or the caller must pass both locks in. The discipline is rigid, but the alternative is a program that runs correctly a million times and freezes on the million-and-first, in production, at the load that finally interleaved two threads the wrong way.

A hash map turns a key into an integer, then uses that integer as an index into an array. The function that does this — the hash function — maps a large domain (strings, objects, numbers) onto a small range (0 through the array length minus one). Two different keys can land on the same index. That is a collision, and every hash map has a strategy for it.

**Chaining** stores a linked list at each array slot. When two keys hash to the same index, both entries live in that slot's list. A lookup walks the list and compares keys one by one. The cost is proportional to the list length. If the hash function spreads keys evenly and the table stays below its load factor, lists stay short — one or two nodes — and lookups stay near O(1). If the function clusters keys or the table overfills, a single list can grow long and a lookup degrades toward O(n).

**Open addressing** stores all entries in the array itself. On collision, the map probes another slot according to a fixed sequence. Linear probing checks the next slot, then the next, until it finds an empty one. Quadratic probing jumps by squares of increasing size. Double hashing uses a second hash function to set the probe step, which breaks up clustering patterns that linear probing creates. Deletion is the hard part: removing an entry and leaving a bare gap breaks the probe chain, so the map writes a tombstone marker that a later insert can reclaim but a probe treats as occupied.

The two approaches trade off differently. Chaining wastes memory on list nodes but tolerates load factors above 1.0 — more entries than slots — because lists simply grow. Open addressing uses memory more tightly, since every byte is array space, but degrades sharply past about 70% full, when probe sequences lengthen and reads touch more cache lines. Most standard-library implementations (Java's `HashMap`, Python's `dict`, Rust's `std::collections::HashMap`) use chaining or a variant of it, though Python switched its `dict` to a combined open-addressing-plus-compact-key-array layout in 3.6 to preserve insertion order and cut memory.

When the load factor crosses a threshold — typically 0.75 for chaining, lower for open addressing — the map allocates a larger array, often double the size, and re-inserts every entry. Rehashing is O(n) but amortized O(1) per insert, because it happens rarely relative to the number of operations between resizes. A map that never resizes, or one given a fixed capacity at construction, avoids the rehash cost but pays in collision rate if the estimate is low.

A database index is a second data structure stored alongside the table. The table holds rows in the order they were written. The index holds key-to-location pairs in an order that makes lookup fast.

The commonest shape is a B-tree. It sorts the indexed column — last name, order date, product ID — and stores each sorted value beside a pointer to the row it came from. A query that filters on that column walks the tree, finds the matching keys, and follows the pointers to the rows. Without the index, the database reads every row in the table and checks each one. With the index, it reads a handful of tree pages.

The gain shows in the numbers. A table of ten million rows, searched for one employee ID, reads perhaps four B-tree pages with the index and ten million rows without it. On disk, that is the difference between milliseconds and seconds. The index also serves any query whose `WHERE` clause tests a range on the indexed column — all orders between two dates, all prices above a threshold — because the sorted order groups those rows together.

The cost is paid in three places.

Storage. The index is a copy of part of the table, sorted and pointered. Indexing five columns on a wide table can double the disk footprint. A table that fits in memory unindexed may not fit once the indexes land, and the spill to disk slows everything.

Write speed. Every `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, or `DELETE` that touches an indexed column must update the index too. One row in, two B-trees to maintain. A table that takes a thousand inserts per second unindexed might take three hundred with four indexes, because each insert re-sorts into each tree. The read gain on lookups trades directly against write cost on mutations.

The wrong query. An index helps when the query narrows the result set. A query that selects most of the table — all employees in a company of fifty thousand, where forty-eight thousand match — gains nothing from the index and loses the cost of reading the index pages plus the table rows. The optimizer, seeing this, often skips the index and scans the table directly. But an index built for a query that no longer runs, or built on a column with three distinct values across a million rows, sits on disk doing nothing, soaking up writes, and never earning its keep. A column storing `active`/`inactive` across a million rows has no useful sort order; the index there is dead weight.

The rule is arithmetic, not principle. If the indexed column appears in queries that return few rows relative to the table size, and the table is read more often than it is written, the index pays for itself. If the column is written heavily, queried rarely, or returns most of the table when queried, the index is a tax with no benefit. Dropping it reclaims the storage and the write cycles.

TCP sends data as numbered bytes, not as messages. Each byte gets a sequence number from a counter that starts at a random value chosen during the handshake — the initial sequence number — and increases by one for every byte sent. A 1400-byte segment carrying sequence number 10001 covers bytes 10001 through 11400.

The receiver acknowledges what it has. When a segment arrives, the receiver sends back an acknowledgment number: the sequence number of the *next* byte it expects. If it receives bytes 10001 through 11400 in order, it replies with 11401. That single number tells the sender everything received is contiguous up to that point.

Gaps are where ordering breaks and gets repaired. If bytes 10001–11400 arrive, then 12801–14200 arrives next, the receiver has a hole from 11401 to 12800. It stores the out-of-order segment in a receive buffer and sends back 11401 again — the same acknowledgment it sent before. This is a duplicate ACK. It tells the sender: everything up to 11401 is fine, and something after that is missing.

The sender keeps a send buffer and a list of which bytes are acknowledged. When it sends a segment, it starts a timer. If the timer fires before an acknowledgment for those bytes arrives, it retransmits. If it receives three duplicate ACKs for the same number — three messages all saying 11401 — it treats that as a faster signal than the timer: a segment was lost, and later segments got through. It retransmits the missing segment without waiting for the timer to expire. This is TCP's fast retransmit.

The receive buffer is where reassembly happens. Segments can arrive in any order because they took different paths through the network or one was dropped and retransmitted. The receiver places each segment's bytes at the position its sequence number specifies, like numbered tiles in a slot rack. Bytes 12801–14200 sit in the buffer waiting. When 11401–12800 finally arrives — retransmitted or merely delayed — it fills the hole. The receiver now has a contiguous run from 10001 through 14200. It passes that run to the application in order and sends a single ACK for 14201.

The application above TCP never sees the gaps. It receives a byte stream in the order the sender wrote it, regardless of how the segments arrived on the wire. The sequence numbers, the buffer, and the acknowledgments do the reordering work below that interface.

Flow control sets the pace. Each ACK carries a window size — the number of bytes the receiver has room to buffer. A receiver reading slowly, with its buffer filling up, advertises a small window. The sender stops or slows so the buffer does not overflow and drop segments that would then need retransmission. A window of zero tells the sender to wait until the receiver drains the buffer and advertises a nonzero window again. This keeps the sender from burying a slow receiver under data it cannot hold, which would create more gaps and more retransmits.

Congestion control does the same job for the network between them. The sender tracks a second window — the congestion window — sized by how fast the network seems to be carrying data. It grows the window as segments are acknowledged and shrinks it on loss. Where flow control protects one receiver's buffer, congestion control protects the shared routers and links, so the sender does not push more bytes into the network than the network can deliver. Both windows apply at once; the sender uses the smaller of the two.

The ordering guarantee rests on three pieces working together. Sequence numbers stamp every byte with its position. Acknowledgments report the contiguous frontier and signal gaps through duplicates. The receive buffer holds out-of-order segments until the missing ones arrive, then releases the repaired run to the application. The wire delivers segments in whatever order it manages. TCP turns that into an ordered stream.

A mutex protects one thing: two threads touching the same memory at the same time and corrupting it.

The corruption is concrete. A counter at 0 is read by two threads, each adds 1, each writes 1. The counter should be 2. It is 1. A linked list has its head pointer updated by one thread while another walks the list, and the walker follows a pointer into freed memory. A buffer is read as it is being written, and the reader gets half of one value and half of the next. These are data races, and their results are nondeterministic: the program produces different outputs on different runs depending on which thread the scheduler ran first.

The mutex — short for mutual exclusion — is a lock with one rule. Only one thread can hold it at a time. A thread that wants to enter the protected section calls `lock`. If no one holds the mutex, it acquires it and enters. If another thread holds it, the caller blocks — the operating system parks it until the mutex is free, then wakes it. When the holder leaves the section, it calls `unlock`, and the mutex passes to one of the waiting threads.

The section between `lock` and `unlock` is the critical section. Everything inside it is serialized. Two threads that both lock the same mutex before touching the counter cannot both read it at 0, because the second one cannot enter until the first unlocks. The increment becomes atomic with respect to other lockers: read, add, write, all behind the lock, no interleaving.

What the mutex does not protect is everything else. A thread that never locks the mutex and writes the counter anyway races against the threads that do. The mutex is a convention, not a memory fence. It guards access only for callers that acquire it first. A second mutex on a second lock does not protect against a thread holding the first. Locking mutex A then waiting for mutex B, while another thread holds B and waits for A, is deadlock: both block forever, each holding what the other needs.

The cost is the wait. A mutex turns concurrent access into serial access. Ten threads that contend on one mutex run that section one at a time, and the other nine sit idle. If the critical section is a four-line counter update, the wait is microseconds and the cost is invisible. If the section holds the mutex across a network call or a disk read, nine threads wait seconds for one, and the program's throughput drops to the speed of a single thread. The discipline is to hold the lock for the shortest scope that covers the shared memory and no longer.

A mutex protects against interleaved access to shared state. It does not protect against the thread that skips the lock, the lock held too long, or the two locks acquired in opposite orders. Those are the failures the mutex cannot prevent, because they are failures to use it correctly.

Garbage collection finds memory the program no longer reaches and returns it to the allocator. The question is how it knows what is unreachable, since a pointer and a freed pointer look the same until something follows them.

Every collector starts from a fixed set of roots. The roots are the things the running program can touch directly: the CPU registers, the call stack of every thread, and the global or static variables. These are the entry points. Anything reachable from a root is live. Anything not reachable from a root is garbage, no matter what it was used for a millisecond ago.

The collector treats memory as a graph. Each object is a node. Each pointer from one object to another is an edge. Starting at the roots, the collector walks every edge it can find, marking each object it reaches. When the walk finishes, every marked object is live and every unmarked object is dead. This is tracing, and it is the core of every modern collector — Java's G1 and ZGC, Go's runtime, .NET's GC, V8's heap.

The walk has to know where the pointers are. An object header that records the field offsets, a compiler that emits a stack map of pointer locations, a conservative mode that treats any word that looks like a heap address as a pointer — these are the mechanisms that let the collector follow edges rather than scanning blindly. A collector without this metadata either cannot move objects or risks keeping dead objects alive because a stray integer happened to look like a pointer.

After tracing, the collector reclaims the unmarked memory. Two strategies divide here.

A sweeping collector walks the entire heap and adds every unmarked object back to a free list. The heap stays in place; objects keep their addresses. The cost is proportional to the total heap size, not the amount of garbage, because the collector must look at every object to find the dead ones. CPython's reference-count-plus-cycle-collector works this way, and so do many older stop-the-world collectors.

A copying collector does not walk the whole heap. It takes the live — marked — objects and copies them into a new region of memory, one after another, packing them tight. The old region is then reclaimed wholesale: one free operation, no per-object walk. Copying costs proportional to the amount of live data, which is usually small, and it defragments the heap as a side effect. The cost is that every pointer to a moved object must be updated to its new address, which is why copying collectors need exact pointer maps and cannot run in conservative mode.

Most production collectors combine both, split by age. Objects are allocated in a young region. Most objects die young, so the young region is collected often with a copying collector — few survivors, little to copy, fast pause. Objects that survive several young collections are promoted to an old region. The old region is collected less often, usually by sweeping or mark-compact, because old objects tend to stay alive and copying them would be expensive. This generational split rests on the weak generational hypothesis: most objects die young. The hypothesis holds well enough in practice that every major runtime uses it.

The pause is the cost the program pays. While the collector traces or copies, the application threads either stop entirely or must cooperate at safe points — places the compiler has marked safe to pause because no object is mid-update. A stop-the-world collector pauses every thread, runs the full trace, and resumes. The pause length scales with heap size and live-object count. A concurrent collector traces while the application runs, which shortens or eliminates the pause but pays in overhead: barriers on every pointer write to tell the collector when the graph changes, and a fixup pass to catch objects that died during the trace. Go's collector runs concurrently and targets sub-millisecond pauses by spending more CPU on bookkeeping. ZGC in Java colors pointers and does most work concurrently to keep pauses under a millisecond on multi-gigabyte heaps.

Reference counting is the other lineage, and it does not trace. Each object carries a count of incoming pointers. When a pointer is created, the count rises. When a pointer is dropped, the count falls. At zero, the object is unreachable by definition — no one points to it — and is freed immediately. The cost is paid on every pointer assignment rather than in batch pauses. The failure mode is cycles: two objects pointing at each other keep each other's count at 1 forever, even when nothing else reaches either. A cycle collector must run periodically to find and break those rings, which means reference-counting systems still need a tracing pass for correctness. Swift uses reference counting without a cycle collector and pushes the problem to the programmer with `weak` and `unowned` references. CPython uses reference counting plus a cycle detector.

The collector finds unused memory by starting at what the program can still touch, walking every pointer to everything reachable, and reclaiming everything the walk never reached.
