The differences between collectors are differences of strategy — sweep versus copy, generational versus flat, stop-the-world versus concurrent, tracing versus reference counting — not of principle. The principle is reachability.

A race condition is what happens when two threads act on the same data and the result depends on which one the scheduler runs first. The program is correct under one ordering and wrong under another, and the scheduler does not promise an ordering.

The example is a bank balance. Two threads transfer money into one account at the same time. The balance starts at 100. Thread A reads 100, adds 50, writes 150. Thread B reads 100, adds 30, writes 130. Both threads ran. Both additions happened. The balance is 130, not 180. Twenty dollars vanished — not stolen, just never recorded, because B read the old value before A wrote the new one.

The failure is silent. No exception fires. No log entry appears. The code returns a number that looks plausible and is wrong. Run the same transfer a thousand times and the error appears on some runs and not others, depending on thread timing, CPU load, and which core the scheduler chose. A test that passes today fails tomorrow on a faster machine, because faster machines expose tighter interleavings that slower ones never hit.

The fix is to make the read-add-write atomic — one thread finishes before the other starts. A mutex around the balance update serializes the two threads: A locks, reads, adds, writes, unlocks; B waits for the lock and then reads the value A wrote. The result is 180 every time. The cost is that the two transfers no longer run in parallel; they queue at the lock. For a balance update that is microseconds, and the correctness is worth it.

The race exists because the three operations — read, add, write — are separate instructions, and the scheduler can switch threads between any of them. What looks like one step in the source code is three steps in the machine, and another thread can land between them.

A CPU cache is a small block of fast memory sitting between the processor and main memory. Main memory — DRAM — takes roughly 100 nanoseconds to deliver a byte. The cache — SRAM — delivers in 1 to 2 nanoseconds. The cache exists because the processor can do work only as fast as it gets data, and DRAM is fifty times too slow to keep up.

The cache holds copies of the data main memory already has. When the processor reads an address, it checks the cache first. If the address is there — a cache hit — the read completes in 1 or 2 nanoseconds and main memory is never touched. If the address is not there — a cache miss — the processor fetches it from DRAM, pays the 100-nanosecond cost, and stores a copy in the cache so the next read hits. A program that hits 95% of the time averages 6 nanoseconds per read instead of 100. That factor of sixteen is the entire reason the cache exists.

The cache does not copy one byte at a time. It copies a cache line — 64 bytes on most x86 and ARM processors. When the processor reads one byte from a new address, the hardware pulls the 64-byte block surrounding it into the cache. If the next read lands inside that same block, it is already cached. This is why reading an array front to back is fast and jumping through it by large strides is slow. A loop that sums `array[0], array[1], array[2]` in order loads one cache line and gets eight 8-byte values from it. A loop that sums `array[0], array[8], array[16]` loads a new cache line for each value and pays the DRAM cost each time.

Caches are layered. The L1 cache is smallest and closest — 32 kilobytes on a typical core, 1-nanosecond access, one per core. The L2 cache is larger and one step farther — 256 kilobytes, 4-nanosecond access, one per core. The L3 cache is shared across all cores — 8 to 32 megabytes, 12-nanosecond access. A read checks L1, then L2, then L3, then DRAM. Each miss costs more time. The hierarchy works because most programs touch a small set of addresses repeatedly — a tight loop, a struct, a small hash table — and that set fits in L1 or L2.

The cache also speeds up writes. A store writes to L1 and returns immediately; the processor does not wait for DRAM. The cache line is marked dirty, and the hardware writes it back to main memory later, in a batch. A program that writes a thousand values to a contiguous array fills twelve and a half cache lines, marks them dirty, and moves on. The DRAM writes happen in the background.

Cache misses come in three kinds, and the distinction matters for tuning. A compulsory miss is the first read of an address — nothing was cached yet, so the fetch is unavoidable. A capacity miss happens because the working set is larger than the cache; data is loaded, evicted to make room, then loaded again. A conflict miss happens because the cache maps memory addresses to a limited set of slots, and two hot addresses land in the same slot, evicting each other even when the cache is not full. Loop tiling — breaking a large matrix operation into blocks that fit in L1 — attacks capacity misses. Padding a struct so its hot fields do not share a cache line with its cold ones attacks conflict misses.

The cache speeds up a program by being close, being fast, and exploiting the fact that programs touch the same memory over and over. The processor runs at the speed of its cache hits, not the speed of its memory bus. A program written to stay inside the cache lines it has already loaded runs at the cache's 2-nanosecond pace. A program that jumps through memory at random runs at DRAM's 100-nanosecond pace. Same processor, same clock speed, fifty times slower.

Idempotency means a client can send the same request twice and the server ends up in the same state as if it were sent once. The second call does not duplicate the first. It does not charge the card twice, create two rows, or append a second record. It either repeats the original result or reports that the result already exists.

HTTP defines `GET`, `PUT`, and `DELETE` as idempotent. `GET` reads; calling it ten times changes nothing. `PUT` sends a full resource representation; sending the same `PUT` twice writes the same data twice, and the second write overwrites the first with identical content, leaving one resource. `DELETE` removes a resource; deleting the same ID a second time finds nothing to remove and returns 404, but the server state — resource gone — is the same as after the first call.

`POST` is not idempotent. Each `POST` typically creates a new resource with a new server-generated ID. Two identical `POST` requests create two resources. A checkout form submitted twice charges the card twice, because the server treats each request as a new action rather than a replay of the first.

The practical problem is the gap between the client sending a request and the client receiving the response. The network drops the response, or the client times out before it arrives, or the user clicks submit twice. The client does not know whether the server processed the request, so it retries. If the operation is not idempotent, the retry doubles the work.

The fix is an idempotency key. The client generates a unique identifier — a UUID — and sends it in a header, typically `Idempotency-Key`. The server stores the key alongside the result of the first request. When a second request arrives with the same key, the server recognizes it as a replay and returns the stored result instead of running the operation again. Stripe's API uses this pattern on its charge endpoints: a key sent once processes the payment, the same key sent again returns the original charge object, and no second charge occurs.

The key makes a non-idempotent operation safe to retry. `POST /payments` with key `abc-123` runs the charge. A retry with key `abc-123` returns the cached charge. A different `POST /payments` with key `def-456` runs a new charge. The server tracks keys for a window — 24 hours in Stripe's case — and expires them after, so the same key reused a day later starts a fresh operation.

Idempotency is a contract about state, not about the response. A `DELETE` that succeeds returns 200 the first time and 404 the second. The status codes differ, but the server state — resource absent — is identical. A retry that receives a 404 can stop retrying, because the deletion already happened. The idempotency guarantee is that the state holds, not that the bytes match.

DNS turns a name into an address by walking a tree of servers, each one answering a smaller piece of the question until one server knows the whole answer.

The browser asks the resolver. The resolver is the first server in the chain, usually run by the ISP or a public provider like Cloudflare at 1.1.1.1 or Google at 8.8.8.8. The browser sends it the name — `www.example.com` — and waits.

The resolver does not know the address. It knows where to start. The start is the root servers, thirteen of them, named A through M, operated by ICANN and scattered across the world. The resolver asks a root server for `www.example.com`.

The root server does not know the address either. It knows the top-level domains. It reads the name right to left, finds `.com`, and hands back a list of the `.com` servers — the servers authoritative for every name ending in `.com`. Verisign runs two of them; the rest are spread among other registrars.

The resolver asks a `.com` server for `www.example.com`. The `.com` server does not know the address. It knows who runs `example.com`. It hands back the name servers for `example.com` — the servers that hold the actual records for that domain, the ones the domain owner configured at their registrar.

The resolver asks `example.com`'s name server for `www.example.com`. This server knows the answer. It looks up the `www` record and returns an A record — an IPv4 address, `93.184.216.34` — or a CNAME, which is a redirect to another name that the resolver must then resolve from scratch.

The resolver takes that address and gives it to the browser. The browser opens a TCP connection to that address and sends the HTTP request.

Each step is cached. The browser caches the answer for the time-to-live the authoritative server specified — minutes or days. The operating system caches it. The resolver caches it. A second request for `www.example.com` in the next hour never reaches the root or the `.com` server; the resolver answers from memory. The TTL is what lets DNS survive the load of eight billion devices asking for names. Without caching, the root servers would drown.

The walk is four questions: root, top-level domain, authoritative name server, answer. The resolver asks all four the first time and remembers the result. The next asker gets the memory.

Okay — explain deadlock and one avoidance strategy, in plain register.

A deadlock is two threads frozen, each holding a lock the other needs. Thread A locks mutex 1, then tries to lock mutex 2. Thread B locks mutex 2, then tries to lock mutex 1. A waits for B forever. B waits for A forever. Neither lets go. The program stops.

The failure needs four conditions, all present at once. Mutual exclusion: a lock is held by one thread at a time. Hold and wait: a thread holding one lock asks for another. No preemption: locks release only when the holder chooses, not by force. Circular wait: a ring of threads each waiting on the next one's lock. Break any one and the deadlock cannot form.

The cleanest break is lock ordering. Pick one global order for every mutex in the program. Every thread acquires locks in that order, always. If mutex 1 ranks before mutex 2, any thread needing both locks 1 first, then 2. Thread A locks 1, then 2. Thread B wants both — it also locks 1 first. B blocks on 1 until A releases it. A gets 2, finishes, releases both. B proceeds. The circular wait never closes, because no thread holding a lower-ranked lock waits for a higher-ranked one.

The cost is discipline. Every new mutex takes a rank, and every code path that locks two or more must follow the ranking. A thread that locks out of order, even once, reopens the ring. The Linux kernel enforces this with a lockdep validator that flags any acquire violating the global order, catching violations before they ship.

A hash map turns a key into an integer, then uses that integer as an index into an array. The hash function spreads keys across the array's slots, but two different keys can produce the same integer. When that happens, the map has a collision, and the design has to answer one question: where does the second entry go?

**Separate chaining** gives each slot its own list. The slot at index 4 does not hold a single entry; it holds the head of a linked list, and every key that hashes to 4 gets appended there. A lookup hashes the key, walks the list, and compares keys one by one until it finds a match. The cost of a lookup is the cost of walking that list, so if every key lands in the same slot the map degrades to a linear search. To keep lists short, the map watches its load factor — the ratio of entries to slots — and when it crosses a threshold, the map allocates a larger array and re-hashes every entry into it. Java's `HashMap` uses this approach, and when a list grows past eight entries it converts the list to a balanced tree to bound worst-case lookup at log n rather than n.

**Open addressing** keeps one entry per slot. When a key hashes to an already-occupied slot, the map probes other slots according to a fixed rule and places the entry in the first empty one it finds. Linear probing checks the next slot, then the next, then the next — slot 4, 5, 6 — until it finds a gap. This is fast because nearby slots are close in memory, but it builds clusters: a run of occupied slots grows longer with each insertion, because a new key that lands anywhere inside the run has to walk past it. Quadratic probing jumps by growing offsets — 1, 4, 9, 16 — which breaks up the clusters but can miss empty slots if the table size and the step pattern share a factor. Double hashing sidesteps that by using a second hash function to compute the probe step, so the step size depends on the key itself and the probe sequence spreads out.

A lookup in an open-addressed map follows the same probe sequence the insertion used. It checks each slot until it finds the key, finds an empty slot — which means the key was never inserted — or has checked every slot. Deletion has a catch: removing an entry and leaving the slot empty would break the probe chain, because a later lookup for a key that was probed past this slot would stop at the gap and conclude the key is absent. The fix is a tombstone, a marker that says "occupied, but deleted." A tombstone keeps the chain intact for lookups but still accepts a new insertion. Tombstones accumulate, though, and a map with many of them slows lookups because probes have to skip past them, so the map re-hashes to clear them out.

The choice between the two turns on memory locality and load. Open addressing puts every entry in the array itself, so a probe sequence walks a contiguous block of memory, which cache prefetch handles well. It also carries no pointer overhead per entry. But it degrades badly as the load factor approaches one, because probes get long and tombstones pile up, so it needs a lower load-factor threshold — typically around 0.7 — before it re-hashes. Separate chaining tolerates load factors above one, since each slot's list can grow independently, and it handles deletions without tombstones. The cost is a pointer chase on every step through the list, which is a cache miss more often than not. Python's `dict` uses open addressing with a perturbed probe sequence derived from the hash, and it keeps the load factor at two-thirds before it grows the table.

A database index is a second data structure stored alongside the table. The table holds rows in the order they were written; the index holds key values in sorted order, each paired with a pointer back to its row. A query for `users WHERE email = 'x'` without an index reads every row in the table and compares the email field — a full table scan, cost proportional to row count. With a B-tree index on `email`, the database walks a balanced tree of height four or five, does binary comparisons at each level, and lands on the matching entry in roughly log n steps. A table of ten million rows becomes four or five disk reads instead of ten million.

The index earns its cost back when queries select a small fraction of the table. A query that returns fifty rows out of ten million hits the index, fetches those fifty rows by their pointers, and stops. The same query without the index scans all ten million rows to find the fifty. The break-even point sits around five to ten percent of the table: if a query returns more than that fraction, the planner often skips the index and scans anyway, because random row fetches by pointer cost more disk seeks than a sequential sweep.

Indexes hurt in three places. First, every insert, update, and delete that touches an indexed column must update the index as well as the table. A table with six indexes pays seven writes for one row insertion — one to the table's heap, one to each index tree. A bulk load into an empty table runs faster if the indexes are dropped and rebuilt after the load rather than maintained row by row. Second, each index is a separate structure on disk. A B-tree index on a wide text column can approach the size of the table itself; six such indexes triple the storage footprint. Third, an index that the query planner never uses — a column that appears in no `WHERE`, `JOIN`, or `ORDER BY` clause — pays both costs and returns nothing. Indexes built "just in case" are the common case of this waste.

A composite index on `(last_name, first_name)` serves queries that filter on `last_name` alone, because the tree sorts on `last_name` first. It does not serve queries that filter on `first_name` alone, because the tree's secondary sort only holds within each `last_name` group — `first_name` values are scattered across the whole tree. This is the leftmost-prefix rule: a multi-column index is usable only for query predicates that test its columns from left to right.

A partial index adds a `WHERE` clause to the index definition itself: `CREATE INDEX active_users ON users(email) WHERE status = 'active'`. It indexes only the matching rows, so it stays small if the active set is a small fraction of the table. A query that asks for active users by email uses it; a query that asks for inactive users cannot, because those rows were never indexed. PostgreSQL, SQLite, and SQL Server support partial indexes; MySQL does not.

The planner's decision to use or skip an index depends on table statistics — row counts, value distribution, estimated selectivity — which the database gathers by sampling. Stale statistics lead to bad choices: the planner picks an index that returns more rows than expected, does more random fetches than a scan would have done, and the query runs slower. Running `ANALYZE` after large data loads refreshes those statistics and lets the planner choose again.

Okay — explain how TCP keeps data in order, in plain White/Orwell register.

TCP sends data as a stream of bytes, not as a sequence of independent messages. An application hands ten kilobytes to TCP; TCP may split that into seven segments or pack it into one, depending on what the connection's window allows at the moment of sending. The application on the other end receives the same ten kilobytes in the same order, regardless of how the bytes were divided on the wire. The mechanism that holds this promise is the sequence number.

Every byte in a TCP connection has a sequence number. The first byte the sender transmits gets a number chosen at connection setup — the initial sequence number, a 32-bit value the sender picks to make sequence prediction hard. Each subsequent byte increments by one. A segment carrying bytes 1000 through 1099 carries the sequence number 1000 in its header, and the receiver knows that the next byte it expects is 1100.

The receiver keeps a variable called the expected sequence number. When a segment arrives, the receiver compares the segment's sequence number against the expected value. If they match, the bytes fill the next gap in the receive buffer, the expected number advances by the byte count, and the receiver sends an acknowledgment back: "I have everything up to byte 1100, send 1100 next." That acknowledgment is cumulative — it confirms all bytes before the acknowledged number, not just the ones in the latest segment.

If a segment arrives out of order, the receiver still knows where its bytes belong. A segment carrying bytes 1200 through 1299 that lands before the segment carrying 1100 through 1199 goes into the buffer at offset 1200, and the expected number stays at 1100. The receiver acknowledges 1100 again — the highest contiguous byte it has received — which tells the sender that everything from 1100 onward is still missing. The sender retransmits the gap.

A lost segment produces the same signal. If bytes 1100 through 1199 never arrive, the receiver gets 1200, 1300, 1400, and acknowledges 1100 each time. The sender sees duplicate acknowledgments for 1100 — three of them, by TCP's common fast-retransmit rule — and retransmits the missing segment without waiting for its retransmission timer to expire. When the gap fills, the expected number jumps forward across any later segments already sitting in the buffer, and one acknowledgment covers all of them.

The receive buffer is what makes reordering tolerable. The receiver holds out-of-order segments in memory until the missing piece arrives, then hands the whole contiguous run to the application. The application never sees a gap. If the buffer fills before the gap closes — the sender is transmitting faster than the missing segment can be retransmitted — the receiver advertises a zero window in its acknowledgments, and the sender stops until the buffer drains.

The sequence number, the cumulative acknowledgment, and the receive buffer together enforce the contract. Bytes may cross the network in any order, in segments of varying size, separated by retransmissions. The receiver reassembles them by number and delivers one contiguous stream to the application.

Okay — explain what a mutex protects against, in plain White/Orwell register.

A mutex protects one thing: the interleaving of reads and writes on shared state across two or more threads running on the same memory. Without it, a thread can read a value mid-update from another thread, or two threads can write the same memory cell at the same instant, and the final value depends on which instruction landed last. The mutex makes the critical section — the block of code between the lock and the unlock — run as one indivisible step. Whatever happens inside it happens fully before the next thread enters.

The concrete case is the increment. A counter at 0 lives in memory. Thread A reads 0 into a register. Thread B reads 0 into its own register. Thread A adds 1, writes 1. Thread B adds 1, writes 1. Two increments produced a count of 1. The mutex prevents this: A takes the lock, reads, adds, writes, releases. B waits at the lock until A releases, then reads the 1 A wrote, adds, writes 2. The counter is correct.

A mutex does not protect against reentrancy from the same thread. If a function takes the lock and then calls a second function that also takes the same lock, the second acquire blocks forever — the lock is already held, and the holder is waiting on itself. A recursive mutex permits this by tracking ownership and acquire count, releasing only when the count returns to zero. A plain mutex deadlocks.

A mutex does not protect against deadlock across multiple locks. Thread A holds lock 1 and waits for lock 2. Thread B holds lock 2 and waits for lock 1. Both sleep forever. The fix is lock ordering: every thread acquires locks in the same sequence, so the cycle cannot form. The mutex itself has no opinion on this; the discipline lives in the calling code.

A mutex does not protect memory it does not cover. If thread A mutates a structure under the lock and thread B reads the same structure without taking the lock, B can see a torn or half-updated value. The lock is a convention — it works only when every access to the protected state passes through it. A lock that guards half the accesses guards nothing.

A mutex does not protect against priority inversion. A low-priority thread holds the lock; a high-priority thread spins waiting for it; a medium-priority thread preempts the low-priority thread and runs, so the high-priority thread waits behind work that has nothing to do with the locked resource. The priority-inheritance protocol hands the low-priority thread the high-priority thread's priority for the duration of the hold, so it runs sooner and releases sooner. Not all operating systems implement this.

What the mutex does guarantee is mutual exclusion in the literal sense: at most one thread executes inside the critical section at a time. The state touched inside that section sees a single thread's reads and writes in that thread's program order, with no other thread's operations interleaved. Everything else — reentrancy, multi-lock deadlock, uncovered accesses, priority effects — is outside its scope and must be handled by the code that uses it.

Okay — explain how garbage collection finds unused memory, in plain White/Orwell register.

Garbage collection reclaims memory that the program can no longer reach. The question it answers is narrow: which objects are dead? An object is dead when no path of references from a live root leads to it. The roots are the things the program can touch directly — local variables on every thread's stack, static and global fields, the CPU registers that hold pointers. Everything reachable from a root, by following fields and array elements, is alive. Everything else is garbage.

**Mark-and-sweep** is the direct implementation of that idea. The collector starts at the roots and walks the reference graph, marking every object it reaches. It sets a bit on the object's header or in a separate bitmap. When the walk stops, every marked object is live and every unmarked object is dead. The collector then sweeps the heap: it walks every allocated block, and for each unmarked block it returns the memory to the free list. The mark phase touches only live objects; the sweep phase touches every object. A heap with ten million objects, nine million of them dead, does ten million marks and ten million sweeps.

**Copying collection** avoids the sweep. It divides the heap into two halves, only one of which holds objects at a time. The collector walks the live graph from the roots and copies each reachable object into the other half, packing them contiguously as it goes. It leaves a forwarding pointer in the old copy so that references to the object update to the new address. When the walk finishes, the entire old half is garbage — every byte of it — and the collector frees it in one move by flipping the two halves. The cost is proportional to the number of live objects, not the total heap. A heap with ten million objects, one million live, touches one million objects and reclaims nine million for free. The cost is that the heap uses half its memory as scratch space.

**Generational collection** rests on an observation about object lifetimes: most objects die young. A function allocates a temporary list, builds it, returns a result, and the list is never touched again. The collector splits the heap into a young generation and an old generation. New allocations go into the young generation, which is small and collected often. A young-generation collection is fast because the space is small and most objects in it are already dead. Objects that survive several young-generation collections get promoted to the old generation, which is large and collected rarely. The old generation fills slowly, because promotion is rare, so the expensive full-heap collection runs infrequently.

The hard part of generational collection is the remembered set. A reference from an old object to a young object is a root for a young-generation collection, but the collector does not want to scan the entire old generation to find them — that would defeat the point. So the runtime maintains a remembered set: whenever the program writes a reference from an old object to a young object, a write barrier records the old object in the set. The young-generation collection then treats the remembered set as additional roots. The write barrier is a few instructions on every pointer write into old memory, and it is the price of not scanning the old heap.

**Concurrent collection** moves work off the application's threads so pauses stay short. The collector runs alongside the program, marking or sweeping while the program mutates the heap. The problem is that the program can change the graph mid-walk: the collector marks object A, then the program stores a reference from A to unmarked object B and drops the last other reference to B. B is reachable but unmarked, and a sweep would reclaim it — a live object, freed. Collectors solve this with a write barrier that catches the new reference and marks B, or with a snapshot-at-the-beginning protocol that treats the graph as it stood when the collection started. The trade is throughput: the barrier adds overhead to every mutation, and the collector and the program contend for CPU.

**Reference counting** is a different lineage. Every object carries a count of references to it. A new reference increments the count; a dropped reference decrements it. When the count hits zero, the object is unreachable and can be freed immediately — no walk, no sweep. The failure mode is cycles: A references B, B references A, both counts are one, both are unreachable from the roots, and neither count ever reaches zero. A reference-counting collector either accepts this and leaks cycles, or runs a periodic cycle collector that does a reachability walk anyway. The second case is mark-and-sweep added on top. Reference counting also pays on every assignment of a pointer, not just at collection time, which makes it expensive for programs that churn references but have long-lived objects.

The common thread is the reachability test. Every collector distinguishes live from dead by asking whether a path exists from a root to the object. The strategies differ in how they walk that graph, when they walk it, and what they do with the answer — mark and sweep, copy and flip, collect the young generation and defer the old, run concurrently and patch the gaps, or count references and catch the cycles. The heap is the graph, and the roots are the entry points. Everything unreachable is reclaimable; the collector's job is to find it without stopping the program for longer than the program can tolerate.

Okay — explain what a race condition is, with a concrete example, in plain White/Orwell register.

A race condition happens when two threads read and write the same memory cell, and the final value depends on which thread's instruction landed last. The program has no single correct output. Run it twice with the same inputs and the result changes.

The example is the bank transfer. An account holds a balance of 100. Thread A reads 100, subtracts 30, writes 70. Thread B reads 100 at the same instant, adds 50, writes 150. The balance is 150. Thirty dollars vanished. The correct result — 120 — required A's write to finish before B's read, or B's write to finish before A's read. Either order works. The interleaving does not.

The defect is not in the arithmetic. Each thread's logic is sound in isolation. The defect is in the timing: the read and the write are two separate instructions, and another thread can slip between them. A mutex around the balance fixes it. A takes the lock, reads, writes, releases. B waits at the lock until A finishes, then reads the 70 A wrote, adds 50, writes 120. The lock collapses the read-modify-write into one indivisible step.

Race conditions do not always corrupt data. Some races produce the right answer by luck on most runs and the wrong answer on one run in a million. Those are the hardest to find. A test that passes ten thousand times proves nothing, because the losing interleaving may require a specific thread schedule that the test never triggered.

Okay — explain how a CPU cache speeds up a program, in plain White/Orwell register.

A CPU executes instructions at three to four gigahertz. Main memory, DDR4 SDRAM, responds in about sixty nanoseconds. That is roughly two hundred clock cycles the CPU spends idle, waiting for a single load to come back. The cache sits between the two.

A cache is a small amount of fast memory built into the CPU die. It holds copies of the data the program has touched recently. When the CPU needs to read a memory address, it checks the cache first. If the address is there — a cache hit — the data comes back in one to four cycles. If it is not — a cache miss — the CPU fetches from main memory, pays the two-hundred-cycle cost, and stores a copy in the cache so the next read hits.

The cache is small because fast memory is expensive. A typical L1 cache is 32 kilobytes, split into 32 KB for data and 32 KB for instructions. L2 is 256 KB to 1 MB. L3 is 8 to 32 MB, shared across all cores on the die. Each level is larger and slower than the one above it. The CPU checks L1, then L2, then L3, then main memory, and stops at the first hit.

Caches work because of two patterns in how programs access memory. The first is temporal locality: if a program reads a variable now, it will probably read it again soon. A loop counter is read and written on every iteration. The counter stays in the cache for the whole loop. The second is spatial locality: if a program reads address 1000, it will probably read 1004, 1008, 1012. An array processed element by element touches consecutive addresses. The cache exploits this by moving data in blocks, not single bytes. A cache line is 64 bytes on most x86 and ARM processors. One miss pulls 64 bytes from main memory, and the next seven reads of that block hit in the cache.

The speedup is the hit rate. A program that hits 95% of the time pays the one-cycle cost on 95 of 100 loads and the two-hundred-cycle cost on five. The average load takes eleven cycles. The same program with no cache pays two hundred cycles on every load. The cache made memory eighteen times faster for that access pattern.

This is why the order in which a program touches memory changes its speed by an order of magnitude. A loop that walks a two-dimensional array row by row hits the cache on every element, because each row is contiguous in memory. The same loop walking column by column misses on every element, because each column element is 64 or more bytes from the last — a different cache line. The arithmetic is identical. The cache behavior is not. The row-wise loop runs ten to twenty times faster on a large array.

The cache does not speed up computation. It speeds up data access, which is what the CPU spends most of its time doing. A program that fits its working set into L1 runs at the CPU's full clock rate. A program that spills to L2 runs slower. A program that misses to main memory on every access spends most of its time stalled, and the CPU's three gigahertz becomes irrelevant.

Okay — explain what idempotency means for an HTTP API, in plain White/Orwell register.

Idempotency means a client can send the same request twice and the server ends in the same state as if it had been sent once. The second call does not duplicate the first. It does not create a second charge, a second row, a second email. It either repeats the first call's effect — which is harmless because the effect already happened — or it recognizes that the effect already happened and does nothing.

The case that forces the issue is the network failure. A client sends `POST /payments` to charge a card. The server receives it, processes the charge, and sends back a 200 response. The response is lost in transit. The client does not know whether the charge happened. It retries. Without idempotency, the server processes the charge again — the card is billed twice. With idempotency, the server recognizes the retry and returns the original result without charging again.

The mechanism is an idempotency key. The client generates a unique string — a UUID — and sends it in a header: `Idempotency-Key: 7a3f9b2c-...`. The server stores the key alongside the result of the first request. When a second request arrives with the same key, the server looks it up. If it finds a stored result, it returns that result. If it does not, it processes the request and stores the result. The key turns a duplicate delivery into a cached response.

HTTP's standard methods carry idempotency at the protocol level, without a key. `GET` is idempotent by definition: it reads a resource and changes nothing, so a second `GET` returns the same data and leaves the server untouched. `PUT` is idempotent because it replaces a resource wholesale — `PUT /users/42` with the same body produces the same final state whether it runs once or ten times. `DELETE` is idempotent because deleting a resource that is already deleted leaves the server in the same state as deleting it once. `POST` is not idempotent. `POST /orders` creates a new order each time it is called, and each order gets its own ID. Two calls produce two orders. This is why idempotency keys apply to `POST` endpoints — the method itself gives no guarantee, so the application adds one.

The distinction matters at the boundary between safe and idempotent. A safe method changes no state — `GET` and `HEAD` are safe. An idempotent method may change state on the first call but not on subsequent calls — `PUT` and `DELETE` change state but are idempotent. `POST` is neither safe nor idempotent. `PATCH` is neither by default, though a specific `PATCH` that sets a field to a fixed value is idempotent in practice.

Idempotency has a time limit. A server cannot store every key forever. It keeps keys for a window — hours or days — and expires them. A retry after expiry is treated as a new request and processed again. The window has to cover the longest plausible retry interval: a client that retries after a network outage of thirty minutes needs a key that survives at least that long. Stripe's idempotency keys last twenty-four hours. A retry on the twenty-fifth hour creates a second charge.

Idempotency also has a scope. The key identifies the operation, not the resource. Two different clients sending the same key are asking for the same operation, and the server should return the same result to both. A client that sends the same key with a different request body has a bug — the server should reject it, not process the new body, because the key already committed to a result. The key binds the client to one attempt at one operation, and retries of that attempt are free.

Okay — explain how DNS turns a name into an address, in plain White/Orwell register.

A browser asks for `www.example.com`. The operating system hands that name to a resolver, and the resolver's job is to come back with an IP address. The address is what the browser needs to open a TCP connection. Names are for humans; sockets take numbers.

The resolver first checks its own cache. If it has answered this query recently, it returns the cached address and stops. If not, it goes to the root servers. The root servers do not know the address for `www.example.com`. They know the servers authoritative for every top-level domain — `.com`, `.org`, `.net`, the country codes. The root server reads the `com` suffix and returns a list of the `.com` servers' addresses.

The resolver takes those addresses and asks a `.com` server the same question. The `.com` server does not know `www.example.com` either. It knows the servers authoritative for `example.com` — the name servers that the operator of `example.com` registered with their registrar. The `.com` server returns those addresses.

The resolver asks the `example.com` name server for `www.example.com`. This server holds the actual record. It reads the `www` subdomain, finds an A record — a mapping of a name to a 32-bit IPv4 address — and returns `93.184.216.34`. The resolver caches that answer for the record's time-to-live, hands the address to the operating system, and the operating system hands it to the browser. Three round trips: root, top-level, authoritative.

The time-to-live governs how long a cached answer stays valid. A TTL of 3600 means the resolver can reuse the address for one hour. After that it discards the entry and repeats the full lookup. Short TTLs — sixty seconds, three hundred seconds — let an operator move a service to a new address quickly, because resolvers pick up the change within minutes. Long TTLs — 86400, one day — reduce lookup traffic but make changes slow to propagate. A resolver that ignores the TTL and caches longer than it should serves stale addresses after a move.

The lookup is recursive from the resolver's perspective but iterative on the wire. The resolver sends three queries — to root, to `.com`, to `example.com` — and each server points it to the next. The resolver does the walking. The authoritative servers do not query each other on the resolver's behalf. A caching resolver that has already walked the chain for `www.example.com` can answer a later query for `mail.example.com` without going back to root, because it has cached the `example.com` name-server addresses from the first walk.

The system is a tree. The root is the top of the tree. Each top-level domain is a branch. Each registered domain is a smaller branch off that. Each subdomain is smaller still. The resolver walks down the tree one level at a time, and each level delegates authority for the next to the servers below it. No single server holds the whole map. The map is distributed, and the delegation is what makes the walk possible.

Okay — explain what a deadlock is and one way to avoid it, in plain White/Orwell register.

A deadlock is two or more threads stuck waiting for locks each other holds. Thread A holds lock 1 and waits for lock 2. Thread B holds lock 2 and waits for lock 1. Both sleep. Neither releases. The program hangs.

Four conditions must hold at once for a deadlock to exist. Mutual exclusion: each lock is held by one thread at a time. Hold and wait: a thread holding one lock requests another. No preemption: locks are not taken by force; a thread releases only voluntarily. Circular wait: a cycle of threads exists where each holds a lock the next one needs. Break any one and deadlocks cannot form.

The example is the transfer function. A bank account has a balance and a lock. To transfer money from account X to account Y, a thread locks X, then locks Y, then moves the money. Two threads run at the same time. Thread A transfers from X to Y: locks X, requests Y. Thread B transfers from Y to X: locks Y, requests X. A holds what B needs. B holds what A needs. Deadlock.

The fix is lock ordering. Every thread acquires locks in the same global sequence. If the rule is "lock the account with the lower ID first," thread A locks X first because X has ID 100 and Y has ID 200. Thread B, transferring from Y to X, also locks X first — same rule. Thread A takes X. Thread B blocks on X. Thread A takes Y, moves the money, releases both. Thread B proceeds. The cycle never forms because both threads line up at the same lock in the same order.

Lock ordering breaks the circular-wait condition. No cycle is possible when every thread enters the lock graph in the same direction. The cost is a constraint on the code: every caller must know the ordering rule and follow it. A single function that takes locks in the wrong order reopens the deadlock. The discipline is global, not local.

A hash map stores values at array slots chosen by a key's hash. Two keys that hash to the same slot collide. Four methods resolve this: separate chaining, open addressing with linear probing, open addressing with quadratic probing, and Robin Hood probing.

**Separate chaining** keeps a linked list at each slot. On insert, the map hashes the key, walks the list, and appends a new node if the key is absent. On lookup, it walks the same list and compares keys. The list grows with collisions; a load factor of 0.75 means the average list holds under one entry, but an adversarial key set can force every key into one slot, degrading lookup to O(n). Java's `HashMap` before Java 8 used this shape exclusively; after Java 8 it converts a long chain to a red-black tree, capping the worst case at O(log n).

**Linear probing** stores entries in the array itself. On collision, the map walks forward one slot at a time until it finds an empty cell and writes there. Lookup follows the same path from the hashed slot until it hits the key or an empty cell. The weakness is clustering: as filled slots accumulate, probes grow longer because a run of occupied cells forces every colliding key past the whole run. Donald Knuth analyzed this in *The Art of Computer Programming* Vol. 3 (1973): expected probe count for a successful lookup is roughly (1 + 1/(1−α))/2, where α is the load factor. At α = 0.75 that is about 3 probes; at α = 0.9 it passes 5.

**Quadratic probing** jumps by squared distances — 1, 4, 9, 16 — instead of stepping by one. This breaks up the primary clusters that linear probing forms. It introduces a different problem: the probe sequence visits fewer slots than the table holds, so the map can report "full" while empty cells remain. This is fixed by choosing a table size that is prime and a probe step that covers all slots, a result proven by Radke and refined in Knuth Vol. 3.

**Robin Hood probing** is linear probing with a twist: on insert, if the key being placed has probed farther from its home slot than the key already sitting in the current cell, the two swap. The displaced key continues probing. This minimizes the variance in probe length — every key travels roughly the same distance from its hash. The worst-case lookup improves accordingly. The method was described by Celis, Larson, and Munro in a 1985 conference paper; Python's `dict` does not use it, but Rust's `HashMap` did before switching to SwissTable in 1.36 (2019).

**Resizing** governs all four. When the load factor crosses a threshold — 0.75 in Java's `HashMap`, 0.6875 in Python's `dict` — the map allocates a larger array, rehashes every entry, and places it in the new table. A resize turns a pathological O(n) lookup into a one-time O(n) cost spread across many inserts. The threshold trades memory for speed: a lower threshold wastes space but shortens probe sequences; a higher one packs the table but lengthens them.

A database index is a second data structure stored alongside the table. It trades disk space and write speed for read speed.

The structure is usually a B-tree. A B-tree keeps sorted keys in blocks, with each block holding many keys and pointers to child blocks. A lookup touches four or five blocks instead of scanning the whole table. On a table with ten million rows, that is the difference between reading forty kilobytes and reading seven hundred megabytes.

An index helps when a query filters on the indexed column. `SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 417` reads a handful of blocks if `customer_id` carries an index. Without one, the database reads every row in `orders` and discards the ones that do not match. The planner chooses the index when it estimates the index path costs fewer disk reads than the scan.

An index hurts in three places.

**Writes.** Every `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, and `DELETE` must update the index as well as the table. A B-tree insert splits a block when it fills, writing two blocks where there was one. A table with six indexes takes seven writes per insert. On a log table that absorbs ten thousand rows a second, those six extra writes dominate the cost.

**Low-selectivity columns.** An index on a column with few distinct values — a boolean flag, a status code with three states — rarely helps. The query `WHERE active = true` matches most of the table, so the planner skips the index and scans anyway. The index consumed writes on every insert and returned nothing.

**The wrong query.** An index on `(last_name, first_name)` does not serve `WHERE first_name = 'Ada'`. B-tree lookups must start from the leftmost column. The database scans the whole index or falls back to the table scan. A separate index on `first_name` alone would serve that query, at the cost of another write per insert.

Dropping an unused index reclaims the writes it consumed. The cost is visible in the database's own statistics: PostgreSQL's `pg_stat_user_indexes` counts reads per index. An index with zero reads across a representative workload is dead weight.

TCP sends each byte with a sequence number. The sender picks an initial sequence number at connection setup — the `ISN` in the SYN segment — and numbers every subsequent byte from there. A 1400-byte segment carrying sequence 1001 covers bytes 1001 through 2400.

The receiver reads that number from the segment header and places the payload in the correct position in its receive buffer. If segments arrive out of order — 2401 before 1001, because a later packet took a faster route — the receiver holds 2401 in the buffer and waits. It does not deliver bytes to the application until a contiguous run from the last delivered position is complete.

The receiver tells the sender what it has. The acknowledgment number in the receiver's next segment is the next byte it expects. An ACK of 2401 means bytes 1 through 2400 have arrived in order. A gap means the receiver keeps the out-of-order data and repeats the same ACK number on every subsequent segment, a signal called a duplicate ACK.

The sender retransmits to fill the gap. It starts a timer when it sends a segment. If the timer expires before an ACK covers that segment's bytes, the sender sends them again. Faster feedback comes from duplicate ACKs: three duplicate ACKs for the same number tell the sender a later segment arrived but an earlier one did not, and it retransmits the missing segment without waiting for the timer. This is TCP fast retransmit, specified in RFC 5681.

Once the gap closes, the receiver releases the contiguous run to the application. The sequence numbers make the ordering explicit; the buffer holds the out-of-order pieces; the ACKs report the frontier; retransmission fills the holes. The application sees a byte stream in the order the sender wrote it, regardless of the order the wire delivered it.

A mutex protects a critical section: a span of code that must run alone, because it reads or writes shared state that a second thread could corrupt mid-operation.

The problem is interleaving. Two threads running `balance = balance + 100` look atomic in source but are three instructions on the machine: load `balance` into a register, add 100, store it back. If thread A loads 500, thread B loads 500 before A stores, both add 100, and both store 600, one deposit vanishes. The lost update is the race condition.

The mutex fixes this by serializing access. A thread calls `lock` before the section and `unlock` after. While one thread holds the lock, a second call to `lock` blocks — the operating system parks the second thread until the holder releases. Only one thread is ever inside the section. The lost update cannot occur because the load-add-store sequence cannot be interleaved.

What a mutex does **not** protect is everything outside the section. If thread A guards `balance` with mutex M but thread B writes `balance` without locking M, the race remains. The mutex protects the section, not the variable; every code path that touches the shared state must acquire the same lock, or the lock is decorative.

A mutex also does not protect against deadlock. Two threads each holding one mutex and waiting for the other's will block forever. Thread 1 locks A then waits for B; thread 2 locks B then waits for A. Neither releases. The fix is a lock-ordering protocol — always acquire A before B — or a single lock that covers both, trading concurrency for safety.

The cost is contention. Every `lock` call is a kernel transition when the lock is already held, and the parked thread consumes no CPU until it wakes. A mutex on a hot path serializes that path: ten threads contending for one lock run that section ten times in sequence, not in parallel. The section should be as short as the correctness requires and no shorter.

Garbage collection reclaims memory the program can no longer reach. It works because every allocated object is reachable from a fixed set of roots — stack variables, static fields, CPU registers — through a chain of pointers. An object unreachable from the roots is garbage, because no code path can ever touch it again.

**Mark-and-sweep** is the original method, described by John McCarthy in 1960 for Lisp. The collector walks the object graph starting at the roots, marking each object it visits. When the walk finishes, it sweeps the heap: every unmarked object is dead, and its memory returns to the free list. The walk touches only live objects; the sweep touches the whole heap. The pause is proportional to the live set plus the heap size.

**Copying collection** splits the heap into two halves. The program allocates in one half until it fills. The collector then copies every reachable object from the full half to the empty half, compacting them into a contiguous run. The old half becomes the new free space. This costs time proportional to the live set, not the garbage — dead objects cost nothing because they are never copied. The trade is memory: the program uses half the heap. C. J. Cheney described an efficient version in 1970 that copies without an explicit stack, using the already-copied objects as the work queue.

**Generational collection** rests on the weak generational hypothesis: most objects die young. A program that allocates a million short-lived temporaries and ten long-lived caches has a heap dominated by garbage in the young region and stable data in the old. The collector splits the heap into generations and collects the young one frequently, cheaply, and alone. Objects that survive several young collections promote to the old generation, which the collector scans rarely. The young collection is fast because it touches little live data; the old collection is rare because old data changes slowly.

The hard part is the roots. The collector must find every pointer on every stack and in every register, or it will free an object that a live pointer still references. A conservative collector — Boehm's libgc, the one used by the Mono runtime — scans the stack for anything that *looks* like a pointer and treats it as one. It cannot free an object whose address happens to appear on the stack, even if the value is actually an integer. A precise collector knows exactly which stack slots and registers hold pointers, which the compiler records at every safe point. HotSpot's JVM is precise; it can free objects a conservative collector would retain.

The pause is the cost. A mark-and-sweep or copying collection stops every application thread while it runs. A heap of eight gigabytes with two gigabytes live can pause for hundreds of milliseconds. Concurrent collectors — the JVM's G1, .NET's background GC — do most of the marking work while the program runs, shortening the stop-the-world phase to the final relabeling. The trade is throughput: concurrent marking spends CPU that the application could have used, and the barrier instructions it inserts at every pointer write slow the program slightly even outside a collection.

A race condition is a bug where a program's output depends on the order in which two operations run, and that order is not controlled.

Two threads share a bank balance of 500. Thread A deposits 100. Thread B deposits 100. The deposit code reads the balance, adds 100, and writes it back. If A reads 500, then B reads 500 before A writes, both threads hold 500 in their registers. A writes 600. B writes 600. The balance should be 700. It is 600. One deposit vanished.

The machine interleaved the two deposits. The source code looked atomic — `balance = balance + 100` is one statement — but the hardware ran it as three: load `balance` into a register, add 100, store the register back. Nothing forced A's three instructions to finish before B's began. The lost update is the visible result.

The fix is a mutex around the read-add-write sequence. A thread locks before the deposit and unlocks after. While one thread holds the lock, the second blocks, and the operating system parks it. The load-add-store runs alone. The balance reaches 700.

The race exists because the two threads shared mutable state and nothing serialized their access to it. A single-threaded program cannot race against itself. The bug appears only when a second thread can touch the same memory between the load and the store — the window where the shared state is inconsistent.

A CPU cache is a small, fast memory that sits between the processor and main memory. It speeds up a program by keeping the data the processor is most likely to need next.

Main memory is slow. A modern processor can execute several instructions per nanosecond, but fetching a value from DRAM takes roughly 100 nanoseconds. That gap means a load instruction can stall the processor for hundreds of cycles while it waits. The cache closes that gap. An Intel Core i7 has three cache levels: L1, L2, and L3. L1 is 32 kilobytes and returns data in 4 cycles. L2 is 1 megabyte and takes 14 cycles. L3 is 8 megabytes and takes 50 cycles. DRAM takes 300.

The cache works because of locality. Programs do not read memory at random. They read the same addresses repeatedly — a loop variable, a struct field, a running sum — and they read nearby addresses — the next array element, the next instruction. The first pattern is temporal locality: a value used once will likely be used again. The second is spatial locality: a value near a used value will likely be used soon. The cache exploits both. When the processor requests a byte, the cache loads a block of 64 contiguous bytes, called a cache line. If the program then reads the next byte in the array, it is already in the cache.

A cache hit returns data from the cache. A cache miss fetches it from the next level down. The hit rate determines the speedup. A program that reads a 10,000-element array sequentially hits the cache on every element after the first, because each 64-byte line holds 8 eight-byte doubles. The first load in each line misses; the next seven hit. The miss rate is 1 in 8. A program that jumps through the same array in strides of 64 bytes misses on every access, because each load touches a different line. The miss rate is 100 percent. Same array, same size, ten times slower.

The cache also governs how data should be laid out. A C struct with a hot field and a cold field wastes cache space if the hot field sits in a line with data the program never reads. Splitting the struct into a hot struct and a cold struct packs the frequently used fields into fewer lines. The technique is called data structure splitting, and it is why game engines store positions and velocities in separate arrays rather than arrays of objects. The positions fit in cache. The velocities fit in cache. An array of objects, each containing both, spills both out because each cache line carries fields the loop does not touch.

The cache is invisible to the program's logic but visible to its performance. Two algorithms with the same big-O complexity can differ by a factor of ten because one walks memory in cache-line order and the other walks it at random. The cache turns memory access patterns into a cost the instruction count does not measure.

Idempotency means a client can send the same request twice and the server ends in the same state it would after one. The second call does not duplicate the first.

`PUT /users/42` with body `{"name": "Ada"}` is idempotent. The first call sets the name. The second call sets the name to the same value. The stored row is identical whether the request arrives once or ten times. RFC 9110 section 9.2.2 defines `PUT` this way: the server stores the representation at the target URI, replacing any prior state.

`POST /users` with body `{"name": "Ada"}` is not. The first call creates a user and returns its ID, say 101. The second call creates a second user, ID 102. Two requests, two rows. A client that retries the POST after a network timeout produces a duplicate account. This is why payment APIs reject a second charge with the same `Idempotency-Key` header: the key marks the second request as a retry of the first, and the server returns the original result instead of running the charge again.

`DELETE /users/42` is idempotent. The first call removes the user. The second call finds no user at 42 and returns 404 or 204, depending on the server's convention. The server state — user 42 absent — is the same after both. The response status differs, but idempotency governs server state, not the bytes returned.

`PATCH` is the ambiguous case. A patch that sets `name` to `Ada` is idempotent. A patch that appends `Ada` to `name` is not: the first call produces `Ada`, the second produces `AdaAda`. RFC 9110 does not guarantee idempotency for `PATCH`, so a client cannot assume it without reading the API's documentation.

The property matters because networks drop responses. A client sends a request, the server processes it, the response vanishes in transit, and the client does not know whether the work happened. With an idempotent method, the client retries the identical request and the server's state stays correct. With a non-idempotent method, the retry risks a second side effect, so the protocol demands a separate mechanism — the idempotency key, a deduplication token, or a check-then-act flow — to make the retry safe.

DNS resolves a hostname through a hierarchy of servers, each answering one piece of the question. A laptop typing `example.com` into a browser starts by asking its stub resolver, a small library routine built into the operating system. The stub resolver checks its local cache first. A hit returns the address in microseconds. A miss sends the query upstream.

The upstream target is a recursive resolver, typically the one operated by the ISP or a public alternative like Cloudflare's 1.1.1.1. The recursive resolver does the full walk on the client's behalf. It begins at the root nameservers, the 13 logical servers whose addresses are compiled into every resolver as a starting point. The root servers do not know `example.com`, but they know which servers handle the `.com` top-level domain, and they return those addresses.

The recursive resolver now asks a `.com` TLD nameserver the same question. The TLD server does not know the address for `example.com` either, but it knows which nameservers are authoritative for `example.com` — the ones the domain owner configured when registering the domain. It returns those.

The final query goes to the authoritative nameserver for `example.com`. That server holds the actual record: an A record mapping `example.com` to `93.184.216.34`, or a CNAME redirecting to another name that restarts the walk. The recursive resolver takes that answer, caches it for the duration specified in the record's TTL field, and hands the address back to the stub resolver. The browser opens its TCP connection.

The hierarchy exists because no single server could hold the roughly 350 million registered domains. The root delegates to TLDs, TLDs delegate to registrants, and each layer caches the answers it receives. A second lookup for `example.com` within the TTL window never reaches the authoritative server; the recursive resolver answers from memory. The system trades a small amount of staleness — a DNS change can take as long as the TTL to propagate — for a drastic reduction in query volume at the top of the tree.

A deadlock is a state where two threads each hold a resource the other needs and neither will give up what it has. Both wait forever.

Thread 1 locks mutex A, then tries to lock mutex B. Thread 2 locks mutex B, then tries to lock mutex A. Thread 1 sits waiting for B, which thread 2 holds. Thread 2 sits waiting for A, which thread 1 holds. Neither thread can proceed. The program hangs.

The four conditions were named by Edward Coffman in 1971: mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, and circular wait. Break any one and the deadlock cannot form.

The cleanest fix breaks circular wait with a lock-ordering protocol. Every thread acquires the mutexes in the same global order. If the rule is "A before B," thread 2 must release B before it can acquire A. Thread 1 holds A and waits for B. Thread 2 releases B and acquires A, finishes its work, and releases both. Thread 1 then takes B. The cycle never closes.

The protocol costs nothing at runtime. It costs discipline: every code path that takes two locks must know the order, and a single violation reintroduces the deadlock. On a large codebase the discipline breaks down, which is why kernel developers prefer a single coarse lock or lock-free structures where the ordering problem does not arise.

A hash map turns a key into an integer with a hash function, then uses that integer as an index into an array of slots called buckets. Two different keys can produce the same index. The map has to store both. That situation is a collision, and every hash map handles it by attaching a small structure to each bucket to hold the extra entries.

The two structures in common use are a linked list and an array of pointers.

**Chaining.** Each bucket points to the head of a singly linked list. An entry stores the key, the value, and a pointer to the next entry. A lookup hashes the key, walks the list at that bucket, and compares keys with `strcmp` or its equivalent until one matches or the list ends. A new entry goes at the head because that is O(1). Deletion unlinkes the node and frees it. The list grows without a fixed cap, so the map degrades gracefully under a bad hash: lookups slow to O(n) in the worst case but never fail to store an entry.

**Open addressing.** There is no per-bucket list. The entries live in the array itself, one per slot. On a collision the map probes other slots according to a fixed sequence. Linear probing checks the next slot, then the next, stepping by one. Quadratic probing steps by 1, 4, 9, 16 — squared offsets that spread entries out. Double hashing computes a second hash from the key and uses it as the step size, which breaks up the clustered patterns the first two produce. Lookup follows the same probe sequence until it finds the key or hits an empty slot. Deletion is the hard part: removing an entry and leaving an empty slot would break the probe chain for any key that was inserted after it, so the map marks the slot with a tombstone flag instead. Tombstones accumulate and slow probes, so the map rehashes to clear them once they cross a threshold.

Both methods share one cost control. The map tracks its load factor, the ratio of entries to buckets. When the factor crosses a set point — 0.75 in Java's `HashMap`, 0.7 in Python's `dict` — the map allocates a larger array, typically twice the size, and moves every entry into its new bucket. That rehash spreads entries thin again and keeps the average probe length near one. Without it, a chained bucket's list or an open-addressing probe chain grows long enough to erase the difference between a hash map and a list scanned front to back.

A database index is a second, smaller copy of one or more columns from a table, kept in a structure that finds rows by value fast. The database builds it from a B-tree or a hash table, stores it alongside the primary table, and updates it on every insert, update, and delete that touches the indexed columns.

Without an index, finding rows that match a condition requires scanning every row in the table. A table with ten million rows means ten million comparisons. With an index on the filtered column, the database walks the B-tree in O(log n) steps, reads a handful of disk pages, and fetches only the matching rows. A query that took seconds drops to milliseconds.

The index on a foreign key column turns a join between a million-row parent table and a million-row child table from a nested loop of a trillion comparisons into a million B-tree lookups. The difference is minutes versus hours.

Indexes cost in three ways.

**Write speed.** Every insert, update, or delete on an indexed column writes to the table and to every index on that column. A table with five indexes takes six times the write work of a table with none. On a system that logs thousands of rows per second, that overhead determines whether the system keeps up or falls behind.

**Storage.** Each index is a full data structure on disk. An index on a wide text column in a hundred-million-row table can occupy gigabytes. Five such indexes can double the storage footprint of the table itself.

**Planner misfires.** The query planner picks an index when it estimates the index reads fewer pages than a scan. That estimate depends on statistics about how many rows match a given value. When the statistics are stale or the data is skewed, the planner picks an index that matches most of the table, and the database reads the index, then reads most of the table's pages anyway. That is slower than scanning the table once. A query on a column with two values in a hundred-million-row table, where ninety-five million rows hold value A, will use an index on that column if the planner's statistics are wrong and read ninety-five million index entries plus ninety-five million rows — twice the work of a plain scan.

The rule that falls out: an index earns its place when it serves queries that read a small fraction of the table. An index on a column with low cardinality — few distinct values relative to row count — serves no query well, because every lookup returns a large fraction of the table. An index on a column written constantly and read rarely costs writes on every transaction and pays back nothing. An index that duplicates another index's leading columns wastes storage and write capacity for queries the first index already serves.

The database's own tools name the waste. Postgres's `pg_stat_user_indexes` shows how many reads each index served. An index with zero scans across a representative workload window is a cost with no benefit, and dropping it reclaims write headroom and storage without changing any query's result.

TCP sends data as a stream of numbered bytes, not as a sequence of independent messages. The sender attaches a 32-bit sequence number to the first byte in every segment it transmits. That number is not a segment index — it is the byte offset within the connection's data stream.

The receiver collects these segments. They can arrive out of order. A segment carrying bytes 4000 through 4099 can reach the receiver before the segment carrying bytes 3000 through 3999, because IP routes each datagram independently and a later segment can take a faster path.

The receiver puts arriving bytes into a buffer at the position their sequence numbers specify. Bytes 4000 through 4099 sit in the buffer waiting. Bytes 3000 through 3999 arrive next and fill the gap. The receiver tracks the highest contiguous byte it has received — the cumulative acknowledgment point. It sends back an ACK bearing that number plus one, which tells the sender "I have everything up to byte N; send me byte N+1 next."

The application reading from the connection sees only bytes from the contiguous point forward. The socket layer holds the out-of-order bytes in the kernel's receive buffer and does not deliver them to the application until the gap fills. The application reads a stream in the order the sender wrote it, regardless of the order the segments crossed the wire.

A missing segment stalls delivery. If bytes 3000 through 3999 never arrive, the receiver buffers bytes 4000 through 8999 as they come in but delivers nothing past byte 2999 to the application. The receiver keeps sending the same ACK — the number of the last contiguous byte plus one — for every out-of-order segment that arrives. The sender interprets duplicate ACKs as a signal that a segment was lost and retransmits the missing one. Once the gap fills, the cumulative point jumps forward, and the buffered bytes deliver to the application in one flush.

The sequence number space is finite: 32 bits, zero through 4,294,967,295. It wraps. A connection sending data fast enough to cycle through the space in less than the maximum segment lifetime — about four minutes on the open internet — would confuse an old, delayed segment with a new one. TCP prevents this by refusing to open a connection until the previous incarnation's segments have aged out, enforced by the TIME_WAIT state and the four-minute wait that precedes closing a connection's control block.

A mutex protects one thing: the invariant a thread relies on while it touches shared state.

A thread that reads and writes shared memory does so through a sequence of instructions. Between the read and the write, the processor can pause that thread and run another. The second thread sees memory in a half-updated state. A bank transfer that debits one account and credits another, interrupted between the two writes, leaves the total balance wrong. A linked list insertion that links a new node but has not yet set the node's data pointer, interrupted and read by another thread, dereferences garbage.

The mutex fixes this by giving the sequence a boundary. A thread locks the mutex before it starts and unlocks after it finishes. The operating system and hardware together guarantee that only one thread holds the mutex at a time. A second thread that calls lock blocks — the kernel suspends it — until the first calls unlock. The critical section, the code between lock and unlock, runs uninterrupted with respect to any other critical section guarded by the same mutex.

The protection is narrower than it looks. The mutex guards the section, not the data. Two threads can read and write the same variable without any mutex if their critical sections never overlap in time, and a mutex held during a long computation serializes that computation even when no shared data is involved. The mutex also does nothing for a thread that accesses the data without locking. A third thread that writes to the balance variable directly, bypassing the mutex, corrupts the state the mutex was supposed to protect. The discipline is voluntary, and it is only as strong as every code path that touches the data.

The mutex does not protect against reentrancy from the same thread. A function that locks a mutex and then calls another function that locks the same mutex deadlocks — the second lock call blocks waiting for the first to release, which it will not do until the second returns. A recursive mutex permits this by tracking ownership and incrementing a count on each lock, decrementing on each unlock, and releasing only when the count reaches zero. That solves the reentrancy problem at the cost of a stricter invariant: every lock call must pair with an unlock call, or the mutex never frees.

The mutex does not protect against deadlock across multiple locks. Thread A locks mutex 1 then mutex 2. Thread B locks mutex 2 then mutex 1. Each holds one and waits for the other. The fix is a lock-ordering protocol: every thread acquires mutexes in the same global order, so no cycle can form. The fix is a discipline, not a mechanism — the mutex itself cannot detect or prevent the cycle.

Garbage collection finds memory the program no longer reaches, then frees it. Two algorithms do the finding, and they disagree about what "unused" means.

**Tracing.** The collector starts from the roots: the stack's local variables, the CPU's registers, the global variables, and every object a running thread can name directly. It follows every pointer from those roots to the objects they reference, then every pointer inside those objects to the objects they reference, and so on until it has walked the entire graph of reachable memory. Every object the walk touches is alive. Every object the walk never touches is garbage — nothing in the running program can get to it. The collector frees those. This is what Java, Go, and JavaScript use. Go's collector stops the program for a few milliseconds at a time to do this work, then runs it again seconds later.

**Reference counting.** Each object carries a counter. When a variable points at the object, the counter goes up by one. When the variable goes out of scope or is reassigned, the counter goes down. When the counter hits zero, no variable anywhere points at the object, and the collector frees it on the spot. Python and Swift use this. It frees memory the instant it becomes unreachable, with no pause to walk a graph.

Reference counting breaks on cycles. Object A points at object B, and object B points back at object A. Both have a count of one. Neither is zero. Both stay alive forever, even though no root reaches either of them. Python handles this with a second pass that detects cycles and breaks them. Swift handles it by making the programmer choose: a `weak` reference does not increment the counter, so a cycle of weak references frees normally.

Tracing has no such problem. A cycle of objects that no root reaches is simply unreachable, and the walk never visits it. The cost is the walk itself. A program with ten million objects in memory runs the collector's fingers over all ten million to find the five thousand that are garbage. That work takes time, and the collector either stops the program while it does it or interleaves the work with the program's own execution at the cost of complexity.

Both methods share one blind spot. An object that is reachable but never used again stays alive. A cache that grows without bound, a map that accumulates entries without a removal policy, a list that the program appends to and never trims — the collector sees a root pointing at it and keeps it. The collector finds memory the program cannot reach. It does not find memory the program forgot it had.

A race condition is a bug where a program's result depends on the order in which two operations run, and that order is not controlled.

Two threads share a bank balance. It starts at 100. Thread A reads the balance, adds 50, and writes 150 back. Thread B reads the balance, subtracts 30, and writes 70 back. Each thread does three steps: read, compute, write. The steps interleave. Thread A reads 100. Before A writes, thread B reads 100. B computes 70 and writes it. A computes 150 and writes it. The final balance is 150. The withdrawal of 30 vanished. The balance should be 120.

The balance is wrong because "read, compute, write" is not one operation. It is three. The processor can pause thread A between the read and the write and run thread B in that gap. Thread B sees the old balance because A has not written the new one yet. Both threads read the same starting value, and the last one to write wins. The other thread's update is lost.

The fix is a mutex. Thread A locks the mutex, reads, computes, writes, and unlocks. Thread B locks the mutex and blocks until A unlocks. The three steps become one indivisible step with respect to the other thread. The balance goes 100 to 150 to 120, or 100 to 70 to 120, depending on which thread locks first. Either order gives 120.
