The race is gone because the order of operations is now controlled.

The bug is not that the threads run at the same time. Two threads reading a value that never changes can run in any order and get the same result. The bug is that one thread reads a value, depends on it staying current while it computes, and writes it back — and nothing stops another thread from changing the value in that window. The window is the race. The mutex closes it.

A CPU cache is a small amount of fast memory sitting between the processor and main memory. It speeds up a program by storing copies of the data and instructions the processor is likely to need next, so the processor does not wait on main memory to fetch them.

Main memory is slow. A modern processor running at 3 GHz completes an instruction in about a third of a nanosecond. Fetching a value from DDR4 memory takes roughly 80 nanoseconds — 240 instruction cycles spent idle. The cache, built from SRAM on the same die as the processor, returns a value in 1 to 3 nanoseconds. That is the difference between the processor working and the processor stalling.

The cache works because of a property called locality. Programs do not access memory at random. They access the same addresses repeatedly — a loop variable incremented each iteration, a function's local variables read and written dozens of times in a single call. That is temporal locality: if an address was used recently, it will be used again soon. They also access nearby addresses — walking through an array element by element, reading the fields of a struct one after another. That is spatial locality: if an address was used, an adjacent address will be used soon.

The cache exploits both. When the processor requests a byte from main memory, the memory controller does not send just that byte. It sends a block of 64 contiguous bytes — a cache line — and the cache stores the whole block. The requested byte goes to the processor, and the other 63 sit in the cache. The next request, for the byte at the next address, hits the cache instead of main memory. A loop summing an array of four-byte integers loads the first element from main memory and the next fifteen from the cache. Fifteen of sixteen reads are fast.

The cache is small because SRAM is expensive. A typical L1 cache holds 32 to 48 kilobytes. L2 holds 256 kilobytes to 2 megabytes. L3, shared across cores, holds 8 to 64 megabytes. Main memory holds 16 to 128 gigabytes. The hierarchy trades size for speed at each level: L1 is fastest and smallest, main memory is largest and slowest. The processor checks L1 first, then L2, then L3, then main memory. A request that finds its data in L1 is a hit. A request that misses every level and fetches from main memory is a miss, and it costs those 80 nanoseconds.

The miss is what makes a program slow. A program whose data fits in L1 runs at full speed. A program that streams through a gigabyte of data, touching each byte once, misses on nearly every access because the cache fills, evicts old lines to make room for new ones, and never reuses a line before it is evicted. The cache helps when data is reused. It does nothing for a program that reads each value exactly once.

The layout of data in memory determines whether the cache helps or sits idle. A struct holding an integer and a 60-byte string, stored in an array of ten thousand, occupies 640 kilobytes. A loop that sums the integers touches one byte of useful data per 64-byte cache line and pulls 640 kilobytes through the cache to read 40 kilobytes of integers. Splitting the struct into two parallel arrays — one of integers, one of strings — lets the same loop touch 40 kilobytes, fit in L1, and run fifteen times faster. The computation is identical. The memory layout changed the cache hit rate, and the cache hit rate changed the running time.

Idempotency means a client can send the same request twice and the server ends in the same state as sending it once.

`PUT /users/42` with body `{"name": "Ada"}` sets the name to Ada. Sending it ten times sets the name to Ada. The second through tenth requests overwrite the same field with the same value. The stored row does not change after the first. That is idempotent.

`POST /users` with body `{"name": "Ada"}` creates a new user. Sending it ten times creates ten users named Ada. Each request appends a row. The server's state grows with every call. That is not idempotent.

`DELETE /users/42` removes user 42. The first call deletes the row. The second call finds no row and returns 404. The server's state after the second call is the same as after the first: user 42 is gone. The response differs — 200 then 404 — but idempotency is about state, not about the response body or status code. `DELETE` is idempotent.

`POST /users/42/deactivate` flips a flag from active to inactive. The first call changes the flag. The second call finds the flag already inactive and changes nothing. The state after two calls matches the state after one. The operation is idempotent even though it uses `POST`, because idempotency is a property of what the handler does, not of the verb in the method line.

The property that matters for the client is this: a retried request is safe to send. A network timeout leaves the client uncertain whether the server received the request. With an idempotent endpoint, the client retries the identical request and risks nothing — no duplicate charge, no duplicate row, no second email. With a non-idempotent endpoint, a retry can double the work. A payment of $50 sent twice charges $100. The client cannot tell whether the first request landed, so it cannot safely retry, and it needs a separate mechanism — an idempotency key, a transaction id, a deduplication table — to make the second call a no-op.

That mechanism works by giving the server a way to recognize the retry. The client sends a unique key in a header. The server stores the key with the result of the first request. On the second request with the same key, the server skips the work and returns the stored result. `POST /charges` with key `abc123` charges $50 and returns a receipt. A second call with key `abc123` finds the key, skips the charge, and returns the same receipt. The endpoint is still `POST`, still non-idempotent by nature, but the key makes the retry safe. Stripe and Square use this pattern, passing the key in an `Idempotency-Key` header.

The HTTP spec names `GET`, `PUT`, `DELETE`, and `HEAD` as idempotent and `POST` and `PATCH` as not. The spec describes what the verbs mean in the abstract. A specific handler can violate the contract — a `DELETE` that logs each attempt to a separate table is not idempotent in state, because the log grows. The contract is a default the handler can break.

DNS turns a domain name into an IP address through a hierarchy of servers, each answering a narrower question than the last.

A program asks the operating system to resolve `www.example.com`. The resolver — a library inside the OS, or a stub like systemd-resolved — checks its local cache first. If the cache holds the address and the entry has not expired, the resolver returns it and the lookup ends. No network traffic crosses the wire.

On a cache miss the resolver contacts a recursive resolver, usually the one the ISP runs or a public one like Cloudflare's 1.1.1.1 or Google's 8.8.8.8. The recursive resolver does the work of walking the hierarchy on the client's behalf. It starts with the root servers, thirteen clusters of machines operated by ICANN and other organizations, scattered across the globe and reachable at well-known anycast addresses. The root servers know only the top of the tree: which servers hold each top-level domain.

The recursive resolver asks a root server, "Where is `www.example.com`?" The root server does not know the answer. It returns a referral — the names and addresses of the servers authoritative for the `.com` top-level domain. There are about a thousand of these, run by Verisign and managed under contract with ICANN.

The recursive resolver caches that referral and asks a `.com` server the same question. The `.com` server also does not know the answer. It returns a referral to the servers authoritative for `example.com` — the machines the domain's owner configured when registering the name, listed in the registrar's records.

The recursive resolver asks the `example.com` server for `www.example.com`. This server holds the actual record. It reads the zone file, finds an A record mapping `www` to `93.184.216.34`, and returns that address. The recursive resolver caches the answer with the record's time-to-live — the number of seconds the owner permits the cache to hold it — and hands the address back to the client.

Three round trips, three servers, one address. The root server answered a question about `.com`. The `.com` server answered a question about `example.com`. The `example.com` server answered the real question. Each server in the chain knows only its own layer and delegates the rest downward.

The caching is what keeps the system standing. Thirteen root servers and a thousand `.com` servers could not answer a lookup for every browser tab on earth. The recursive resolver caches every referral and every answer it receives, keyed by name and bounded by TTL. A site visited by a million users behind the same recursive resolver generates one miss and 999,999 cache hits. The authoritative servers see one query. The root servers see none, because the `.com` referral is almost always already cached from some prior lookup.

The records themselves carry types. An A record maps a name to an IPv4 address. An AAAA record maps a name to an IPv6 address. A CNAME record maps one name to another, deferring the final answer to the target — `www.example.com` as a CNAME for `example.com` sends the resolver back to the `example.com` server to resolve the target. An MX record names the mail server that handles a domain. The resolver asks for a specific type, and the authoritative server returns the matching record or a signal that no record of that type exists.

The whole system runs over UDP port 53. A query fits in a single 512-byte datagram, and so does the response in the common case. A response that exceeds 512 bytes — a zone with many records, a DNSSEC signature chain — triggers a fallback to TCP, or the newer EDNS0 extension that lifts the UDP limit to 4096 bytes. The choice of UDP was deliberate: a lookup is one request and one reply, and TCP's three-way handshake would triple the round trips for every name resolution.

A deadlock is a state where two threads each hold a resource the other needs, and neither will give up what it holds. Both wait forever. The program stops.

Two threads, two locks. Thread A locks the account mutex, then tries to lock the transfer-log mutex. Thread B locks the transfer-log mutex, then tries to lock the account mutex. A holds the account lock and waits for the log lock. B holds the log lock and waits for the account lock. Neither thread can proceed. Neither thread can release what it holds until it gets what it waits for. The cycle closes and there is no way out of it.

Four conditions must hold at once for this to happen. The locks must be mutually exclusive — one thread at a time. The threads must hold while waiting — a thread does not release its lock before asking for the next. The resources must be held in a circular chain — A waits for B, B waits for A. And the scheduler must not force a release — the operating system will let a blocked thread sit indefinitely. Break any one of the four and the deadlock cannot form.

The simplest way to break the cycle is a lock-ordering protocol. Every thread acquires the locks in the same sequence. If the rule is "account lock before log lock," thread A locks the account, then the log. Thread B locks the account, then the log. Thread B blocks at the account lock and waits. It does not pick up the log lock while it waits, because it has not finished with the account lock yet. Thread A gets the log lock, does its work, and releases both. Thread B proceeds. No cycle forms because no thread holds a lock that appears later in the order while it waits for one that appears earlier.

The protocol is a discipline, not a mechanism. The locks themselves cannot detect a violation. A thread that grabs the log lock first, ignoring the rule, can still deadlock against a thread that follows it. The rule works only when every code path that touches both locks obeys it. The cost is small — a comment above each lock call naming the order — and the benefit is total. A cycle that cannot form is a cycle that does not need breaking.

A hash map stores key-value pairs in an array. It computes an integer from the key, maps that integer to an array index, and places the entry there. Two keys can produce the same index. That is a collision, and the map needs a rule for what happens next.

**Chaining** hangs a linked list off each array slot. When a new entry lands on an occupied slot, the map appends it to that slot's list. A lookup walks the list and compares keys. The list stays short while the array has spare room; it grows as the load factor rises, and lookups degrade from constant time toward linear. Some implementations swap the linked list for a small array or a balanced tree once a bucket gets heavy, which holds the worst case down to O(log n) rather than O(n). Java's HashMap takes this route: buckets cross a threshold of eight entries and become red-black trees.

**Open addressing** keeps one entry per slot. On collision, the map probes a sequence of nearby slots and takes the first empty one. The probe sequence defines the variant. Linear probing steps forward by one: simple, but it clusters filled slots, and clusters merge as the table fills, so each insertion walks a longer run. Quadratic probing jumps by 1, 4, 9, 16…, which breaks up primary clusters but can cycle through the same slots without covering the table unless the capacity is prime. Double hashing computes a second hash from the key and uses it as the step size, scattering probes across the table and avoiding both clustering patterns.

Deletion in an addressing scheme cannot just empty a slot. A later probe may have skipped past that slot, and zeroing it would break the chain. The map marks the slot as a tombstone: occupied for probing, vacant for insertion. Tombstones accumulate and slow lookups, so the map rehashes to clear them once they cross a fraction of the table.

Every scheme hits a load factor where performance collapses. The map allocates a larger array, typically double the capacity, and reinserts every entry at its new index. This rehash is O(n) but amortized O(1) across insertions, so individual operations stay constant on average. The choice between chaining and addressing comes down to memory layout and workload: chaining tolerates high load factors and handles deletion cleanly but spends a pointer per entry; addressing keeps data packed in the array for cache locality but demands a low load factor and careful tombstone management.

A database index is a second data structure stored alongside a table to make lookups fast without scanning every row. The common form is a B-tree: a sorted search tree whose leaves hold pointers back to table rows. A query with a `WHERE` clause on an indexed column walks the tree in O(log n) comparisons, follows the leaf pointers, and reads only the matching rows. Without the index, the database reads the entire table from disk and filters in memory — a sequential scan that costs O(n) row reads.

The index earns its keep when queries select a small fraction of the table. A query returning 50 rows from 50 million uses the index and touches a few hundred pages. The same query without the index reads every page of the table, which can be millions of pages on disk. The difference between a ten-millisecond lookup and a ten-second scan is the difference between an index that pays for itself and a table scan that does not.

Indexes cost storage and write speed. Every index is a copy of part of the table, sorted and persisted. A table with five indexes stores six sorted structures on disk. Each insert, update, or delete that touches an indexed column must update every one of those structures, not just the table. A workload that writes ten thousand rows per second and reads them once pays for indexes it never uses: the writes are slower, the reads are no faster, and the disk holds five copies of data that serve no query.

An index hurts in three specific situations. First, on a column with low cardinality — a boolean flag, a status field with three values — the B-tree partitions the table into a few huge buckets, and the database still reads most of the table to satisfy the query, plus the index pages on top. The planner recognizes this and skips the index, but the index still consumes write bandwidth and storage at insert time. Second, on a write-heavy table where the indexed column changes often: each update deletes and reinserts an entry in every index on that column, fragmenting the B-tree and forcing page splits that write more pages to disk than the update itself touched. Third, when two indexes on the same table serve queries that run rarely: the storage and write cost is paid on every write, the read benefit is collected on a query that runs once a week.

The database query planner decides whether to use an index per query, based on table statistics it gathers. An index that the planner never chooses is pure overhead. The way to find one is to read the query plans for the actual workload, not to index every column that appears in a `WHERE` clause. A table carrying indexes the planner ignores is a table paying a tax for nothing.

TCP sends data as a stream of numbered bytes, not as a sequence of independent messages. The sender attaches a sequence number to the first byte in every segment it transmits. That number is not a segment counter — it is a byte offset into the stream, and it tells the receiver where these bytes belong relative to everything that came before.

The link between two hosts is not a single wire. IP packets travel through routers, and any two packets can take different paths, arrive in different orders, or vanish entirely. A segment sent early can land after a segment sent late. Without sequence numbers, the receiver would have no way to tell which bytes came first.

The receiver holds a buffer and a counter called the expected sequence number. When a segment arrives, the receiver checks its sequence number against the counter. If the number matches, the bytes are in order: the receiver writes them to the buffer, advances the counter by the number of bytes received, and delivers the contiguous run to the application above. If a segment arrives with a number higher than expected, the bytes are ahead of their place — a gap. The receiver stores them but does not deliver them. It waits for the missing bytes to fill the gap.

A segment can also arrive twice. Networks duplicate packets. The receiver catches this with the same check: a segment whose sequence number falls below the expected counter is a duplicate or a retransmission of already-delivered bytes, and the receiver drops it.

Every segment the receiver gets, in order or out, earns an acknowledgment back to the sender. The acknowledgment carries the next sequence number the receiver expects — the counter value after the bytes it has assembled. An ACK of 5001 means "I have everything through byte 5000; send 5001 next." Cumulative acknowledgments make this robust: if ACKs 4001 and 5001 both arrive, the sender knows everything up to 5000 is settled, even if intermediate ACKs were lost.

The sender keeps a send window of bytes it has transmitted but not yet acknowledged. Each unacknowledged byte has a timer. If the timer fires before an ACK covers that byte, the sender retransmits the segment. This handles loss, which is the common cause of gaps at the receiver: the missing segment did not arrive out of order, it did not arrive at all, and the retransmission fills the hole.

Order is not a property of the network. The network delivers packets however it likes. Order is a property the receiver reconstructs from sequence numbers, holding early bytes in reserve and releasing them only when the gap closes. The application above TCP never sees the disorder — it sees a byte stream in the order the sender wrote it.

A mutex protects one thing: the interleaving of reads and writes on shared state.

Two threads running on separate cores can touch the same variable at the same instant. Thread A reads `count`, gets 7, adds 1, writes 8. Thread B reads `count` in the nanosecond between A's read and A's write, also gets 7, adds 1, also writes 8. Two increments produced one. The lost update is a race condition, and the mutex exists to prevent it.

A mutex is a lock with one owner. A thread acquires the mutex before entering the critical section — the block of code that reads or writes the shared variable. If a second thread tries to acquire the mutex while the first holds it, the second thread blocks: the operating system suspends it, takes it off the CPU, and parks it in a wait queue. When the first thread releases the mutex, the scheduler wakes one waiting thread and hands it ownership. The second thread enters the critical section only after the first has left it.

The result is mutual exclusion: at most one thread executes the critical section at a time. The lost update cannot happen because the read-modify-write sequence runs uninterrupted. Thread A acquires, reads 7, writes 8, releases. Thread B acquires, reads 8, writes 9, releases. Two increments produced two.

A mutex protects against data corruption, not logic errors. If the critical section computes the wrong value, the mutex ensures the wrong value is computed atomically. It serializes access; it does not make the access correct.

The mutex also protects against memory reordering. On a weakly-ordered architecture like ARM, a CPU can reorder a store before a load, or a write before another write, if the hardware sees no dependency between them. A thread could write `data = 42` and then set `ready = true`, but another core observes `ready` as true before `data` as 42. Acquiring and releasing a mutex inserts memory barriers: the acquire prevents reads and writes inside the critical section from moving before the lock, and the release prevents them from moving after the unlock. A thread that sees the mutex released sees every write the previous owner made inside the section.

What a mutex does not protect against is deadlock. Thread A holds mutex 1 and waits for mutex 2. Thread B holds mutex 2 and waits for mutex 1. Neither releases. The lock that prevented the race has now frozen both threads permanently. The mutex is a discipline imposed by the programmer — acquire locks in a consistent order across all threads, or the locks themselves become the hazard.

A mutex is not free. Each acquire and release is a pair of system calls when the lock is contended, and a context switch costs microseconds. A critical section that does no work but lock and unlock still pays that cost under contention. Uncontended, most implementations use an atomic compare-and-swap in userspace and skip the kernel entirely — the fast path is tens of nanoseconds. The slow path, where threads queue, is where the cost lives.

Garbage collection reclaims memory that a program can no longer reach. The question is how it knows what is unreachable, and the answer is that it traces from the roots.

The roots are the entry points: registers on the CPU, local variables on each thread's stack, static and global fields that hold object references. Every object directly referenced by a root is live. Every object referenced by a live object is also live. The collector walks this graph — roots to fields to the objects those fields point to — and marks each one it reaches. When the walk finishes, any object without a mark is garbage. No root path leads to it. No running code can ever read its fields or call its methods again. The collector sweeps the unmarked objects and returns their memory to the heap.

That pair of phases, mark and sweep, is the classic formulation. It handles arbitrary object graphs and never frees something still reachable, but it leaves the heap fragmented: live objects scattered among holes of freed space. Allocation must find a hole that fits, and as the heap fragments, that search slows.

A copying collector solves fragmentation by splitting the heap into two halves. Only one half is active at a time. When it fills, the collector walks the roots, copies every live object into the other half, and leaves the dead ones behind. The live objects land packed, contiguously, with no gaps between them. Allocation in the new half is pointer bumping: advance the free pointer by the object's size, return that address. The cost is that half the heap is always unused, held in reserve for the next copy.

Generational collection rests on an observation about real programs: most objects die young. A function allocates a temporary list, builds a string, returns a result, and the temporaries are garbage before the next allocation. The collector splits the heap into a young region and an old region. New objects go to the young region, which is collected frequently and cheaply. The few that survive several young-region collections are promoted to the old region, which is collected rarely. The win is that a small, frequently collected region reclaims most of the garbage, and the large, stable region is left alone.

The hard part is the roots. A generational collector that wants to collect only the young region must still know which old objects point into the young region, or it will miss a live path and free something reachable. Maintaining that set — the remembered set — costs write barriers: every store of a reference into an old object's field triggers a small bookkeeping update that records the old object as a root for the young-region collection. The barrier is overhead on every pointer write, paid so the young collection can skip scanning the entire old heap.

Concurrent collection adds another tension. A collector that runs while the application's threads are still mutating the object graph can miss a death or, worse, free an object that a mutator thread just acquired a reference to. The standard fix is a write or read barrier that forces the mutator to reconcile with the collector: if a thread reads or writes a reference the collector is about to move, the barrier traps into the collector, which updates the reference to the new location. The collector can relocate objects and fix the mutator's pointers on demand. This is how the JVM's G1 and ZGC and .NET's server GC keep pause times in single-digit milliseconds on heaps of hundreds of gigabytes — the work of tracing and relocation happens off the application's threads, and the barriers are the synchronization points where the two views of the heap meet.

The collector never knows whether an object is logically dead. It knows only whether a path exists from a root to the object. A cache that holds references it will never read again keeps those objects alive, because the reference is there and the collector follows it. A listener registered on an event source keeps the listener's owner alive, because the source holds the listener and the listener holds the owner. These are not bugs in the collector. They are reachable objects that the program has stopped using, and no collector can distinguish them from objects the program needs.

A race condition is a bug where the result of a program depends on the order in which two threads execute, and that order is not controlled.

Two threads share a bank balance of 100. Thread A reads the balance, sees 100, subtracts 10 for a withdrawal, and writes 90. Thread B reads the balance at the same instant, also sees 100, subtracts 20, and writes 80. Two withdrawals happened. The balance dropped by 30, not 10. The bank lost 20.

The defect is not in the arithmetic. It is in the gap between reading and writing. Thread A reads 100, then Thread B reads 100, then Thread A writes 90, then Thread B writes 80. The read and the write are separate operations, and the operating system can pause a thread between them. When it does, a second thread sees a stale value and acts on it. The lost update is the race.

The name comes from the metaphor of a contest. Two threads race for the same memory. The winner's write survives. The loser's write overwrites it, and the loser's read happened so long ago that it no longer reflects the state of the balance. The program's output depends on which thread the scheduler happened to run first, and the scheduler is not fair, not deterministic, and not under the programmer's control.

A mutex fixes the race by making the read and the write atomic. Thread A acquires the lock, reads 100, writes 90, releases the lock. Thread B acquires the lock, reads 90, writes 70, releases the lock. The balance is 70. Two withdrawals produced a 30-dollar drop, and the order no longer matters because the lock serialized the operations.

Races are hard to find because they do not reproduce on every run. The scheduler picks a different order each time, and most orders are correct. Only the one where both threads read before either writes produces the lost update, and that order might appear once in a million executions. A test that runs a thousand times and passes has not proven the race absent. It has proven the race did not trigger on those thousand runs, on that hardware, with that scheduler. The bug sits in the code, waiting for the right timing.

A CPU cache is a small, fast memory that sits between the processor and main memory. It speeds up a program by holding copies of the bytes the program is about to read.

Main memory is slow. A modern CPU core runs at three or four billion cycles per second, and a fetch from DRAM takes two hundred of those cycles. If the CPU waited for main memory on every load, it would spend ninety-five percent of its time idle. The cache closes that gap. A load that hits the cache returns in three or four cycles, and the core keeps working.

The cache works because programs do not read memory at random. They read addresses close together, and they read the same addresses more than once. A loop that sums an array walks through memory in order, hitting each element once. A loop that searches a hash table reads the same bucket array on every lookup. The cache keeps the nearby bytes and the recently used bytes, and the program finds them there.

Hardware exploits this pattern with three levels of cache, each larger and slower than the one before. The L1 cache is 32 or 48 kilobytes, sits on the core, and answers in one nanosecond. The L2 cache is 256 kilobytes to a megabyte and answers in four. The L3 cache is shared across all cores on the chip, holds 8 to 64 megabytes, and answers in twelve to forty. DRAM, the fallback, answers in eighty. The hierarchy catches most reads: a well-behaved program hits L1 ninety percent of the time and misses to DRAM less than one percent.

The cache does not load one byte at a time. It loads a cache line — 64 contiguous bytes — on the first miss. When the program reads the first element of an array, the hardware fetches the next fifteen elements alongside it. If the program walks the array in order, the next fifteen reads hit the cache for free. If the program jumps through the array by strides larger than a cache line, each read misses, and the cache becomes a tax: the hardware loads 64 bytes, the program uses 4, and the other 60 travel across the bus to die unused.

The cache is finite, and new data evicts old data. The L1's 32 kilobytes hold 512 cache lines. When the 513th arrives, the hardware discards a line to make room, and the choice of which line to discard determines whether the program runs fast or slow. The common policy is least-recently-used: throw out the line that went longest without a read. This works because the access pattern that filled the cache — locality in space and time — is the same pattern that will refill it. A program that reads the same small array in a tight loop keeps it in L1. A program that streams through a hundred megabytes of data evicts everything behind it, and the cache stops helping.

A program that fights its own cache is slower than one that fits it. A matrix multiplied row by column touches two arrays in non-sequential order and misses on every access. The same matrix transposed and multiplied row by row walks both arrays in order and hits the cache on every element. The arithmetic is identical. The memory access pattern is not, and the memory access pattern decides the speed.

Idempotency in an HTTP API means a client can send the same request twice and the server ends up in the same state as if it received it once.

`GET` is idempotent by design. It reads a resource and changes nothing, so ten identical GETs return the same body and leave the server untouched. `PUT` is idempotent by contract. A PUT sends a full representation of a resource, and the server stores it at the named URI. Sending the same PUT twice overwrites the same resource with the same data, and the second request produces the same end state as the first. `DELETE` is idempotent in its outcome. The first DELETE removes the resource. The second DELETE finds nothing to remove and returns 404, but the server state — resource absent — is identical to the state after the first call.

`POST` is not idempotent. A POST submits data to a handler, and the handler decides what to do. A POST to `/orders` creates a new order. Sending it twice creates two orders, each with its own ID, each charging the customer. The server state after two requests differs from the state after one. This is why payment endpoints carry the most risk: a duplicated POST, whether from a network retry, a double-click, or a client timeout followed by a resend, charges the customer twice.

The practical fix for non-idempotent POST is an idempotency key. The client generates a unique token — a UUID — and sends it in an `Idempotency-Key` header. The server stores the key on first receipt, processes the request, and persists the response. The second request with the same key arrives, the server finds the stored response, and returns it without reprocessing. Stripe's API documents this pattern: the key persists for 24 hours, and a repeat request within that window returns the original response's status code, headers, and body. The server must store the key before processing, not after, or a crash between processing and storage lets the retry create a second order.

Idempotency is a property of the server's state, not the response. A DELETE that returns 200 the first time and 404 the second is still idempotent. The responses differ, but the resource is gone in both cases. What matters is that no additional side effect occurs. A PUT that returns 200 on the first call and 200 with a different `Last-Modified` on the second is still idempotent if the stored resource is byte-identical, though a strict implementation returns the same representation both times.

The HTTP specification defines idempotency as a property of the method, not the implementation. `PUT` is declared idempotent in RFC 9110, which means a client or proxy can retry a failed PUT without worrying about duplicating state. But the declaration is a contract the server must honor. A PUT handler that appends to a list instead of replacing it breaks the contract, and a retrying client will duplicate entries. The method label tells the client what to expect. The server code determines whether the expectation holds.

DNS turns a human-readable name into a 32-bit or 128-bit network address. The work is distributed across thousands of servers, and the lookup proceeds in stages.

A program calls a resolver, usually a library function like `getaddrinfo`. The resolver checks its local cache. If the cache holds an address for the requested name and the entry has not expired, the resolver returns it without contacting any server. The cache is the first and fastest tier.

On a cache miss, the resolver sends a UDP query to a recursive resolver, typically the one configured by the operating system or provided by the ISP. The recursive resolver does the walking. It starts with no knowledge of the requested name and finds the address by following a chain of delegations from the root of the DNS hierarchy downward.

The recursive resolver begins at a root nameserver. The root nameserver does not know the address for `www.example.com`, but it knows which nameservers are authoritative for the `.com` top-level domain. It returns those nameserver addresses. The recursive resolver sends the same query to a `.com` nameserver. The `.com` nameserver does not know the address for `www.example.com` either, but it knows the nameservers authoritative for `example.com`. It returns those. The recursive resolver queries the authoritative nameserver for `example.com`, and that server holds the actual record. It returns the IP address.

Each answer carries a time-to-live value in seconds. The recursive resolver stores the address in its cache and uses it for subsequent queries until the TTL expires. A short TTL, like 60 seconds, forces frequent re-queries and lets the domain owner change the address quickly. A long TTL, like 86400 seconds, reduces load on the authoritative servers but delays propagation of any change.

The query and response are DNS messages carried over UDP port 53. Each message is a structured packet with a 12-byte header, a question section listing the name and record type, and space for answers. The name is encoded as a sequence of length-prefixed labels, not a null-terminated string. A query for the A record of `www.example.com` asks for a 32-bit IPv4 address. A query for the AAAA record asks for a 128-bit IPv6 address.

The most common record types are A for IPv4 addresses, AAAA for IPv6, CNAME for aliases, and MX for mail servers. A CNAME record maps one name to another, and the resolver restarts the lookup at the new name. `www.example.com` might be a CNAME pointing to `example.com`, which holds the A record. The resolver follows the chain until it reaches an address record.

The distribution is what makes the system scale. The root zone has 13 logical nameserver addresses, served by over a thousand physical instances using anycast routing. The `.com` TLD serves hundreds of millions of domains. Each domain's authoritative server answers only for its own zone. No single server holds the entire namespace, and no query traverses more than a few hops. A full recursive lookup from root to authoritative takes three round trips, and the cache collapses that to zero on a hit.

Okay — explain what a deadlock is and one way to avoid it.

A deadlock is a state where two or more threads are stuck, each waiting for a resource another holds, and none will give up what it has.

Thread A holds lock 1 and asks for lock 2. Thread B holds lock 2 and asks for lock 1. A cannot proceed until B releases lock 2, and B cannot proceed until A releases lock 1. Neither releases, because a thread must acquire the second lock before it can finish its work and release the first. The two threads sit forever. The program halts at that point, and no error is raised — the threads simply stop.

Four conditions must hold at once for a deadlock to exist. The threads must hold resources while waiting for more — *hold and wait*. The locks cannot be taken away by force — *no preemption*. Each resource has one owner at a time — *mutual exclusion*. And the wait forms a circle — *circular wait*. Break any one of the four and the deadlock cannot occur.

The cleanest way to break the cycle is to impose a global lock order. Every thread in the program acquires locks in the same sequence. If lock 1 must be acquired before lock 2 everywhere, Thread A takes lock 1, then lock 2. Thread B also takes lock 1, then lock 2. Thread B blocks at lock 1 while Thread A holds it, and Thread A proceeds to lock 2, finishes its work, and releases both. Thread B then acquires lock 1 and continues. The circular wait never forms, because no thread holds a later lock while waiting for an earlier one.

The discipline is simple to state and hard to enforce. A program with a hundred lock-pair sites must order every pair consistently. A single thread that acquires lock 2 before lock 1, while every other thread does the reverse, reintroduces the cycle. Lock ordering is a convention the code must honor everywhere, and the compiler does not check it. Tools like Thread Sanitizer can detect lock-order violations at runtime, but they find the bug only when the violating path executes — the same timing dependence that makes deadlocks rare and hard to reproduce.

A hash map stores values in an array of buckets, keyed by a hash of the key. Two distinct keys can produce the same bucket index. That is a collision, and the map has to resolve it.

The common resolution is chaining. Each bucket holds a pointer to a linked list of entries. When a key hashes to an occupied bucket, the map walks that list, comparing keys, and either updates the matching entry or appends a new node. Lookup follows the same path: hash, index, walk, compare. Deletion unlinks the node.

Chaining degrades gracefully. A map with *n* entries across *m* buckets has an average chain length of *n*/*m*, the load factor. At a factor of 0.75, the average lookup touches under two nodes. The worst case is *O*(*n*), when every key lands in one bucket, but a reasonable hash function spreads keys evenly and the worst case stays theoretical.

Open addressing is the other resolution. All entries live in the array itself. On collision, the map probes for the next open slot according to a fixed sequence. Linear probing checks the next index, then the next, until it finds room. Quadratic probing jumps by squares of the probe count. Double hashing uses a second hash function to set the step size, which spreads entries more evenly than a fixed stride.

Probing makes the array the whole structure. No lists, no separate node allocations, no pointer chasing. Cache locality is good because entries sit contiguously in memory. The cost is fragility under high load: as the array fills, probe sequences lengthen, and a map near capacity slows for every operation. Deletion is awkward because removing an entry can break a probe chain, so implementations mark slots as tombstones and reclaim them later.

Both methods trigger a resize when the load factor crosses a threshold. The map allocates a larger array, re-hashes every entry into it, and discards the old one. This keeps the average chain short or the probe distance small, which is what preserves constant-time average performance as the entry count grows.

A database index is a separate structure that stores one or more columns of a table in a form optimized for fast lookup. The most common form is the B-tree, which keeps the indexed values sorted and balanced so that finding a row by that column takes logarithmic time rather than a full scan.

Without an index, the database reads every row in the table to find the ones matching a condition. With an index on the filtered column, it traverses the tree, lands on the matching entries, and fetches only those rows. On a table of ten million rows, a query filtering by an indexed column might touch a few dozen pages instead of all of them.

Indexes hurt in three ways.

First, they cost storage. Each index is a copy of part of the table, organized differently. A table with five indexes can occupy several times its raw size on disk.

Second, they slow writes. Every insert, update, or delete that touches an indexed column must update every index on that column in addition to the table itself. A table with five indexes pays five extra maintenance operations per write. Workloads that ingest high volumes of data and query it rarely will run slower with indexes than without.

Third, they can be useless or harmful at query time. An index on a column with low cardinality — a status field with three values, a boolean flag — rarely helps, because the tree points to large fractions of the table anyway, and the database may decide a sequential scan is cheaper than the random reads the index implies. A query that selects most of the rows in a table will also bypass the index for the same reason: reading the whole table in order beats jumping through a tree to reach most of it.

The decision to add an index rests on the workload. Read-heavy tables with queries that filter or join on specific columns benefit. Write-heavy tables, or columns that rarely appear in predicates, do not. An index that no query uses is pure overhead: it consumes space and slows every write for nothing.

TCP sends data as a stream of numbered bytes, not as a series of messages. Every byte gets a sequence number. The first byte's number is chosen randomly during the three-way handshake that opens a connection, and each byte after it increments that number by one.

A sender transmits segments, each carrying a range of bytes and the sequence number of the first byte in that range. The network can deliver these segments out of order. A segment taking a longer network path arrives after a segment sent later, and IP, the protocol underneath TCP, makes no guarantee about delivery order.

The receiver puts segments back in order using those sequence numbers. It holds incoming bytes in a receive buffer. If segment 200 arrives before segment 100, the receiver stores the bytes from 200 and waits. When segment 100 lands, the receiver places it ahead of 200 in the buffer, closing the gap.

The receiver tells the sender what it has. Every acknowledgment segment carries the sequence number of the next byte the receiver expects, which is the first byte after the contiguous, in-order block it holds. An acknowledgment of sequence number 500 means the receiver has every byte up to 499, regardless of the order the segments arrived in.

Gaps trigger retransmission. The sender starts a timer when it sends a segment. If an acknowledgment for those bytes does not arrive before the timer expires, the sender transmits the segment again. A segment lost in transit never arrives, so the receiver never advances its acknowledgment past the missing byte, and the sender's timer eventually fires.

The sender also tracks duplicate acknowledgments. When a receiver gets a segment that fills a gap ahead of a hole, it sends an acknowledgment for the byte at the start of that hole. Several segments arriving out of order produce several copies of the same acknowledgment. The sender treats three duplicate acknowledgments as evidence that the segment at that sequence number was lost, and it retransmits that segment without waiting for the timer.

Order emerges from this accounting. The sequence numbers give every byte a fixed position in the stream. The buffer holds bytes that arrived early. Acknowledgments report the contiguous frontier. Retransmission fills the holes. The application reading from the connection sees an unbroken, ordered stream of bytes, identical to what the application wrote at the other end.

A mutex protects one thing: shared state being touched by two threads at once.

Threads run concurrently. Two threads can read and write the same memory location, and without coordination, their operations interleave. A thread reads a balance of 100, another thread reads 100, both add 50, both write 150. The second deposit is lost. The final value should be 200.

A mutex — mutual exclusion lock — makes that impossible. Before touching the shared data, a thread acquires the mutex. If another thread already holds it, the caller blocks until that thread releases it. Only one thread holds the mutex at a time, so only one thread executes the code between acquire and release. That section is the critical region.

The mutex does not lock the data itself. It locks access to it. The protection holds only if every thread that touches the data acquires the same mutex first. A thread that bypasses the lock and writes directly faces no barrier, and the data corrupts as if the mutex did not exist.

Mutexes guard against race conditions, where the outcome depends on which thread runs first. They do not guard against deadlocks, which they themselves cause. Two threads each holding one mutex and waiting for the other's will both wait forever. The discipline is to acquire mutexes in a consistent order across all threads, or hold one at a time.

The cost is serialization. While one thread holds the mutex, every other thread that needs it waits. A long critical region turns parallel work sequential. The lock is only as fine-grained as the region it protects, and a mutex covering a whole hash table under heavy contention can make a four-core program run at the speed of one.

Garbage collection reclaims memory that a program can no longer reach. The collector's job is to distinguish what is alive from what is not, and free the rest.

The root set is the starting point. It consists of the pointers the program can use right now: registers, stack frames, global variables. Anything reachable from the roots is live. Anything reachable from something reachable from the roots is live too. The collector follows pointers transitively, and what it never touches is garbage.

Two algorithms do this. Both assume the collector can tell which words in memory are pointers and which are data, a property called type information or pointer tagging.

Mark-and-sweep walks the graph. The collector starts at the roots, follows every pointer it finds, and marks each object it reaches. It then sweeps the heap: every unmarked object is freed, and every mark is cleared for the next cycle. The heap fragments, because freed objects leave gaps of varying sizes between the survivors. Allocation must later find a gap that fits, or the heap compacts.

Copying collection avoids fragmentation. The heap is split into two halves. The collector walks the graph from the roots, but instead of marking objects, it copies each reachable object into the other half, packing them contiguously. It leaves a forwarding pointer in the old location so other references can be updated. When the walk finishes, the old half is entirely free space. The new half holds only live objects, packed. Fragmentation is impossible. The cost is that half the heap is unused at any moment, and long-lived objects get copied every cycle.

Generational collection exploits a pattern: most objects die young. The heap is divided into a young region and an old region. New allocations go to the young region. A collection of just the young region is frequent and cheap, because it scans few objects and most of them are already garbage. Objects that survive several young collections are promoted to the old region, which is collected rarely. The hard part is pointers from old objects to young ones: a young collection must know whether an old object still references a young one, or it will free something still in use. Collectors handle this with remembered sets, write barriers that record when an old-to-young pointer is created, so the young collection scans only those old objects rather than the entire old region.

Concurrent collectors run alongside the program instead of pausing it. The trade is complexity. The program can mutate the graph while the collector walks it, changing a pointer the collector already visited or moving an object the program is about to read. Collectors solve this with read and write barriers — small fragments of code inserted at every pointer access — and by treating certain mutations as reasons to re-examine part of the graph. The pauses shrink, sometimes to sub-millisecond, but the throughput drops because every pointer access carries a little extra work.

What every variant shares is the core invariant. An object is garbage if and only if no path of pointers leads from the roots to it. The collector's task is to compute that set precisely and free it, and to do so without stopping the program long enough to matter.

A race condition is a bug where the result of a program depends on the order in which concurrent operations run, and that order is not controlled.

Two threads share a bank balance of 100. Both read it at the same instant. Both see 100. The first thread adds 50 and writes 150. The second thread adds 50 and writes 150. The balance should be 200. It is 150. One deposit vanished.

The loss happens because read and write are separate operations. The hardware executes them one at a time, and the scheduler can switch threads between any two of them. Thread A reads 100. The scheduler switches to thread B. Thread B reads 100, adds 50, writes 150, and finishes. The scheduler switches back to thread A. Thread A still holds the 100 it read earlier, adds 50, and writes 150. The value B wrote is overwritten and lost.

The balance is correct only if one thread finishes its read-add-write before the other starts. Nothing in the code enforces that. The outcome depends on timing, and timing is not a reliable input.

The fix is a mutex around the read-add-write sequence. A thread acquires the lock, reads, adds, writes, and releases. The second thread blocks at the acquire until the first releases. The operations no longer interleave, and the balance reaches 200 regardless of which thread runs first.

A race exists whenever two threads access the same memory and at least one of them writes, and nothing forces their operations to be atomic. The bug is not that the program runs slowly or crashes. The bug is that it produces a wrong answer some of the time, and the times it does are unpredictable.

A CPU cache is a small, fast memory that sits between the processor and main memory. It holds copies of the data and instructions the processor is most likely to need next. When the processor requests a byte, the cache checks whether it already holds that address. If it does, the request is satisfied at cache speed. If it does not, the processor fetches from main memory, which is slower, and the cache stores a copy on the way back.

The speed difference is large. A register access completes in under a nanosecond. An L1 cache hit takes one to two nanoseconds. Main memory takes fifty to a hundred. A program that keeps its working data in cache runs an order of magnitude faster than one that does not, because the processor spends time computing instead of waiting for memory.

Caches work because of locality. Programs do not access memory at random. They access the same locations repeatedly, and they access nearby locations in sequence. A loop that sums an array reads element 0, then 1, then 2, all adjacent in memory. A cache that loads a block of 64 bytes when the program touches the first byte has the next seven integers ready before the program asks for them. The first access is slow. The next seven are fast.

The cache is organized into levels. L1 is smallest and closest, typically 32 to 64 kilobytes per core, split into separate caches for data and instructions. L2 is larger, around 256 kilobytes to one megabyte, and may be private to each core. L3 is largest, several to tens of megabytes, and shared across all cores on the die. A request checks L1, then L2, then L3, then main memory. Each miss costs more time than the last.

A program's data layout determines how well the cache serves it. An array of structures, where each element contains a name, an age, and an address, loads all three fields into cache when the program reads any one. If the program loops over ages, it pulls in names and addresses it never uses, wasting cache capacity and memory bandwidth. An array of separate arrays — one for names, one for ages, one for addresses — loads only ages during the age loop. The cache holds more of what the program needs, and fewer bytes travel from main memory.

The same principle governs traversal order. A two-dimensional array stored in row-major order, as in C, lays each row contiguously in memory. Walking the array row by row hits cache on every element after the first in each row. Walking it column by column jumps across memory by the width of a row, and each jump lands in a different cache line. The column traversal can be ten times slower on a large array, not because the processor does more work, but because it waits for main memory on nearly every access.

The cache turns the slow, distant bulk of main memory into something the processor can reach at a useful fraction of its own speed. The program that fits its working set inside the cache gets that speed. The program that does not pays the memory latency, and no amount of processor clock rate fixes the wait.

Okay, explain idempotency in the context of an HTTP API, in plain register.

An HTTP method is idempotent when a client can issue the same request twice and leave the server in the same state as issuing it once. The second request does not duplicate the effect of the first. It produces the same result, or an equivalent one, without compounding the original action.

`GET` is idempotent because it reads. Two reads do not change the resource, so the state after the first is identical to the state after the second. `PUT` is idempotent because it replaces. A `PUT` to `/users/42` with a given body sets that resource to that body. Issuing it again sets the resource to the same body. The second call overwrites the first, and the end state matches the end state after a single call.

`POST` is not idempotent. A `POST` to `/users` creates a new user. Issuing it twice creates two users. The server state after the second request differs from the state after the first, because the second request added something the first did not. `DELETE` is idempotent in a specific sense: deleting resource 42 once removes it, and deleting it again leaves it removed. The second call returns 404 instead of 200, but the server state — resource 42 absent — is the same.

The property matters because clients and networks retry. A proxy drops a connection mid-request, and the client cannot tell whether the server received the message before the drop. The client retransmits. If the method is idempotent, the retry is safe. The server applies the request once or twice, and the result is the same. If the method is not idempotent, the retry doubles the effect. A payment gets charged twice, an order gets placed twice, a record gets duplicated.

Idempotency is a contract about server state, not about the response. The two requests can return different status codes or different response bodies. The first `DELETE` returns 200 with the deleted resource. The second returns 404. Both leave the resource absent, so the method is idempotent. The guarantee is about what the server holds, not what the client sees in the reply.

The contract is also a statement about the method's semantics, not about a specific implementation. A poorly written `PUT` handler that appends to a log on every call breaks the contract, even though `PUT` is defined as idempotent. The definition tells the client what it can rely on. The server's job is to honor it.

Okay, explain how DNS resolves a hostname to an IP address, in plain register.

A browser asks the operating system to resolve `example.com`. The operating system hands the query to a resolver, usually a program run by the ISP or a public resolver like Google's 8.8.8.8 or Cloudflare's 1.1.1.1.

The resolver does not know the address. It knows where to find it. The domain name system is a tree. At the root sit thirteen logical name servers, operated by separate organizations and identified by the letters A through M. Below the root sit the top-level domain servers, one cluster per extension: `.com`, `.org`, `.net`. Below those sit the authoritative servers for each registered domain.

The resolver starts at the top. It queries a root server for `example.com`. The root server does not have the address, but it holds the names and addresses of the `.com` top-level domain servers. It returns those.

The resolver queries a `.com` server. The `.com` server does not have the address either, but the registrar recorded the authoritative name servers for `example.com` when the domain was purchased. The `.com` server returns those.

The resolver queries `example.com`'s authoritative server. That server holds the actual records for the domain. It finds an A record mapping `example.com` to `93.184.216.34` and returns that address.

The resolver caches the answer. It stores the address with a time-to-live, a number of seconds the record stays valid. The next request for `example.com` within that window gets the cached answer without a single query traveling up the tree. The authoritative server also tells the resolver how long to cache the `.com` server addresses and the root server addresses, so later lookups for other `.com` domains skip the root step.

The browser receives the address and opens a TCP connection to it. The whole walk, when the cache is cold, takes four round trips: one to the root, one to `.com`, one to the authoritative server, one to the target. When the cache is warm, it takes one.

Okay, explain what a deadlock is and one way to avoid it, in plain register.

A deadlock is a state where two threads each hold a resource the other needs, and both wait forever for the other to release it. Neither moves. The program stalls.

Thread A acquires mutex 1. Thread B acquires mutex 2. Thread A now tries to acquire mutex 2, and blocks, because thread B holds it. Thread B tries to acquire mutex 1, and blocks, because thread A holds it. Each thread holds the lock the other wants. Each waits for a release that never comes. The scheduler moves neither forward.

Four conditions produce this. Mutual exclusion: the locks are held by one thread at a time. Hold and wait: each thread holds one lock while requesting another. No preemption: the scheduler cannot force a lock release. Circular wait: the wait graph forms a loop, A waiting on B, B waiting on A. Break any one and the deadlock cannot form.

The cleanest break is lock ordering. Every thread acquires the mutexes in the same global order. If the rule is "acquire mutex 1 before mutex 2," thread A takes 1 then 2, and thread B takes 1 then 2. Thread B cannot hold 2 while waiting for 1, because it would have had to acquire 1 first. The circular wait never forms, because the wait graph can only point one direction along the shared order.

The discipline costs little when the lock order is obvious, and it costs more when the order crosses module boundaries a thread does not know it is inside. A thread in the billing module calling into the inventory module may not see that inventory takes its lock second. Document the order where the locks are declared, and enforce it where they are acquired.

A hash map turns a key into an array index, then stores the value at that index. Two different keys can produce the same index. That is a collision, and the map has to keep both.

**Chaining** hangs a linked list off each bucket. When a second pair lands on an occupied slot, it joins the list. Lookup walks the list and compares keys. The list stays short if the load factor — pairs divided by buckets — stays under one. Java's `HashMap` and C++'s `std::unordered_map` both chain. The cost is a pointer chase per node and poor cache locality, since list nodes scatter across the heap.

**Open addressing** stores every pair inside the bucket array itself. A collision sends the new pair to the next open slot, found by a probe sequence. Linear probing checks `i+1, i+2, i+3…` — fast on modern CPUs because it walks contiguous memory, but it grows clusters: a run of filled slots lengthens with every collision, and every probe into the cluster walks past every member. Quadratic probing jumps `1, 4, 9, 16…` to break clusters up, but can skip over open slots in a small table. Double hashing uses a second hash function to set the step size, which spreads probes more evenly than either. Robin Hood hashing, a variant of open addressing, evicts the pair with the shorter probe distance on each collision; this bounds the worst-case probe length and lets the table stay dense. Python's `dict` uses open addressing with a perturbed probe sequence; Rust's `HashMap` uses Robin Hood hashing (specifically the SwissTable design).

The load factor decides when the table rebuilds. Open addressing degrades fast past 70% full — probes lengthen, and a table near capacity turns every insert into a scan. Chaining tolerates load factors above one because extra pairs just lengthen lists. Both schemes double the bucket array and rehash every pair when the threshold trips. Rehashing is O(n) but amortized O(1) per insert, since it happens rarely.

Deletion has one wrinkle under open addressing: removing a pair and leaving its slot empty breaks the probe chain for anything that was inserted past it. The fix is a tombstone — a marker that says "occupied for probing, empty for storage." Tombstones accumulate, so the table needs periodic rehashing to clear them. Chaining has no such problem; a deletion unlinks the node.

A database index is a second data structure stored alongside the table. It holds a sorted copy of one or more columns, each entry paired with a pointer back to the full row. The database walks this structure instead of scanning the table when a query filters on those columns.

Without an index, a query for `WHERE user_id = 414` reads every row in the table to find the matches. With a B-tree index on `user_id`, the database descends a balanced tree of comparisons and lands on the matching entries in O(log n) time. On a million-row table, that turns one million disk reads into roughly twenty.

The cost is storage and write speed. Every index is a file. A table with five indexes occupies six times the space of the table alone. Every `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, and `DELETE` must update the table and every index that covers the changed column. A write-heavy table with many indexes slows in direct proportion to the index count.

An index hurts when the query cannot use it. A query like `WHERE LOWER(last_name) = 'smith'` bypasses an index on `last_name` because the function changes the value the index sorted. The same applies to `WHERE created_at + 1 = 86400`. The index was built on the raw column; the query asks about a transformation of it. The database falls back to a full scan, and the index consumed disk and write bandwidth for nothing.

Multi-column indexes carry an ordering constraint. An index on `(last_name, first_name)` sorts by surname, then by given name within each surname. It serves `WHERE last_name = 'Smith'` and `WHERE last_name = 'Smith' AND first_name = 'Jane'`. It does not serve `WHERE first_name = 'Jane'`, because first names are sorted only within each surname group, not across the table. The query planner scans the whole index or ignores it.

Indexes also hurt when they are redundant. A query that returns a large fraction of the table — say 20% of a million rows — often runs slower with an index than without. The index points the database to scattered row locations, producing random disk reads. A full table scan reads sequentially, and sequential I/O is an order of magnitude faster on spinning disks and still meaningfully faster on SSDs. The planner knows this and will sometimes choose a scan even when an index exists, but the index still sits on disk, still slows every write, and still serves no purpose.

The decision rests on the workload. A table read by filtered queries and written rarely wants indexes on every column that appears in a `WHERE` clause. A table written a thousand times per second and read by full scans wants none. Most tables sit between those poles, and the indexes that earn their keep are the ones the query planner actually uses — visible in the query plan, not guessed from the schema.

TCP sends data as a stream of numbered bytes, not as a series of messages. Every byte gets a sequence number. The first byte the sender transmits carries an initial sequence number agreed on during the three-way handshake; each byte after it increments by one.

The sender writes bytes into segments. Each segment's TCP header records the sequence number of its first byte. The receiver reads that number, checks it against what it expected, and decides where the segment belongs.

If segments arrive in order, the receiver places them in its buffer and sends an acknowledgment naming the next byte it wants. An ACK of sequence number 1000 tells the sender: "I have everything up to 999; send 1000 next." This is a cumulative acknowledgment. It does not confirm individual segments; it confirms the highest contiguous byte received.

If segment 1000 arrives, then segment 3000, then segment 2000, the receiver holds all three. It cannot deliver 3000 or 2000 to the application yet, because the stream has a gap at 1001. It buffers the out-of-order data and sends a duplicate ACK for 1000 — the same number it sent before, because the next expected byte has not changed. Each out-of-order segment triggers another duplicate ACK.

The sender notices the duplicates. Three duplicate ACKs for the same number mean the segment after that number was probably lost. The sender retransmits that segment without waiting for its timer to expire. This is fast retransmit.

When the missing segment arrives, the gap closes. The receiver now holds bytes 1000 through 3000 contiguously. It sends a single ACK for 3001, releasing all the buffered data to the application in order. The application never sees the gap. It receives a byte stream that looks unbroken, regardless of what happened on the wire.

The sequence number space is 32 bits, which wraps after 4,294,967,296 bytes. TCP handles this with timestamps — the PAWS option, Protection Against Wrapped Sequence numbers — which tags each segment with a clock value so an old, delayed segment cannot be mistaken for a new one after the counter rolls over. Without PAWS, a segment delayed long enough in the network could arrive after the sequence space has cycled and land in the wrong place in the stream.

The receive buffer is finite. The receiver advertises its current window size in every ACK — the number of bytes it can accept. A window of zero tells the sender to stop until the application drains the buffer. This keeps the sender from flooding a slow reader, and it keeps the ordering machinery intact: the receiver only promises to hold and reorder what it has room for.

A mutex protects one thing: shared state touched by more than one thread at the same time.

Two threads run the function `balance = balance - 100`. The CPU executes it as three steps: read `balance` into a register, subtract 100, write the register back. If thread A reads `balance` at 500, and thread B reads `balance` before A writes, both compute 400. The final write is 400. Two withdrawals happened; one was lost. This is a data race.

A mutex fixes it by serializing access. The thread calls `lock(m)` before touching `balance` and `unlock(m)` after. While one thread holds the mutex, every other thread that calls `lock(m)` blocks — it stops running until the holder calls `unlock`. The subtraction becomes atomic with respect to other threads using the same mutex: it completes fully before the next one starts.

A mutex protects only the threads that acquire it. A thread that reads `balance` without locking `m` races against every thread that does lock it. The mutex is a convention, not a fence. It does not guard memory by address; it guards memory by agreement.

The scope of what a mutex protects is whatever runs between its `lock` and its `unlock`. A mutex held too long serializes too much — threads queue where they could have run in parallel. A mutex held across a blocking call — a disk read, a network wait — stalls every thread waiting for it for the duration of that call. The lock should span the shared access and nothing else.

A mutex does not prevent deadlock on its own. Thread A locks `m1` then tries to lock `m2`. Thread B locks `m2` then tries to lock `m1`. Both wait forever. The fix is a lock order: every thread acquires the same set of mutexes in the same sequence, so the cycle never closes.

A mutex does not protect against reentrancy from the same thread. A thread that holds `m` and calls `lock(m)` again deadlocks itself on most implementations — the holder is already the holder, so it blocks on itself. A recursive mutex permits this, incrementing a count on each `lock` and decrementing on each `unlock`, releasing only when the count reaches zero. Recursive mutexes mask design problems: a function that locks a resource it already holds is usually a function calling another function without a clear contract about what it locks.

A mutex is not a memory barrier by intent, but on modern hardware acquiring one issues the barriers needed to make the protected region's reads and writes visible to the next thread that acquires it. The visibility comes with the lock; it is not free, and it is not the reason the mutex exists. The reason is exclusion.

Garbage collection finds memory the program no longer reaches, then frees it. The program allocates objects on a heap. It holds some objects directly — local variables, static fields, the roots of every reachable graph. It holds the rest indirectly: an object is reachable if a chain of references leads from a root to it.

**Tracing** walks those chains. The collector starts at the roots — registers, the call stack, global variables — and follows every pointer it finds. Each object it reaches gets marked alive. Everything it does not reach is garbage. This is mark-and-sweep, the scheme Smalltalk used in 1980 and the Java Virtual Machine uses today. The mark phase colors objects; the sweep phase scans the heap and reclaims the uncolored ones. The program must pause while both phases run, because the collector cannot follow moving pointers while the program changes them.

**Moving collectors** solve fragmentation. Mark-and-sweep leaves gaps — objects freed between survivors, too small to hold new allocations. A compacting collector copies every live object into a contiguous block after marking, then points the roots at the new locations. The old space becomes one free range. Copying takes time proportional to the live set, not the garbage, which is an advantage when most objects die young — the generational hypothesis, observed in most programs: 80 to 95 percent of objects allocated do not survive one collection.

**Generational collection** splits the heap by age. New objects go in the young generation. The collector scans it frequently and cheaply, since most of its contents are already dead. Objects that survive several young collections move to the old generation, which the collector scans rarely. The JVM's G1 collector divides the old generation into regions and collects the regions with the most garbage first — the "garbage first" the name refers to. This bounds pause time: the collector picks a fixed number of regions to fit a target pause, rather than scanning the entire old generation at once.

**Reference counting** takes a different path. Every object carries a count of references pointing to it. Assignment increments the count; dropping a reference decrements it. When the count hits zero, the object is unreachable and freed immediately — no pause, no scan. PHP and Swift use this. It fails on cycles: two objects referencing each other keep each other's count above zero forever, even if nothing else reaches either. Swift sidesteps this with `weak` references that do not increment the count; Python's cycle detector supplements reference counting with a periodic tracing pass to break loops.

The cost of any scheme is the trade between pause time and throughput. A collector that stops the program for ten milliseconds frees garbage faster than one that interleaves work with the program's own, but the program freezes for those ten milliseconds. Concurrent collectors — Go's, for instance — run most of the marking alongside the program's execution, trading a small constant overhead for short pauses. The program never stops for long, but it runs slower between collections because the collector steals CPU cycles the program could have used.

A race condition is a bug where the program's output depends on the order in which two operations finish, and that order is not controlled.

Two threads run this function:

```
balance = balance - 100
```

The CPU does not subtract 100 from memory in one step. It reads `balance` into a register, subtracts 100 inside that register, and writes the register back to memory. Three instructions. Between the read and the write, anything can land.

Thread A reads `balance` and gets 500. Thread B reads `balance` before A writes. B also gets 500. A subtracts 100, writes 400. B subtracts 100, writes 400. Two withdrawals happened. The account lost 100 dollars. The machine did exactly what it was told, in the order it was told.

The race is the gap between read and write. The CPU scheduled A and B to run at the same time, and neither knew the other had read a stale value. The result is wrong, but no instruction was wrong. The program failed because two operations that should have been sequential ran concurrently, and the hardware let them.

A mutex closes the gap. The thread calls `lock(m)` before reading `balance` and `unlock(m)` after writing it back. While A holds the mutex, B blocks on `lock(m)` and waits. A writes 400 and releases. B reads 400, subtracts, writes 300. The answer is correct. The mutex turned two racing operations into two sequential ones.

Races are not limited to memory. A program checks whether a file exists, then opens it. Between the check and the open, another process deletes the file. The open fails. The check was honest when it ran; the world changed underneath it. This is a TOCTOU race — time-of-check to time-of-use — and it appears wherever a program acts on a condition it does not re-verify. The fix is the same shape: make the check and the use atomic, so nothing can intervene.

A CPU cache is a small amount of fast memory sitting between the processor and main memory. It holds copies of the data and instructions the processor is most likely to need next. When the processor reads a memory address, the cache checks whether it already holds that address. If it does, the read completes in one to three cycles. If it does not, the processor fetches from main memory, which takes two to three hundred cycles on modern hardware. The first case is a cache hit. The second is a cache miss.

The cache is fast because it is built from static RAM, which uses six transistors per bit and responds in a single cycle. Main memory uses dynamic RAM, one transistor per bit, which must be read in rows and refreshed constantly. Static RAM is large, hot, and expensive, which is why a cache holds a few megabytes while main memory holds gigabytes.

Caches exploit two properties of how programs access memory. The first is temporal locality: if the processor reads an address, it will probably read it again soon. A loop variable is read and written on every iteration. The cache keeps it. The second is spatial locality: if the processor reads an address, it will probably read nearby addresses soon. An array processed element by element walks through contiguous memory. The cache exploits this by fetching in blocks — typically 64 bytes — not single addresses. One miss pulls a whole cache line, and the next seven reads on a 64-bit machine hit the cache for free.
