Modern processors have three cache levels. L1 is smallest and closest, 32 to 64 kilobytes, one cycle away, split into separate caches for data and instructions. L2 is larger, 256 kilobytes to one megabyte, roughly ten cycles. L3 is shared across all cores on the die, several megabytes to tens of megabytes, thirty to fifty cycles. A read that misses L1 checks L2, then L3, then main memory. Each miss costs more time. A program that fits its working set in L1 runs at full speed. A program that spills to L2 slows by a factor of ten on every access that spills. A program that misses all three levels waits two hundred cycles per read, and the processor stalls.

The cost shows up directly in two kinds of code. The first walks memory in the order it is laid out. An array of one million integers summed left to right hits the cache on every element after the first, because each 64-byte cache line holds eight integers and the loop consumes them in sequence. The same array summed by striding through it — every sixteenth element, say — touches a new cache line on almost every access. The processor fetches a full line from memory and uses one value from it. The computation does the same number of additions either way. The strided version takes ten to twenty times longer on a million-element array, because it spends its time waiting on memory, not doing arithmetic.

The second kind of cost comes from pointer chasing. A linked list node can live anywhere in memory. Walking a linked list touches a new cache line on every node, because the next node's address bears no relation to the current one's. Walking an array of the same data touches one cache line per eight elements. This is why a vector outperforms a list for sequential traversal even though both are O(n): the vector does eight reads per cache miss, the list does one.

Cache misses also dominate function call cost in large codebases. A function whose code is not in the instruction cache takes tens of cycles to load before its first instruction executes. A hot function that loops stays in the cache and runs at full speed. A function called once in a cold path pays the full miss penalty. This is why virtual function calls and indirect jumps cost more than direct calls on modern hardware — not because the dispatch itself is expensive, but because the target code is often not in the cache.

The cache turns the memory hierarchy into a performance question about access patterns. A program that reads what it just read, walks memory in order, and keeps its working set small runs from cache and is fast. A program that scatters its reads across memory, follows pointers, and touches more data than the cache holds spends its time waiting for DRAM. The arithmetic unit is rarely the bottleneck. The cache is.

Okay — explain idempotency as it applies to HTTP APIs, in plain register.

An HTTP method is idempotent when a client can send the same request twice and leave the server in the same state as sending it once. The second request does not duplicate the first's effect. It either repeats a no-op or re-applies the same result, and the resource ends up where it would have ended up after a single call.

`GET` is idempotent because it reads. Two reads change nothing. `PUT` is idempotent because it replaces. A `PUT /users/42` with the body `{"name": "Ada"}` sets the resource to that exact state. Sending it again sets the resource to the same state again. The server stores one user, not two. `DELETE` is idempotent because it removes. `DELETE /users/42` deletes the user. A second `DELETE /users/42` finds no user and deletes nothing, and the end state — no user 42 — matches the first call.

`POST` is not idempotent. `POST /orders` with the body `{"item": "book"}` creates an order. Sending it again creates a second order. The server holds two orders where one was requested. This is why browsers warn before resubmitting a form: the second `POST` charges the card a second time.

The distinction matters when a request fails mid-flight. A client sends `PUT /users/42`, the server writes the new state, the network drops the response. The client does not know whether the write happened. It retries the same `PUT`. The server applies the same state again. No harm. The same failure on a `POST /orders` produces two orders, because the second request creates again rather than replaces. The client cannot safely retry without a guard — an idempotency key in the request body or header that lets the server recognize the duplicate and return the first order instead of creating a second.

The HTTP specification marks `GET`, `PUT`, `DELETE`, and `HEAD` as idempotent. It marks `POST` and `PATCH` as not. `PATCH` is the subtle one: a patch that sets a field to a value is idempotent, but a patch that adds one to a field is not. Two patches that add one produce a total increase of two. The specification leaves `PATCH` non-idempotent because the method does not define the operation, only the transport.

Idempotency is a contract about server state, not about the response. A second `GET` may return different data than the first if the resource changed between calls. A second `DELETE` may return `200 OK` the first time and `404 Not Found` the second. Both are correct. The server state after the second call matches the state after the first: the resource is gone. The response differs, but the effect does not.

Okay — explain DNS resolution, name to address, in plain register.

A browser asks for `example.com`. The operating system hands that name to a resolver, and the resolver goes looking for a number.

The resolver checks its own cache first. If it has seen `example.com` recently, it returns the address and stops. Most lookups end here. The rest of the system exists for the cache miss.

On a miss, the resolver asks a root nameserver. There are thirteen root addresses, published in a file called the root hints, and every resolver ships with them. The root does not know `example.com`. It knows who knows about `.com`. It returns a referral to the top-level domain servers for `.com`.

The resolver asks a `.com` server. That server does not know the address of `example.com` either. It knows which nameservers are authoritative for `example.com` — the servers operated by whoever registered the domain. It returns those names.

The resolver asks the authoritative server for `example.com`. That server holds the actual record. It returns an A record, which is an IPv4 address: `93.184.216.34`. The resolver hands that address to the browser and caches it for the time the record specifies — the TTL, time to live, measured in seconds.

Three round trips: root, top-level, authoritative. Each asks one question and gets either a referral one step closer or the final answer. The resolver caches every answer it receives, so the next lookup for anything under `.com` skips the root and goes straight to the `.com` servers.

The address record is one type among many. An MX record names the mail server for a domain. A CNAME maps one name to another — `www.example.com` to `example.com` — and the resolver restarts the lookup at the target. An AAAA record returns an IPv6 address, 128 bits instead of 32. TXT records hold arbitrary strings, used now to verify domain ownership and publish mail policy. NS records name the authoritative servers. Each record type answers a different question about the same name.

DNS runs over UDP port 53. A query and its response each fit in a single UDP packet, which keeps the protocol cheap — no handshake, no connection state, one packet out and one back. When a response exceeds 512 bytes, the resolver falls back to TCP and re-asks. DNSSEC, which signs records so the resolver can verify they were not tampered with, pushes many responses over that limit and onto TCP.

The system is hierarchical because the name is. `example.com` reads right to left. The root owns the empty suffix after the final dot. The `.com` registry owns the next label. The domain owner owns everything to the left. Each layer delegates authority downward, and each resolver walks down the chain until the authority runs out and the address appears.

Okay — explain deadlock and one avoidance, plain register.

A deadlock is a state where two or more threads each hold a resource the others need and each waits for a resource another holds. None can proceed. None releases what it has. The cycle never breaks.

Thread A locks file one. Thread B locks file two. A tries to lock file two and blocks, because B holds it. B tries to lock file one and blocks, because A holds it. A waits for B. B waits for A. Both sleep forever. The program halts at that point with no error message and no crash — the threads simply stop.

Four conditions must hold at once for this to happen. The threads hold resources exclusively: one lock, one owner. They hold while waiting: a thread does not release its lock before asking for the next. They wait in a cycle: A for B, B for A. And the system does not preempt: nothing forces a lock away from a holder. Break any one condition and deadlock cannot occur.

The reliable fix is a lock order. Every thread acquires the same set of locks in the same sequence. If the rule is "lock file one before file two," A locks one, then two. B locks one, then two. B blocks at the first lock while A holds it. A proceeds to the second lock, finishes its work, and releases both. B wakes, acquires one, then two, and proceeds. The cycle never forms because the waiting is linear, not circular.

The cost is discipline. A function that locks a resource must know what locks the caller already holds, or it can violate the order without knowing. A thread that needs a lock out of order must release what it holds, acquire the locks in the correct sequence, and re-acquire the first. The rule is simple to state and hard to enforce across a large codebase, which is why lock-order violations are the most common cause of deadlocks in production.

A hash map turns a key into an array index, then stores the value at that index. Two keys can land on the same index. That is a collision, and every hash map has to resolve it.

**Chaining** hangs a linked list off each bucket. On insert, the map hashes the key, walks the list at that index, and either updates an existing entry or appends a new node. On lookup, it walks the same list and compares keys. The cost grows with list length. If the hash function spreads keys evenly and the table stays half-full, the average list holds one or two nodes and operations stay O(1). If the function clusters keys, lists grow long and performance degrades toward O(n). Java's `HashMap` and C++'s `std::unordered_map` both chain.

**Open addressing** stores entries in the bucket array itself, no list. When a key hashes to an occupied slot, the map probes other slots by a fixed rule until it finds an empty one. Three common rules:

- *Linear probing* checks the next slot, then the next, and so on. Simple, but collisions cluster: a run of occupied slots grows longer with each insert that lands inside it, because every probe in the run extends it.
- *Quadratic probing* jumps by 1, 4, 9, 16… slots, breaking up clusters. It can still cycle through a small set of slots and miss empties if the table size is poorly chosen.
- *Double hashing* uses a second hash function to set the probe step, giving each key its own stride. This scatters probes the most but adds a second hash computation per probe.

Deletion in open addressing cannot just clear a slot, because a probe sequence that passed through that slot would break. The map marks the slot as a tombstone: lookups skip past it, inserts can reuse it, and the map rehashes everything when tombstones accumulate.

**Load factor** is the ratio of entries to slots. Chaining tolerates a load factor above 1.0 because lists can grow indefinitely. Open addressing requires the factor below 1.0 — once the table fills, probes search forever. Both schemes rehash when the factor crosses a threshold, usually 0.75: allocate a larger array, rehash every entry into it, discard the old array. Rehashing is O(n) but amortized O(1) per insert if growth doubles the capacity.

The tradeoff is locality versus worst-case bounds. Chaining handles high load and bad hash functions gracefully because lists absorb overflow. Open addressing keeps all data in one contiguous array, so a probe sequence hits cache lines, but a full or nearly full table makes every operation slow.

A database index is a second data structure stored alongside a table to make lookups fast without scanning every row.

The common form is a B-tree. It holds a sorted copy of one or more columns, each entry pointing to the row that owns those values. A query filtering on an indexed column walks the tree — O(log n) — instead of reading the table top to bottom. A query joining two tables on indexed keys avoids a nested loop that compares every row of one against every row of the other.

The cost is storage and write work. Every index is a file. A table with five indexes occupies roughly six times the disk space of the raw data. Every insert, update, and delete must update the table and every index that covers the changed column. A table that takes 2ms to insert a row with no indexes takes 12ms with five, because each index adds its own B-tree write and its own disk seek.

Indexes hurt in three specific cases.

A table that takes far more writes than reads gains nothing from an index. The index pays its write cost on every insert and never earns a read saving. Logging tables, event queues, and sensor feeds fit this shape.

A query that touches a large fraction of a table is slower through an index than through a full scan. The index points to rows scattered across disk. Following those pointers means random I/O. A sequential scan reads the table in order, which is what disks do fastest. Most query planners skip an index when they estimate it will touch more than 5–20% of rows, and read the table directly instead.

An index on a column with few distinct values — a status field holding "open" and "closed" — selects half the table on either value. The B-tree narrows the search to 500,000 rows, then fetches each one by pointer. A scan would have read the same rows in one pass. The planner usually ignores such an index.

A useful index sits on a column that queries filter by, that holds many distinct values, and that the table reads from more often than it writes to. A users table indexed on email fits: logins look up one row by email, and new users arrive one at a time. An index on a boolean flag does not.

TCP sends each byte as a segment carrying a 32-bit sequence number. That number is the byte's offset from an initial sequence number both ends agree on during the handshake. The receiver reads the sequence number, places the segment's payload at the correct offset in its receive buffer, and delivers bytes to the application in offset order.

Segments can arrive out of order. A packet routed through a slower path lands after a packet sent later. A retransmitted segment arrives after segments that were sent after the original was lost. The receiver handles both the same way: it stores whatever arrived, in the slot the sequence number names, and waits for the gap to fill.

The receiver tells the sender what it has through the acknowledgment number. That number is the next byte the receiver expects — the first offset past all contiguous data it has received. An ACK of 5001 means bytes 0 through 5000 are in the buffer and ready for the application. It says nothing about byte 5002, which may have arrived and is sitting in the buffer waiting for 5001.

This is cumulative acknowledgment. The receiver repeats the same ACK number until the gap fills. If bytes 5001 through 7000 arrived but 5001 is missing, every segment the receiver sends back carries ACK 5001. The sender sees the same number repeated and infers loss: three identical ACKs in a row trigger fast retransmit, which resends the missing segment without waiting for a timeout.

The timeout is the other loss signal. The sender starts a retransmission timer for every segment it sends. If the ACK does not return before the timer expires, the sender resends. The timer adapts to round-trip time, measured from each segment's send time to its ACK arrival.

The receive buffer is the structure that makes ordering work. It is a contiguous byte array indexed by sequence number. Out-of-order segments sit in it at their offsets. When a gap fills, the receiver slides a window forward over the now-contiguous bytes, hands them to the application, and frees that space for new data. The application never sees gaps. It receives a byte stream in the order the sender wrote it.

A mutex protects a critical section: a span of code that reads or writes shared state that two or more threads can reach at the same time.

The problem is interleaving. A thread is not atomic. It loads a value from memory, modifies it in a register, and stores it back. Between the load and the store, the scheduler can pause that thread and run another. Two threads incrementing a counter from 4 to 5 can both load 4, both add 1, and both store 5. One increment is lost. The mutex makes the load-modify-store indivisible by serializing access: one thread enters the section, the other waits outside until the first leaves.

The mutex itself is a small piece of kernel or library state with two operations, lock and unlock. Lock checks a flag. If the flag is clear, the thread sets it and proceeds. If the flag is set, the thread blocks — the kernel parks it off the run queue until the holder calls unlock, which clears the flag and wakes one waiter. The check-and-set must itself be atomic, done with a hardware instruction like compare-and-swap or test-and-set, because two threads reading a clear flag and both setting it is the same race the mutex exists to prevent.

A mutex protects against data races, which are concurrent unsynchronized accesses where at least one is a write. It does not protect against reentrancy from the same thread. A thread that locks a mutex and then calls a function that locks it again will deadlock against itself, because the lock is already held and no other thread will unlock it. Languages that expect this pattern offer a recursive mutex, which tracks owner and count so a second lock by the same thread succeeds.

It also does not make code correct by existing. Locking the wrong mutex protects nothing — thread A locks mutex X, thread B locks mutex Y, both reach the same data. Locking too little protects the wrong thing — locking around a read, releasing, then writing based on that read leaves the value stale by the time the write happens. Locking too much serializes code that did not need it, turning parallel work sequential and erasing the reason threads were there.

Two failure modes follow from misuse. Deadlock: thread A holds mutex 1 and waits for mutex 2, thread B holds mutex 2 and waits for mutex 1. Neither moves. Priority inversion: a high-priority thread waits on a mutex held by a low-priority thread, and the scheduler keeps running medium-priority threads that preempt the low-priority holder, so the high-priority thread waits indefinitely. The Mars Pathfinder rover hit this in 1997; its watchdog timer rebooted it in a loop until the ground team enabled priority inheritance, which temporarily raises the holder's priority to match the waiter's.

A mutex is the narrowest tool for the narrowest problem. It guarantees that one thread at a time executes a given section of code. Everything else — ordering of operations across threads, visibility of writes to other cores, avoidance of deadlocks — is a separate concern that the mutex does not address by itself.

Okay: explain how garbage collection finds unused memory, in the plain register already established.

A garbage collector reclaims memory the program can no longer reach. "No longer reach" has a precise meaning: no path of pointers from a root to the object. The roots are the starting points — static fields, local variables on every thread's stack, CPU registers holding references. If a chain of pointers from a root leads to an object, it is live. If no chain does, it is garbage.

The collector builds that chain by tracing. It starts with the roots, follows every pointer it finds, marks each object it reaches, then follows that object's pointers in turn. When the trace stops, every marked object is live. Every unmarked object is unreachable. The collector then sweeps the heap: walks every object, frees the unmarked ones, clears the marks on the rest, and starts over. This is mark-and-sweep, the scheme McCarthy described in 1960 and the ancestor of most collectors since.

The trace answers the question "is this object reachable?" It does not answer "is this object still going to be used?" A program can hold a reference in a long-lived collection, never read it again, and the object survives every collection. The collector finds what the program *can* reach, not what it *will* use. This is why caches and listener lists leak: the reference exists, so the object lives, whether or not anyone consults it.

Mark-and-sweep fragments the heap. Freed objects leave holes of varying size. New allocations that do not fit any hole trigger a new sweep or grow the heap. **Compacting** collectors solve this by sliding live objects together after the mark phase, leaving one contiguous free region at the end. The collector must update every pointer it moves, which means knowing where every pointer lives — a constraint that some runtimes meet with exact type information and others approximate with conservative scanning that treats any word that looks like a pointer as one.

**Copying** collectors fold compaction into collection. They split the heap into two halves, from-space and to-space. The program allocates in from-space. At collection, the collector copies every reachable object from from-space to to-space, packing them end to end, and leaves behind a single free region. The old from-space becomes the new to-space. This costs half the heap — only one half holds live data at a time — but allocation is pointer bumping: the next free byte is the last allocated byte plus its size, no free-list to search.

Generational collectors exploit one observation: most objects die young. A study by Ungar and Jackson measured allocation lifetimes across Smalltalk programs and found that the majority of objects became unreachable before the next collection. The collector splits the heap into a young region and an old region. New objects go in the young region, which the collector traces frequently and cheaply because it is small. Objects that survive several young collections promote to the old region, which the collector traces rarely.

The hard part of generational collection is the remembered set. A pointer in the old region pointing at a young object keeps that young object alive, but a young-only collection does not trace the old region. The runtime maintains a side table — the remembered set — listing old-to-young pointers. Every write to an old-region field that could hold a young reference must add an entry to that table. This is a write barrier: a small piece of code the compiler inserts after every reference store, checking whether the stored value points into young space and recording it if so. The barrier costs a few instructions per store, paid across the whole program to make young collections fast.

**Concurrent** collectors trace while the program runs, rather than pausing it. The problem is mutation: the program changes a pointer while the collector is following it. If object A points to B, the collector marks A, the program then repoints A to C and drops the pointer to B, and the collector has already passed A, it never traces C. C is reachable but unmarked, and the collector frees it. This is the tricolor problem. The collector treats objects as three colors: white (unseen), gray (seen, children not yet traced), black (seen and children traced). The invariant is that no black object holds a pointer to a white object — a black object has been fully traced, so anything it points to must be at least gray. A write barrier restores the invariant when the program mutates a pointer: it either turns the target gray (the Yuasa barrier, used by Go's collector) or turns the source gray again (the Steele barrier). The collector then re-traces the gray objects before declaring the sweep safe.

The pause is what every collector trades against. A stop-the-world collector pauses every thread, traces, sweeps or copies, and resumes. The pause length grows with the live heap, not the total heap — dead objects cost mark time but not sweep time in a copying collector, and the mark is the expensive part. Concurrent collectors shrink pauses by doing trace work in parallel with the program, at the cost of write barriers on every store and higher total CPU. Go's collector targets sub-millisecond pauses by running the mark phase concurrently and bounding the sweep, accepting that total throughput drops during collection. The JVM's G1 pauses are longer but bounded by region size, because it collects regions rather than the whole heap at once.

What garbage collection does not do is manage resources other than memory. A file handle, a database connection, a lock — these are not memory, and the collector does not know they are scarce. An object holding a file descriptor becomes unreachable, the collector marks it garbage, but the collector may not run for seconds or minutes. The descriptor stays open until the collector happens to run and the object's finalizer (if it has one) closes it. Finalizers are unreliable for this reason: their timing depends on collection timing, which depends on allocation pressure, which the program does not control. The reliable fix is an explicit close or release call, not a finalizer.

A race condition is a bug where the result depends on the order in which two operations run, and that order is not controlled.

Two threads share a bank balance of 100. Both read it. Both see 100. Thread A adds 50, writes 150. Thread B subtracts 30, writes 70. The final balance is 70. One deposit vanished. The operations interleaved: A read, B read, A wrote, B wrote. Had A written before B read, the balance would be 120. The code is correct in isolation and wrong under concurrency because nothing forced one sequence over the other.

The balance lives in memory. A thread does not update it in one step. It loads the value into a CPU register, adds or subtracts, and stores the result back. The scheduler can pause the thread between any of those steps and run another. The window between load and store is the race. Two threads that enter it at the same time both operate on the same stale value, and the second store overwrites the first.

The fix is to make the load-modify-store indivisible. A mutex locks the balance: one thread enters the section, the other waits. A compare-and-swap does it without a lock: the CPU writes the new value only if the memory location still holds the value the thread read, retrying if another thread changed it. Either way the operation becomes atomic, and the second thread sees the first thread's result before it begins.

Races are not confined to counters. A program checks whether a file exists, then opens it. Another process deletes the file between the check and the open. The open fails. A lazy initializer checks whether a singleton is null, then constructs it. Two threads see null, both construct, and the singleton is no longer single. A logger appends a line to a buffer with no synchronization; the lines interleave mid-character. In each case the code assumes the world stays still between two observations, and it does not.

The defining trait is that the program's output changes with timing. Run it twice on the same input and the result differs. A bug that reproduces on every run is a logic error. A bug that appears once in a thousand runs, under load, on a particular core count, is a race.

A CPU cache is a small amount of fast memory sitting between the processor and main memory. It speeds up a program by storing copies of the data and instructions the processor is likely to need next, so the processor does not wait on the slow trip to RAM.

Main memory is far away. A modern processor runs at 3 GHz and can execute an instruction in a third of a nanosecond. Fetching a value from DDR4 RAM takes 60 to 100 nanoseconds — 200 to 300 clock cycles of idle waiting. The cache, built from SRAM on the same die as the processor, returns a value in 1 to 4 cycles. The speed difference is a hundredfold, and it is the reason caches exist.

Caches work because of locality. A program that reads address 0x1000 almost always reads 0x1001 next. That is spatial locality: memory accesses cluster in address ranges. A loop that sums an array touches each element in sequence, and a function that calls another function executes instructions that sit right next to each other in the binary. The cache exploits this by loading data in blocks, not single bytes. A cache line is 64 bytes on most x86 and ARM processors. When the processor requests one byte from RAM, the memory controller ships the whole 64-byte line containing it. The next seven reads hit the cache instead of RAM.

The other half is temporal locality. A value the program just read, it will probably read again soon. A loop variable is touched every iteration. A struct's fields are read together. The cache keeps recently used lines and discards old ones, betting that the near future resembles the recent past. The bet wins often enough that a well-written program hits the cache 95% of the time or more.

The hierarchy has three levels. L1 is smallest and closest: 32 to 48 kilobytes, one or two cycles away, split into separate caches for data and instructions. L2 is larger, 256 kilobytes to 2 megabytes, 10 to 15 cycles, private to each core. L3 is largest, 8 to 64 megabytes, 30 to 50 cycles, shared across all cores on the die. A request checks L1, then L2, then L3, then RAM. Each miss costs more time. A program that fits its working set in L1 runs at full speed. One that spills to L2 slows by a factor of five. One that misses to RAM slows by a factor of a hundred.

The cache cannot hold everything, so it evicts. When a new line arrives and the set is full, the controller picks an old line and discards it. Most caches use least-recently-used: the line that went longest without a read gets thrown out. Eviction is the mechanism behind cache misses that are not cold. A program that streams through a large array fills the cache with early elements, then evicts them to make room for later ones. If it loops back and reads the early elements again, they are gone — a capacity miss. Two arrays that map to the same cache sets can evict each other even when the cache is not full — a conflict miss, the cost of the direct-mapped or low-associativity design that trades hit speed for simpler hardware.

What this means for a program is that the memory access pattern, not the instruction count, often determines speed. A loop that walks a contiguous array hits every cache line and runs at the processor's peak. A loop that follows linked list nodes through scattered heap addresses misses on every node and spends its time waiting on RAM. The linked list and the array hold the same data and do the same arithmetic. The array finishes in a fraction of the time because the cache can predict its access pattern and load ahead.

Prefetching extends that prediction. The hardware detects a stride — sequential access at a fixed distance — and fetches the next cache lines before the program asks for them. By the time the loop reaches the next element, it is already in L1. Prefetching works for regular patterns and fails for random ones. A binary tree traversal jumps to addresses that depend on comparisons, and no hardware can predict where the next pointer points. The cache helps less there, and the program runs at memory speed.

Okay: explain idempotency for an HTTP API, in the plain register already established.

An operation is idempotent when calling it twice produces the same result as calling it once. For an HTTP API, that means a client can retry a request after a network failure without changing the server's state beyond what the first attempt already did.

GET is idempotent by definition. It reads a resource and changes nothing. Ten GETs in a row return the same body, and the server's state is the same after the tenth as before the first. PUT is idempotent by intent. A PUT sends a full representation of a resource, and the server replaces whatever exists at that URI with it. Sending the same PUT twice overwrites the resource with the same content both times. The second call does not duplicate the resource and does not stack a change on top of the first.

DELETE is idempotent in a specific sense. The first DELETE on `/users/42` removes the user. The second DELETE on `/users/42` finds no user there and does nothing, or returns 404. Either way the server's state after the second call is the same as after the first: user 42 is gone. The response codes may differ — 200 the first time, 404 the second — but idempotency is about state, not about the response.

POST is the method that is not idempotent. A POST creates a new resource and lets the server assign its identity. Two identical POSTs to `/users` create two users. The server's state grows with each call. This is why payment APIs and order APIs treat POST with care: a retry after a timeout can double-charge a customer if the first request succeeded but the response was lost.

The practical problem is the gap between the method's contract and what the handler does. A PUT handler that appends to a list instead of replacing it breaks idempotency. A DELETE handler that decrements a counter on each call breaks it. The method tells the client what to expect, but the server's code has to honor it.

Retries are where idempotency earns its cost. A client sends a request. The server processes it and sends a response. The network drops the response. The client does not know whether the server saw the request, so it retries. If the operation is idempotent, the retry is safe: the worst case is the server applies the same change twice and the state is unchanged. If the operation is not idempotent, the retry risks a duplicate charge, a duplicate order, or a duplicate row in the database.

For non-idempotent operations, the common fix is an idempotency key. The client generates a unique token — a UUID — and sends it in a header. The server stores the token with the request's result. On a retry, the client sends the same token. The server recognizes it, skips the work, and returns the stored result from the first call. Stripe's API uses this pattern with an `Idempotency-Key` header. The key turns a non-idempotent POST into an idempotent operation by making the server remember the first outcome and replay it.

The distinction that matters is between idempotent and safe. Safe methods — GET, HEAD, OPTIONS — change no state at all. Idempotent methods may change state, but only once. A GET that logs every access is safe in the HTTP sense but not idempotent in the strict sense, because each call appends a log entry. The spec calls this a side effect that does not alter the resource's representation, and most clients tolerate it. The line is whether the observable resource state converges.

Okay: explain how DNS resolves a name to an address, in the plain register already established.

A program asks the operating system to connect to `example.com`. The OS does not know the address. It hands the name to a resolver, usually a library routine called `getaddrinfo`, which sends a UDP packet to a configured DNS server — typically the one a home router or corporate DHCP server supplied. The packet carries one question: what is the IPv4 address for `example.com`?

The DNS server that receives that question is almost never the one that holds the answer. DNS is a hierarchy, and the resolver climbs it one level at a time.

At the top sit the root servers. There are thirteen logical root server addresses, operated by twelve separate organizations, backed by over a thousand physical instances scattered across the world using anycast routing. The root servers do not know `example.com`'s address. They know which servers hold the top-level domains — the `.com` servers, the `.org` servers, the `.uk` servers. The resolver's first packet goes to a root server, and the root server replies with a referral: a list of authoritative servers for `.com`.

The resolver sends the same question to one of those `.com` servers. The `.com` server does not know `example.com`'s address either. It knows which servers are authoritative for `example.com` — the name servers that the domain's owner configured when registering the domain. The `.com` server replies with a second referral: the list of `example.com`'s authoritative servers.

The resolver sends the question a third time, now to one of `example.com`'s own name servers. That server holds the zone file for `example.com`, a text record mapping names to addresses. It finds the A record for `example.com`, which contains the IPv4 address `93.184.216.34`, and sends that answer back. The resolver hands the address to the OS, and the OS hands it to the program, which opens a TCP connection to that address.

Three round trips to resolve a name from scratch. The system avoids repeating them through caching. Every DNS response carries a time-to-live — a number of seconds the answer may be stored before it must be discarded. The resolver caches the root referral, the `.com` referral, and the `example.com` A record, each with its own TTL. The next lookup for `example.com` returns from cache in zero round trips. A lookup for `example.org` reuses the cached root and `.com` referrals and makes one round trip to `.org`'s servers. A lookup for a different host under `example.com` reuses the cached `example.com` referral and makes one round trip to the authoritative server. The cache is what makes DNS fast in practice; the hierarchy is what makes it scale to billions of names.

The caching resolver that a home router or ISP runs does this climb on behalf of every device behind it, so the first lookup from any device on the network pays the round-trip cost and the rest share the cached answer. Public resolvers like Google's `8.8.8.8` and Cloudflare's `1.1.1.1` do the same work at a larger scale, answering billions of queries per day from caches fed by the same hierarchy.

DNSSEC adds a cryptographic signature to each answer so the resolver can verify it came from the authoritative server and was not modified in transit. The signature chains from the root's public key down through each level, and the resolver validates the chain at every step. Most resolvers still run without validation, accepting answers on trust — a gap the protocol has been closing slowly for over twenty years.

A deadlock is a state where two or more threads are stuck, each waiting for a resource another holds, and none will give up what it has. The system stops. No error fires. No exception propagulates. The threads sit, and the program hangs.

Four conditions must hold at once. A thread holds a resource and asks for another — that is *hold and wait*. A resource can be held by only one thread at a time — *mutual exclusion*. A thread does not release a resource until it finishes its work — *no preemption*. And the wait forms a loop: A waits on B, B waits on C, C waits on A — *circular wait*. Break any one and the deadlock cannot form.

The classic shape is the dining philosophers. Five philosophers sit at a round table with five forks, one between each pair. Each needs two forks to eat. If every philosopher picks up the fork on their left at the same moment, every fork is held, and every philosopher waits forever for the fork on their right. The loop closes. Nobody eats.

One way to avoid it is to impose a total order on the resources and require every thread to acquire them in that order. A thread that needs fork 3 and fork 5 takes fork 3 first, then fork 5. A thread that needs fork 1 and fork 4 takes fork 1 first, then fork 4. The ordering rule breaks circular wait: if two threads both need forks 3 and 5, they both reach for fork 3 first, and only one gets it. The other waits before holding anything the winner needs. The winner takes fork 5, eats, and returns both. The cycle never opens.

The cost is discipline. Every lock in the system must have a rank, and every code path that takes more than one lock must take them in ascending rank. A path that takes lock C then lock A violates the order and reintroduces the deadlock the scheme exists to prevent. The rule is simple to state and hard to enforce across a large codebase, which is why lock-ordering bugs tend to surface under load rather than in review. Static analysis tools exist — Clang's Thread Safety Analysis annotates locks with ranks and checks call sites — but they catch only what the annotations cover.
